title: Energy Transitions in Regulated Markets
authors: Gautam Gowrisankaran, Ashley Langer, Mar Reguant
abstract: Natural gas has replaced coal as the dominant fuel for US electricity generation. However, utilities in regulated US states have retired coal more slowly than others. We build a structural model of rate-of-return regulation during an energy transition where utilities face trade-offs between lowering costs and maintaining and using legacy capacity. A regulated utility facing carbon taxes lowers short-run coal generation 48 percent as much as a cost minimizer would. Thirty years after a sudden energy transition, a cost minimizer has retired 71 percent more coal capacity than the regulated utility. Alternative regulations may jeopardize affordability and reliability goals during energy transitions. (JEL D24, L94, L98, Q35, Q48)

title: Designing Dynamic Reassignment Mechanisms: Evidence from GP Allocation
authors: Ingrid Huitfeldt, Victoria Marone, Daniel Waldinger
abstract: We study the problem of designing a dynamic reassignment mechanism when agents' preferences over objects change over time. In the context of Norway's system for (re)assigning patients to general practitioners (GPs), we provide direct evidence of misallocation under the current mechanism—patients waiting for each others' GPs, but who cannot trade—and estimate a structural model of GP-switching behavior to evaluate alternatives. Introducing top trading cycles (TTC) would, on average, reduce waiting times and increase patient welfare. However, patients endowed with less desirable GPs would be harmed. Prioritizing these patients can avoid these harms while preserving most of the gains from TTC. (JEL D82, H51, I11, I13, I18)

title: The Productivity of Professions: Evidence from the Emergency Department
abstract: This paper studies the productivity of nurse practitioners (NPs) and physicians, two professions performing overlapping tasks but with starkly different backgrounds, training, and pay. Using quasi-experimental variation in patient assignment to NPs versus physicians in Veterans Health Administration emergency departments, we find that, on average, NPs use more resources and exhibit a higher 30-day preventable hospitalization rate than physicians. However, the NP-physician performance difference varies by case complexity and severity. Importantly, even larger productivity variation exists within each profession, leading to substantial overlap between the productivity distributions of the two professions; NPs outperform physicians in 38 percent of random pairs. (JEL I11, I18, J24, J44, M53)

title: Merger Effects and Antitrust Enforcement: Evidence from US Consumer Packaged Goods
authors: Vivek Bhattacharya, Gastón Illanes, David Stillerman
abstract: We document the effects of a comprehensive set of mergers of consumer packaged goods manufacturers on prices, quantities, and product assortment. Across specifications, we find a small average price effect of mergers (−0.5−1.1 percent) but substantial heterogeneity, with a standard deviation between 3.9 and 7.6 percentage points. Through a model of enforcement, we find that agencies act as if they challenge mergers they expect would increase prices more than 4.8 to 6.3 percent. Increases in stringency would reduce prices and the prevalence of completed price-increasing mergers, with minimal impacts on blocked price-decreasing mergers, at significantly greater agency burden. (JEL D43, G34, K21, L13, L41, L66)

title: Talent Hoarding in Organizations
abstract: Most organizations rely on managers to identify talented workers. However, managers who are evaluated on team performance have an incentive to hoard workers. This study provides the first empirical evidence of talent hoarding using personnel records and survey evidence from a large firm. Talent hoarding is self-reported by three-fourths of managers, is detectable in manager ratings of worker talent, and occurs more frequently under stronger hoarding incentives, proxied by performance-related pay, team size, and talent visibility. Using quasi-random exposure to talent hoarding, I show that hoarding deters internal job applications, inhibiting career progression and altering talent allocation in the firm. (JEL D22, J23, L60, M12, M51, M54)

title: Community Engagement and Public Safety: Evidence from Crime Enforcement Targeting Immigrants
authors: Felipe Gonçalves, Elisa Jácome, Emily Weisburst
abstract: We study the role of victim reporting in the production of public safety. We examine the Secure Communities program, a crime-reduction policy that involved police in detecting unauthorized immigrants and increased deportation fears in immigrant communities. We find that the policy reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims report crimes to police and increased offending against Hispanics. The number of reported crimes is unchanged, masking these opposing effects. We show that reduced reporting drives the offending increase and provide the first elasticity of offending to victim reporting in the literature, calculating that a 10 percent decline in reporting increases offending by 7.9 percent. (JEL J15, K37, K42)

title: Uncertainty and Change: Survey Evidence of Firms' Subjective Beliefs
authors: Rüdiger Bachmann, Kai Carstensen, Stefan Lautenbacher, Manuel Menkhoff, Martin Schneider
abstract: This paper studies how managers plan under uncertainty. In a new panel survey of German manufacturing firms, we observe both forecasts of sales growth and a quantitative measure of subjective uncertainty. We show that subjective uncertainty reflects change experienced by firms: It is high when growth is either unusually low or unusually high. Subjective uncertainty is more than conditional volatility; while more volatile firms are typically more uncertain, experienced change alone increases uncertainty, consistent with a model of learning. Uncertainty over our sample is mostly idiosyncratic but varies substantially over time and leads managers to plan lower employment and prices. (JEL C83, D22, E20, E23)

title: Additionality and Asymmetric Information in Environmental Markets: Evidence from Conservation Auctions
abstract: Mechanisms that aim to reduce environmental degradation at low cost can be undermined when participants' conservation actions are not marginal to the incentive—or “additional”—as the lowest-cost participants may not be the highest social value. We investigate this challenge in the Conservation Reserve Program's auction mechanism for ecosystem services, linking bids to satellite-derived land use. Three-quarters of marginal auction winners are not additional. The heterogeneity in counterfactual land use introduces adverse selection. We develop a model of bidding and additionality to quantify welfare implications. Alternative auctions increase efficiency by using scoring rules that incorporate expected land use impacts. (JEL D44, D82, Q24, Q57, R14)

title: Professional Motivations in the Public Sector: Evidence from Police Officers
abstract: We study how public sector workers balance their professional motivations with private economic concerns, focusing on police arrests. Arrests made near the end of an officer's shift typically require overtime work, and officers respond by reducing arrest frequency but increasing arrest quality. Days in which an officer works a second job after their police shift have higher opportunity cost, also reducing late-shift arrests. Combining our estimates in a dynamic model identifies officer preferences over workplace activity and overtime work. Our results indicate that officers' private costs of arrests have a first-order impact on the quantity and quality of enforcement. (JEL K42, J33, J45)

title: Random Utility with Unobservable Alternatives
authors: Haruki Kono, Kota Saito, Alec Sandroni
abstract: The random utility model (RUM), a cornerstone in economics, is typically studied under the assumption that choice frequencies of all alternatives are observable. In practice, however, some alternatives have unobservable choice frequencies and are commonly aggregated into a single category called an outside option. We study RUM in such environments and derive a finite, nonredundant system of inequality constraints on observed choice frequencies that characterizes RU-rationalizability. We show that the conventional practice of aggregating unobserved alternatives can miss key information leading to incorrect conclusions such as that observed choices are rationalizable, even when no RUM is consistent with them. (JEL D11, D44, D83)

title: Remote Work and City Structure
authors: Ferdinando Monte, Charly Porcher, Esteban Rossi-Hansberg
abstract: Relative to remote work, working downtown facilitates valuable interactions with other in-office workers but entails commuting costs. The resulting coordination mechanism can lead to multiple stationary equilibria with varying levels of remote work. Temporary reductions in commuters, as in the COVID-19 pandemic, can lead to persistently large fractions of remote workers. Cell phone-based mobility data for the United States shows commuting trips in the largest cities, which are more likely to exhibit multiplicity, have stabilized at only 60 percent of prepandemic levels, while they are fully back in smaller cities. Cities with permanently low commuting experience average welfare losses of 2.3 percent. (JEL I12, J22, M54, R23, R31)

title: Relational Roots of Civic Fields: Capital Conversion and Organizational Reproduction in a Developing Country
abstract: Social scientists have long studied the emergence of civic organizations through two dominant perspectives: demand-side theories arguing that these groups fill gaps left by government and market failures, and supply-side theories emphasizing resource mobilization and dependence. However, these theories insufficiently account for how contemporary nonprofits and social enterprises arise in increasingly networked, professionalized, and competitive environments. This article interrogates the relational roots of civic fields, centering the concrete ties and interactions through which new organizations are incubated, resourced, and legitimated. Using the case of a dozen new civic organizations in a developing country, I show how founders leverage interpersonal and interorganizational ties to convert social capital into intellectual, economic, human, and symbolic capital. However, this ability for capital conversion depended on actors’ positions in the field and dispositions embedded in their habitus. These processes contribute to the field’s organizational reproduction —that is, reproduction of professional practices, funding models, and state-aligned approaches mirroring founders’ shared social (dis)positions. As civic organizations play increasingly prominent roles in development and governance, understanding their relational origins helps explain whose visions of social change gain organizational form.

title: Education for Mobilization: The Effects of Knowledge about Labor History on Union Support
abstract: The US working class is less organized along class lines than in other advanced democracies. We propose a new explanation: the absence of education on historical class struggle and labor organizing weakens support for the contemporary labor movement. To test this, we conduct two survey experiments exposing respondents to educational videos about the history of an American union and present-day union drives. Our surveys focus on non-college-educated whites in the US South, where union membership is low and racial conflict has historically constrained class-based solidarity. We find that exposure to labor history increases enthusiasm for unions and cross-racial class coalitions. These effects appear to be driven by greater political efficacy, better understanding of unions’ material benefits, linked fate with the working class, and increased allyship with marginalized groups. Our findings suggest that labor history education can shift political attitudes and foster greater class-based mobilization, even in contexts historically resistant to such organizing.

title: Can Authoritarian Electoral Propaganda Compete with the Opposition? Experimental Evidence from Russia
authors: Michael Rochlitz, Koen Schoors, Nikita Zakharov
abstract: We examine the effectiveness of electoral propaganda in an autocracy, using Russia as a unique setting. Exploiting the unexpected release of a pro-regime propaganda video about Vladimir Putin shortly before the presidential election, we conducted a field experiment by randomly promoting the video to voters via a telephone survey and measuring self-reported voting behaviour after the election. Our results show that the pro-regime treatment successfully mobilized offline media consumers to vote for Putin, but failed to persuade online media users, and even backfired among respondents dissatisfied with the regime. Using electoral statistics for all major Russian cities and instrumenting public interest in the propaganda video with rainfall, we find a positive, albeit moderate, causal effect of the video on Putin’s vote share. As an alternative treatment, we used a viral anti-corruption video by opposition leader Alexei Navalny, which consistently undermined regime support among both offline and online media consumers.

title: Concessions and Protest Demobilization
authors: Sasha de Vogel, Jessica S. Sun
abstract: How and why do concessions, or promises to implement reform in the future, affect protest mobilization in autocracies? Concessions are a routine response to protest and generate a puzzling empirical regularity: Although autocrats often renege once protest abates, concessions can produce demobilization. We develop a model showing that concessions demobilize by exploiting heterogeneity among protesters. A subgroup of moderates, who derive symbolic value from the autocrat’s promise to reform, and a subgroup of radicals, who value only implemented reforms, must coordinate to sustain protest after a concession. Concessions undermine the between-group coordination necessary for protests large enough to prevent reneging. Some moderates demobilize in response to promised concessions, and in turn, declining turnout demobilizes radicals. Even autocrats in highly repressive regimes may concede because concessions and repression demobilize through distinct mechanisms. However, concessions lose efficacy as moderates lose trust in the autocrat. Morocco’s Feb20 movement illustrates the theory.

title: Productivity and Entry Regulation in the Service Sector: Evidence from the Universe of Firms in Italy
authors: A Cintolesi, S Mocetti, G Roma
abstract: Burdensome entry regulations can hinder productivity growth, particularly in services where competitive pressures are weaker. We construct a novel measure of entry regulation, varying across narrowly defined sectors, and combine it with firm-level data for the universe of Italian firms. Exploiting reforms that generate variation across sectors and over time, we find that deregulation (reductions in red tape) raises productivity. The effect is driven by incumbent firms, with a smaller role for reallocation and selection. Effects are larger in the lower-middle of the productivity distribution and in sectors with higher entry rates and tighter initial regulation.

title: When Do Shadow Ministers Become ‘Realities’? Evidence from the UK, 1964–2024
abstract: A characteristic feature of Westminster-style democracy is the convention that the opposition frontbench forms the basis of the new executive following changes in the party of government. Yet we know little about how this convention operates when it comes to individual appointments. This paper examines how frequently opposition frontbenchers have become ministers in the UK, the archetypal Westminster system. Across seven incoming governments, we find that around four-fifths of opposition frontbenchers were appointed to ministerial office, and roughly half retained responsibility for the same policy portfolio they had shadowed. At the government level, prime ministers’ idiosyncratic preferences affected overall levels of continuity, but these choices were constrained by electoral and party factors. At the individual level, we find no evidence that prime ministers retained their supporters in greater numbers, but party seniority, prior ministerial experience and time served in an opposition post were closely associated with portfolio continuity.

title: Opposition Distinctiveness in Parliaments: A Longitudinal Analysis
abstract: There are concerns about the distinctiveness of opposition party behaviour in parliaments, but the literature offers mixed findings. This article analyses how distinctive the opposition is from the government in its voting patterns and speech-making in four parliamentary democracies (Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, United Kingdom [UK]) over a long time span (1945–2020). Our results show a diversity of trends in opposition distinctiveness. Overall, the distinctiveness in terms of parliamentary voting behaviour increased up to the 1980s, and slightly decreased or remained stable thereafter in most countries. Opposition sentiment in speech-making follows a different pattern, particularly in the UK and Canada, where the increasingly positive sentiment of governing party MPs and the increasingly negative sentiment of opposition parties has led to significant divergence over time. These trends in opposition distinctiveness in voting and speech-making are shown to be related most strongly to opposition parties’ prior governing experience, in particular in Denmark and the Netherlands.

title: Intermediaries and Informal Migration Pathways of Filipino Migrant Workers in Belgium
abstract: This study examines the migration trajectories of Filipino migrant workers in Belgium, asking how migrants rely on intermediaries across different informal migration pathways. Drawing on Fresnoza‐Flot's humanizing approach to migration studies and based on 20 in‐depth interviews, it traces how migrants navigate legal precarity through intermediaries. Empirically, intermediaries become salient at two critical junctures: (1) facilitating entry into Belgium through invitations, referrals and circulation of information and (2) assisting migrants, to varying degrees, to navigate Belgian legal, social and labour systems after arrival. By centering migrant narratives, the study presents three informal migration pathways: jump ship migration as a shift from regular to irregular status; short‐term visa overstay as legal entry that extends beyond authorized stay; and cross‐border labour mobility as movement through multiple countries before settling in Belgium. Migrant narratives matter analytically because they show how intermediaries shape the terms under which legal precarity is navigated, how legality is interpreted and recalibrated over time and how informal pathways are produced relationally rather than as isolated individual acts.

title: Disrupted Trajectories: COVID ‐19, Transnational Youth Mobility and Unequal Transitions to Adulthood
authors: Simon Chambers, Anita Harris, Loretta Baldassar
abstract: While the impact of COVID‐19 on youth development has been widely studied, less is known about its effects on transnationally mobile young adults. This longitudinal study of Australian outbound and inbound mobility examines how the pandemic disrupted this population's experiences abroad as they navigated transitions to adulthood. It draws on two waves of survey data collected using a convenience sample between July 2020 and September 2022. Our findings reveal that COVID‐19 presented significant challenges to young adults living away from home, with disruptions to their future plans, social connections, and well‐being. However, these impacts were not uniform. The pandemic magnified existing inequalities, with those on short‐term visas, women, and those already facing financial precarity experiencing greater negative effects. Moreover, individuals who experienced higher negative effects also reported increased struggles in achieving personal milestones associated with transitions to adulthood. This study highlights how crises (like the pandemic) amplify the vulnerability of transnationally mobile youth, a population often assumed to be—or actively striving to be—independent and self‐sufficient. It underscores the need for targeted support and interventions that address their specific challenges, including more equitable and inclusive migration and education policies that recognise the differentiated and overlapping vulnerabilities faced by this population.

title: Europe as a Normative Horizon: Migration Aspirations Among Japanese Self‐Initiated Migrants
abstract: This article examines migration aspirations among highly educated Japanese nationals considering migration to Europe, with particular attention to how Europe is imagined as a normative horizon. Drawing on interviews with migration experts and Japanese aspiring migrants, the study shows that migration aspirations are shaped not only by structural constraints in Japan—such as economic stagnation, demanding work cultures, and gender inequality—but also by perceptions of Europe as a space associated with democratic values, social inclusion, gender equality, and alternative ways of organising work and everyday life. By focusing on aspirations rather than realised mobility, the article demonstrates how imaginaries of Europe and perceived constraints in the country of origin interact to shape migration motivations prior to actual movement.

title: Persons Enough to Punish: Illegality, Deportability and the Hierarchy of Personhood in US Immigration
abstract: This paper argues that contemporary United States immigration law and policy construct a hierarchy of personhood for undocumented migrants which better explains their status as opposed to a classic binary framework of citizen/migrant. It develops a four‐layer conceptual framework of personhood including baseline personhood, membership personhood, administrative personhood and social personhood. These layers are argued to be unevenly distributed across legal domains, creating a strong and impactful hierarchization of individuals. Historically situating the current regime within the late‐twentieth‐century turn towards employer sanctions and one‐time legalization, the expansion of deportable offences, the restriction of non‐citizens' access to public benefits, and post‐9/11 securitization, the paper demonstrates the rise of an ‘immigration industrial complex’. It then draws on critical scholarship relating to deportability, the illegality trap, and crimmigration to argue that illegality is actively produced as a tool for governance that keeps migrants exploitable. A section on doctrinal analysis of constitutional and administrative law shows that undocumented migrants are recognized as persons in some contexts, yet denied secure access to the social state and membership. The paper further identifies mechanisms of personhood‐thinning and reads their combined effects through a republican non‐domination lens. It concludes by sketching reforms aimed at thickening personhood and reducing domination to escape the illegality trap and move towards a just immigration law framework.

title: Can Hong Kong Be Home? Sub‐Saharan African Students' Notions and Aspirations of Home in a Global City
abstract: African student migration to China has increased markedly in recent years, driven by China's internationalisation agenda. While existing scholarship has focused largely on African students' educational motivations and precarious transcultural navigation in mainland China, far less is known about how African students experience Hong Kong as a potential site of belonging. This paper asks: Can Hong Kong be home for African students? Drawing on a 3‐year ethnography (2019–2023) with African higher‐education students, complemented by ongoing informal engagements in 2024, the study examines students' everyday experiences, the opportunities and constraints they encounter and the strategies they employ to cultivate belonging. The findings reveal Hong Kong as a distinctive socio‐political and institutional space where shifting governance, racialised encounters and transnational ties intersect to shape aspirations and senses of home. Rather than a fixed endpoint, home emerges as a negotiated, ongoing process. The paper contributes new empirical insights into African student mobility and advances theorisation of belonging by conceptualising home as fluid, iterative and shaped by mobility, marginality and aspiration.

title: Gratitude That Never Was: Migration, Labour and Discontent in Au Pair Experiences
abstract: Conceptions of the ‘ideal immigrant’ as not only compliant but also grateful have long shaped US immigration discourse and material realities. Young immigrant women engaged in service and care work frequently report encountering expectations that they should feel grateful for the opportunities provided by their employers. In this study, I examine the narrated lived experiences of Turkish au pairs, young women on temporary work visas providing child care in U.S. households, with particular attention to how their discontent builds up from the point of hiring through the decision to quit, and the role that perceived expectations of gratitude from the host families play in this process. I employ a qualitative research design drawing on publicly available YouTube videos created by Turkish au pairs since 2020, as well as on in‐depth conversations with a former au pair conducted between 2023 and 2024. Engaging the literature at the intersection of labour, immigration and affect, I use narrative analysis to unpack how resentment emerges at the nexus of blurred work‐life boundaries, undercompensated labour, and social isolation. These tensions become increasingly unmanageable when au pairs realise that their host families, implicitly or explicitly, expect gratitude as part of the labour relationship. Subtle or explicit refusals to perform gratitude by au pairs destabilize labour arrangements and relationships built on unequal foundations and complicate Global North–South encounters, particularly in the context of post‐2015 Turkish youth migration to the United States. In this context, Turkish au pairs seek to understand themselves as participants in cultural exchange, a distinction that is frequently, and perhaps strategically, overlooked by host families. This research advances understandings of the affective dimensions of migration by illuminating how emotional labour expectations intersect with gender, culture, age, economic precarity and centre–periphery relations in transnational care work.

title: Revolutionizing Time, Reforging Social Orders: State-Building Success and the Enforcement of Symbolic Programs in Revolutionary France
abstract: How do state builders reshape society? While existing work shows they often rely on violence, education, elite co-optation, and institution building, this article underscores the importance of symbolic programs. When intensely enforced, symbolic programs reshape social orders by forging new social bonds and socializing individuals into state builders’ governing principles. I test this argument using subnational variation in the enforcement of the French Republican calendar—a symbolic program that politicized time, labor, and rest, rightfully regulated by the state, rather than sacred duties governed by the Catholic Church—and its association with labor conflicts. In departments where the calendar was more strongly enforced, it fostered political understandings of labor and rest, reduced coordination costs, and increased mobilization potential. Using original data and a difference-in-differences design, I find that more intense enforcement of the calendar is associated with a higher likelihood of labor conflict onset, demonstrating the long-term social effects of symbolic state-building programs.

title: Mutually Hurting or Mutually Beneficial Stalemates? Alternative Logics Shaping Conflict Outcomes
abstract: Scores of intrastate conflicts end without military victory or formal peace agreement, yet civil war scholarship lacks a mechanism to explain how these non-decisive outcomes emerge, recur, and endure. Existing “win, lose, or draw” rationalist bargaining frameworks treat settlements as the default outcome when neither party prevails militarily, assuming impasse reliably produces the ripe moment Zartman describes. Yet as conflict systems grow more complex, negotiated settlements continue to decline. This theory note introduces mutually beneficial stalemates—an equilibrium in which conflict parties calculate that maintaining the status quo yields higher returns than renewed fighting or settlements that risk commitment failures—as a mechanism to explain how non-decisive outcomes evolve and are sustained. Where Zartman’s mutually hurting stalemate describes a painful impasse generating pressure toward settlement, the mutually beneficial stalemate explains how parties distribute some benefits of peace—limited or no violence, selective cooperation, and hybrid governance arrangements—without the risks of formal resolution. I develop a logic of joint conflict avoidance that shows how parties protect existing gains and preserve organizations against the risks posed by both escalation and resolution. I extend the framework to multi-actor conflicts, where rebel proliferation and external intervention reinforce non-decisive equilibria.

title: “Communicating in the Air Force”: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication , and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
abstract: This article explores the intertwined history of the National Society for the Study of Communication (NSSC), its Journal of Communication, and U.S. Air Force educational programs. Founded in 1950 (and renamed the International Communication Association in 1969), NSSC developed a close partnership with the Air Force’s Air University in its early days. The growth of the academic society and the expansion of communication courses in military education programs were then mutually reinforcing: NSSC leaders—including several Air Force officers and civilian consultants—helped define and refine military communication curricula. Air University resources supported NSSC projects, most notably the Journal of Communication. Drawing on extensive archival research and a close reading of the Journal’s content during its first decade, this article argues that these collaborations not only nurtured NSSC’s institutional development, but also shaped a specific conception of communication emphasizing vocational training, efficiency, and the transmission of command.

title: Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
authors: Moran Ovadia, Shiri Davidovitch, Romi Sion, Naama Shoham, Nimrod Keren, Sergei Freedman, Cynthia Cabañas, Dov Rubinstein, Mark A Thornton, Jonathan Frome, Liad Mudrik, Tim J Smith, Gal Raz
abstract: Point-of-view (POV) editing—the juxtaposition of a character’s gaze with the object of that gaze—is presumed to function as a unique empathic device that dissolves viewer-character boundaries; however, direct empirical evidence remains scarce. This study provides the first systematic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral investigation into whether POV editing facilitates shared attention and intentionality. 39 adults viewed 8 original narrative movies containing POV sequences or closely matched control conditions. POV sequences increased fixation durations on characters’ faces and enhanced subsequent recognition of gazed-at content. Neurally, POV editing elicited stronger responses in regions implicated in mentalizing and increased shared, item-specific activation patterns across viewers within areas associated with perspective-taking and goal-directed control. Multivariate decoding further indicates that a character’s gaze induced more robust neural signatures of character identity on subsequent target elements. Together, these findings support a functional role for POV editing in promoting joint attention and shared intentionality in audiovisual messages.

title: Diplomats in Camouflage: A Dataset of China’s Military-Diplomatic Engagements
authors: Noel Foster, Zenobia T. Chan, Jackie S. H. Wong
abstract: Face-to-face diplomacy is central to international politics, yet existing research focuses largely on civilian leaders and diplomats. We introduce an original meeting-level dataset of China’s public military-diplomatic engagements from 2000 to 2023. Drawing on four authoritative Chinese-language party, state, and military outlets, the dataset records over 2,500 engagements involving senior Chinese military leaders and foreign counterparts. It classifies engagements as receptions in China, outbound visits, multilateral organization meetings, and defense and security fora, while preserving information on participants, timing, location, sources, and reported content. Official reporting frames these engagements primarily around cooperation and exchange. An illustrative analysis of outbound visits finds little evidence that China concentrates senior-level military outreach on U.S. allies. Outbound visits are instead positively associated with pre-existing security-specific and economic relationships with China. This dataset enables future research on how military diplomacy complements civilian diplomacy, signals strategic priorities, and shapes security cooperation, crisis management, and political influence.

title: Attitudinal impacts of polarized protests: experimental evidence from abortion protests in Poland
abstract: Extensive literature suggests that protests can change citizens’ attitudes through several informational mechanisms. However, protests often occur around deeply polarized issues that are resistant to attitudinal change. In such contexts, do protests instead deepen political and affective divides? Leveraging evidence from an original, preregistered survey experiment conducted in Poland, this study examines how abortion protests influence citizens’ attitudes toward the abortion law, as well as their sentiments toward others holding different views on abortion. The findings indicate that while abortion protests do not significantly change respondents’ positions on the abortion issue itself, they increase in-group favoritism among anti-abortion sympathizers. No comparable effects are observed among pro-abortion supporters. These results highlight that the attitudinal impacts of protests extend beyond attitudes toward the protest issue itself, notably by strengthening positive in-group sentiments among status quo defenders. These insights are valuable for understanding counter-reactions to liberal protests and are especially relevant in the context of rising polarization and the ongoing illiberal backlash observed in many countries worldwide.

title: Oxytocin increases trust in men low in dispositional trust
authors: Bodo Vogt, Paul Bengart, Carolyn Declerck, Ernst Fehr
abstract: In recent years, increasing skepticism regarding oxytocin’s (OT) influence on social behavior arose. Low power, HARKing (hypothesizing after the results are known), and replication failures have clouded the field. Here, we directly address these concerns with a high-powered, preregistered study that offers robust evidence for a causal effect of OT on trust among males with a low disposition to trust. We recruited 359 low-trusting men who participated in a trust game with complete anonymity. Results show that OT administration significantly increased trusting behavior by roughly 15%, with consistent effects across regression models with and without controls for personality traits. A pooled data analysis incorporating a previous sample (n = 219) of low-trusting individuals further strengthens this conclusion, yielding a statistically significant 16.9% increase in trust. No interaction effect was found between OT and the degree of dispositional trust, suggesting OT’s effect may be uniform across the low-trusting spectrum. These findings present a strong case for OT’s selective trust-enhancing role. By isolating OT’s impact within a well-defined subpopulation and experimental context, this study resolves a key question in the debate over neurobiological determinants of trust.

title: Economic preferences predict higher-education choices
authors: Thomas F. Epper, Ernst Fehr, Kristoffer B. Hvidberg, Claus T. Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen, Basit Zafar
abstract: We examine whether individual preferences predict higher-education choices. According to standard human capital theory, differences in individuals’ time and risk preferences lead to differences in educational investments. Testing this hypothesis is challenging, as it requires measuring individuals’ preferences, doing so before they make educational investments, and subsequently observing their educational choices. We combine incentivized, experimentally elicited measures of time and risk preferences for a large, representative sample of 18- to 19-y-old Danes with administrative data on subsequent higher-education choices, program-specific earnings trajectories, prior school performance, and family background. In line with theory, we find that more patient individuals choose longer education programs and programs with steeper early-career earnings profiles, while more risk-averse individuals select programs with lower earnings dispersion and reduced downside risk. These relationships remain strong after controlling for cognitive ability, prior academic performance, and family background. Our findings suggest that preferences have a substantial impact on real-world educational investments and have implications for educational sorting.

title: Implicit biases change more slowly in larger cities
abstract: Implicit biases remain a contributor to discrimination despite widespread endorsement of equality. Although there has been a large-scale reduction in sexuality, race, and skin tone biases in the past two decades, there is a current shortage of quantitative theories that describe how and why biases change. Here, I present a theory of implicit bias change, which focuses on changes in exposure due to cultural information and how the speed of these changes varies geographically. This model makes counterintuitive predictions when compared with previous findings, including 1) that biases change more slowly in larger cities and 2) that one-off interventions are less effective in larger cities. I confirm these predictions using 14 million tests of implicit biases from U.S. residents over 14 y and experimental data from 1,150 individuals. Documenting the typical timescales and patterns that govern implicit bias change is an important step toward designing interventions that can facilitate further reductions in biases and prevent biases from increasing.

title: The undemocratic face of greenwashing and the duty to counter-frame
abstract: Normative research on greenwashing has largely focused on the environmental and economic consequences of false or misleading green claims. This article introduces a new perspective that sheds light on its democratic costs. First, I argue that by interfering with the transmission of a public political culture through deceptive claims, greenwashing constitutes a particularly problematic form of corporate capture of democratic rhetoric. I further contend that greenwashing should also be examined against ordinary patterns of language use, given their capacity to shape the range of communicative possibilities available. At the normative level, I then defend a duty to counter-frame: a duty of ordinary citizens to play their part in avoiding reinforcing the communicative conditions that facilitate corporate capture of public rhetoric. This duty aims to initiate processes of reciprocal reason-giving about responsible language use within everyday conversations.

title: Too burdensome to be acknowledged? How sexism is rendered invisible to women candidates through seven mechanisms
authors: Clémence Deswert, Robin Devroe, Elise Storme, Emilie van Haute
abstract: Drawing on an inductive analysis of 21 interviews with women candidates at the 2024 elections in Belgium, our article questions how the perpetuation of sexism in politics is facilitated by its invisibilization, even among its victims. First, we show that despite an awareness of the prevalence of sexism in politics, women candidates often struggle to clearly identify its expressions. We show how the type of target (candidates’ profile), the type of sexism (benevolent vs hostile), and the context of its expression (online vs offline) affect the type of mechanisms women candidates turn to, but that it ultimately all leads to the same outcome: the invisibilization of sexism and its disconnect from candidates’ experience. We argue that the mechanisms uncovered can serve as an analytical grid in other contexts. Our findings call for a reconsideration of how sexism in politics is defined, understood, measured, and addressed by actors and institutions.

title: Institutional Pressures or Organizational Capacity? Antecedents of Digital Maturity in Local Governments
authors: Sarah Van Impe, Lieselot Danneels, Ben Suykens
abstract: Public administration research has identified institutional pressures and organizational capacity as digital maturity (DM) antecedents, yet these are typically considered in isolation. Taking the proverbial next step, this study draws on primary survey data to explain the variation of DM among local governments in Flanders (the northern region of Belgium) by juxtaposing the explanatory power of institutional pressures on the one hand, and political and administrative capacity on the other hand. Using multiple regression analyses, our findings highlight the critical role of administrative capacity in advancing DM among local governments. In contrast, and somewhat surprisingly, political capacity and institutional pressures appear to play a more limited role. These findings challenge conventional assumptions in existing literature, indicating that institutional pressures may catalyze the initial stages of DT, whereas organizational capacity seems to be more influential in sustaining and advancing DM.

title: A Race to the Top: The Adoption of Net‐Zero City Pledges in Large US Cities
abstract: Many cities have adopted net‐zero emission pledges, yet little is known about why these commitments emerge or how their determinants shift under changing policy environments. Using a panel of 148 large US cities from 2016 to 2022, this study applies the Political Market Framework and employs discrete‐time event‐history models to examine how policy demand, policy supply and institutional conditions shape adoption decisions. Results show that civic capacity, political ideology, and horizontal diffusion drive adoption in the full period, but their influence varies sharply across institutional contexts. During federal disengagement (2016–2018), cities with less population, strong vulnerability signals, supportive state policies, or fiscal cushioning through federal aid are more likely to adopt. When federal engagement returned (2019–2022), education, population size, and neighbor adoption emerged as significant correlates of net‐zero adoption. These findings extend the Political Market Framework by showing how federal contexts condition the adoption of ambitious climate commitments.

title: Social Capital and Policy Compliance in a Polarized Democracy: A Necessary Condition Analysis of COVID Vaccination Rates Across US Counties
authors: Bin Chen, Zhiwei Zhang, Gao Liu, Kun Huang
abstract: Policy compliance, the extent to which citizens adhere to government policies, remains a central test of democratic governance, especially during the COVID‐19 pandemic in the United States. This study examines how distinct forms of social capital—relational, structural (bonding versus bridging), cognitive, and vertical linking—serve as critical preconditions for COVID‐19 vaccination uptake in 2021. Using necessary condition analysis (NCA), we uncover nuanced and context‐specific impacts of distinct social capital on policy compliance. NCA also identifies threshold levels of various social capital required to achieve specific vaccination outcomes, yielding actionable diagnostics for policymakers and administrators. Strategies to raise compliance must align with local social capital configurations, prioritizing bridging in Republican‐leaning counties and relational support and careful use of bridging in Democratic‐leaning counties. The study advances civil society research by pinpointing the civic preconditions under which democratic institutions can function effectively in a polarized environment.

title: Does Political Decoupling Through Fair Market Privatization Improve Managerial and Political Outcomes? Insights From Water Utility Sales
authors: Jesse L. Barnes, Michael A. Powell
abstract: Many U.S. municipalities face environmental service delivery challenges, including aging infrastructure and rising debt. In response, several states have adopted Fair Market Value (FMV) legislation, which aims to incentivize private firms to acquire and invest in municipal utilities—particularly in the water sector. However, the impacts of FMV privatization remain understudied. Guided by political decoupling theory, this study hypothesizes that FMV privatization improves drinking water utility management and local incumbent electoral outcomes. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we analyze fifteen Illinois municipalities that sold their utilities after the state adopted FMV legislation relative to thirty‐four controls. Results suggest that FMV privatization improves personnel and technical management outcomes by reducing violations under the Safe Drinking Water Act but has no significant impact on incumbent vote share. These findings indicate that while FMV privatization may enhance utility management through political decoupling, its presumed political benefits warrant further investigation.

title: Consolidating Liberal Democracy From Within A Theory of Public Institutional Leadership
abstract: Recent developments in also established democracies have made clear that public administration and management research alike have neglected giving scholarly attention to public organizations as institutions. Drawing upon research on leadership of institutions and leadership in public organizations we suggest a theory of public institutional leadership . Public institutional leadership reconnects public management with democracy by suggesting three central dimensions of leadership behaviors that instill and sustain liberal democratic values in public organizations. These behaviors include articulating and reaffirming democratic values through top‐down vision‐setting; building “character” bottom‐up through role modeling and fostering psychological safety to enable dialogue and deliberation around these values as well as demonstrating constrained responsiveness to political principals relative to those values enabled by the cultivation of bureaucratic autonomy. Although the necessity of such behaviors is made salient by rising populism and democratic backsliding, their relevance extends to public management situated in liberal democracies in general.

title: Foreign Exchange Intervention with UIP and CIP Deviations
authors: Philippe Bacchetta, Kenza Benhima, Brendan Berthold
abstract: We examine the welfare-based opportunity cost of foreign exchange (FX) intervention when both CIP and UIP deviations are present. We consider a small open economy that receives international capital flows through constrained international financial intermediaries. Deviations from CIP come from limited arbitrage or through a convenience yield, while UIP deviations are also affected by global risk. We show that the sign of CIP and UIP deviations may differ for safe haven countries. We find that FX reserves may provide a net benefit, rather than a cost, when international intermediaries value the safe-haven properties of a currency more than domestic households. We show that this has been the case for the Swiss franc and the Japanese Yen. We examine the optimal policy of a constrained central bank planner in this context.

title: Marriage, Assortative Mating and Wealth Inequality
authors: Andreas Fagereng, Luigi Guiso, Luigi Pistaferri
abstract: We use population data on capital income and wealth holdings for Norway to measure asset positions and wealth returns before individuals marry and after the household is formed. These data allow us to establish a number of novel facts. First, individuals sort on personal wealth rather than parental wealth. Second, people match also on their personal returns to wealth and assortative mating on returns is as strong as that on wealth. Third, post-marriage returns on family wealth reflect in equal part the pre-marriage returns of the two spouses. However, for households at the top of the wealth distribution at marriage, family wealth is largely managed by the spouse with the highest potential to grow it, providing a microfoundation for the scale dependence in wealth returns documented in several empirical papers. Fourth, marriage lowers the degree of wealth inequality as well as the heterogeneity in returns relative to the counterfactual case of no marriages. We use a simple framework to illustrate how the inequality-attenuating role of marriage is affected by assortative mating on wealth and returns and by wealth management task allocation between spouses.

title: Optimal Age-based Policies for Pandemics: An Economic Analysis of Covid-19 and Beyond
authors: Luiz Brotherhood, Philipp Kircher, Cezar Santos, Michèle Tertilt
abstract: This paper investigates the importance of the age composition for pandemic policy design. To do so, it introduces an economic framework with age heterogeneity, individual choice, and incomplete information, emphasizing the value of testing. Calibrating the model to the US Covid-19 pandemic reveals an 80% reduction in the death toll due to voluntary actions and the lockdown implemented in the US. The optimal lockdown, however, is more stringent than what was implemented. Moreover, the social planner follows an asymmetric approach by locking down the young relatively more than the old. We highlight the role of testing in reducing deaths, lowering economic costs, and allowing for a less restrictive lockdown. A social planner would choose a faster ramp-up in testing capacity relative to what occurred in the US. We use the framework to provide insights into pandemics caused by different viruses (including the Spanish flu), and underline the influence of economic conditions on optimal policies.

title: How should India approach AI?
abstract: In an unstable geopolitical environment, countries are looking to secure access to artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, which are seen as essential to economic growth, scientific research, and national security. Few have placed sovereignty as squarely at the center of their AI strategy as India—and few are as well positioned to achieve it. But to do so, it needs to look beyond infrastructure—chips, data centers, and large language models—and pay more attention to the application layer above them: AI agents, the software and tools that accomplish real-world work. If the effort succeeds, India may pioneer a template for genuine AI sovereignty that other nations can follow.

title: Having a child through medically assisted reproduction: a social stratification perspective
authors: Alice Goisis, Alina Pelikh, Maria Palma, Pekka Martikainen, Niina Metsä-Simola, Hanna Remes
abstract: Prior research documents marked social disparities in births through medically assisted reproduction (MAR), which are often attributed to unequal access to treatment. However, social inequalities may also arise from processes operating after MAR treatments begin. We examine this possibility using population-level administrative register data from Finland, a context where MAR treatments are generously subsidized and access barriers are relatively low. Focusing on all childless women who initiated MAR treatments between 1995 and 2019, we analyze whether and why women with tertiary education are more likely than less-educated women to have a child through MAR. The results show that, among childless women who start MAR treatments, those with tertiary education are more likely to have a child after MAR than women with below tertiary education. This educational gradient is partly explained by differences in early treatment discontinuation, uptake of more invasive and more successful MAR treatments, and per-cycle treatment success rates. The results support the hypothesis that social stratification processes in MAR outcomes continues after the start of MAR treatments.

title: Racism and parent stress in the context of police violence
authors: Ann Meier, Claire Kamp Dush, Alexandra VanBergen, Sierra Clark, Hyunjae Kwon, Chalandra Bryant
abstract: This project assessed parental stress in 2020 and 2021 during a period of racial trauma marked by high-profile, race-motivated murders of people of color. We leveraged the Contextual Model of Family Stress Re-Imaged to understand parents’ stress about children’s interactions with police in the context of racism. Findings indicate higher policing stress among Black parents. To measure racism, we assessed county-level racial segregation and socioeconomic privilege, respondents’ perceptions of community climate, discrimination experiences, and the salience of George Floyd’s murder and its aftermath in their lives. The associations between Black race and discrimination experiences on the one hand and parent policing stress on the other were both direct and indirect. Black respondents and those who experienced more discrimination found more salience in the racialized milieu after George Floyd’s murder, and this was directly associated with more parent policing stress. Other indicators of racism were associated with parent policing stress indirectly. Those living in more socioeconomically privileged contexts reported a more favorable community climate, and this was associated with less policing stress. Those living in more racially segregated contexts experienced the racialized milieu as more salient, which was linked to more policing stress. These findings suggest marginalizing contexts of racism are risk factors for Black parents’ compromised well-being.

title: Framing inclusion: discursive logics of entitlement in immigrant social rights advocacy
abstract: This article investigates how civil society organizations (CSOs) advocate for immigrant access to social assistance in politically charged environments. It explores whether the frame choices of CSOs are shaped by their relationships with government bodies and examines the implications of these narratives for representing a highly diverse group of non-citizens. The article introduces a novel two-dimensional framework that categorizes advocacy frames along two axes: “scope of inclusion” (Targeted Inclusion vs. Universal Inclusion) and “justification for entitlement” (Individual Justification vs. Structural Justification). Findings from document analysis reveal a predominant reliance on frames that call for the inclusion of specific groups basing entitlement on individual characteristics independent of CSOs’ relationship to the state. The most radical frame type (Structural Justification for Universal Inclusion), however, is more frequently used by independent CSOs. Analyses of interviews underscore that CSOs navigate a trade-off: aligning with targeted, individualistic frames can achieve incremental policy gains, but potentially reinforces stratified notions of “deservingness”, contributing to internal hierarchies within immigrant communities. Conversely, advancing structural justification for universal inclusion carries the potential to challenge systemic inequalities yet risks limited immediate resonance within the political mainstream. These insights highlight the tension between short-term policy success and long-term systemic change in CSO advocacy strategies. The empirical findings, alongside theoretical discussions, extend beyond this specific policy field, offering broader insights into civil society strategies in adverse contexts.

title: Democratizing from Within: British Elites and the Expansion of the Franchise
authors: Chitralekha Basu, Carles Boix, Sonia Giurumescu, Paulo Serôdio
abstract: abstract: The authors develop a theory of democratization that relies on political and electoral calculations to explain the franchise choices of political actors in Great Britain. Given their location in the policy space, left-leaning (liberal) politicians are more likely to be supported by newly enfranchised voters, so they favor a broader franchise than conservative politicians do. The preferences of liberal politicians are conditional on the interests of both enfranchised and disenfranchised electors. As those interests become more heterogeneous, policymakers are more reluctant to expand the franchise because they may find it harder to attract new voters while keeping their current supporters. To evaluate this theory, the authors estimate the franchise preferences of British members of parliament (mps) based on their votes on franchise-related issues between 1830 and 1918. The authors then link these preferences to the mps’ personal and constituency characteristics. In line with their theory, the authors find that partisanship, declining inequality, and World War I were crucial factors in democratizing Britain.

title: Who Sets the Agenda? Diplomatic Experience and Small Power Influence in the United Nations
abstract: abstract: Why are some small powers effective in setting the UN agenda, even in the face of large power opposition? The author argues that small states are more likely to be represented by experienced diplomats, who, over time, accumulate influence that can be deployed to shape the international organization’s agenda. To test these claims, the author assembled a data set of proposed agenda items and the tenure of all states’ ambassadors from 1946 to 2018 and conducted interviews with diplomats from forty-nine states. The author finds that smaller powers have more diplomatic experience than larger powers; that individuals with more diplomatic experience are more successful at agenda setting even when accounting for material power; and that random shocks to ambassadorial tenure, such as the death of an ambassador, have negative effects on diplomatic experience and effectiveness. These insights contribute to understanding the role of individuals and diplomacy in international relations and the ways in which small powers influence international politics.

title: The Myth of the Traditional Gender Gap? Evidence from Catholic Countries
abstract: abstract: In rich democracies today, women are less conservative than men. Yet for most of the twentieth century, politicians, pundits, and scholars believed that family life and religiosity tied women to conservative causes and parties. Recent scholarship has reexamined this traditional gender gap hypothesis but has done so in cases in which electorate-wide shifts to the left make it least likely that a conservative gender gap would emerge. This article scrutinizes a hard case, Quebec, a Catholic province in Canada that experienced a dramatic shift to the right after suffrage. Using Gallup polls and ecological inference techniques, the authors show that political geography drove gender preference gaps, with rural women voting more conservatively, and urban women more liberally, than men. In two other Catholic contexts, Austria and Argentina, they show that after suffrage women were not more conservative than men in general, undermining the traditional gender gap thesis in several crucial cases.

title: Peasants and Parliaments: Institutional Foundations of Agrarian Reform in Eighteenth-Century Eastern Europe
abstract: abstract: An influential literature attributes Europe’s economic precocity to what might be termed “good” institutions, such as representative assemblies, which shielded property from governmental predation. This account fails to contend with the diversity of property rights in preindustrial Europe, many of which, like serfdom, were obstacles to growth. The author proposes a role for some—but not all—early representative assemblies in fostering growth by eliminating these “bad” property rights. An assembly’s capacity to extinguish property rights is a product of its decision-making efficiency, which in turn is associated with majority voting and centralized agenda control. The author tests these claims through a controlled comparison of progrowth agrarian reforms in the Russian Baltic province of Livonia and the Danish-ruled duchies of Schleswig and Holstein between 1795 and 1805, finding that the Livonian diet’s efficient organization was key to the successful transformation of serfdom. This analysis suggests that we must evaluate preindustrial representative institutions on the basis of their capacity to orchestrate complex exchanges of property rights and rents.

title: South-South Immigration and Redistribution Preferences: Evidence from Colombia
abstract: abstract: Research on the effects of immigration on redistribution preferences mostly focuses on Western countries and neglects the Global South. The authors argue that immigration shocks may have different effects in South-South migration than they do in South-North contexts. On one hand, the effects should be more muted in the former due to minimal cultural differences and limited development of the welfare state. On the other hand, the impact might be larger due to high economic inequality and scarce resources. To investigate these differences, the authors follow a two-fold strategy. First, they exploit the 2015 Venezuelan immigration shock in Colombia using a difference-in-differences strategy, complemented by an instrumental variable. The authors find null-to-positive effects. Second, a survey experiment reveals that priming citizens on immigration has positive effects on citizens’ social spending preferences. The authors attribute this effect to deservingness considerations. These results challenge some prevailing theories and sug-gest that increased immigration does not necessarily reduce redistribution preferences in South-South contexts.
