title: Late‐Life Mobility in a Rapidly Ageing Middle‐Income Country: Spatial Patterns and Local Demographic Change in Brazil, 1980–2010
authors: Fernando Antonio Ignacio González, Jean Sleifer
abstract: How do older adults reshape the spatial demography of a middle‐income country undergoing one of the fastest population‐ageing transitions on record? Brazil offers a particularly informative case: its share of population aged 60 or above rose from 6.2% in 1980 to 10.8% in 2010 and is projected to reach 25% by 2050, and a nationally administered pension regime makes benefits fully portable across the country's 5565 municipalities. Using large‐sample microdata from four Brazilian Demographic Censuses (1980–2010, 84 million records harmonised to 4298 stable comparable areas) linked to municipal economic accounts, we document a senior counter‐current with the hallmarks of counter‐urbanisation. Senior inter‐area mobility declines with age yet remains substantial through retirement ages, and it is not local boundary‐hopping: the median senior move covers roughly 100 kilometres and nearly a third crosses state lines. Older Brazilians move against the working‐age tide—the largest metropolitan areas lose retirees on net, while small and medium‐sized interior destinations receive them at rates reaching 5%–6% of initial population per 5‐year window. Receiving areas expand demographically—in total population, working‐age cohorts, employment, housing stock and services activity—but GDP per capita and agricultural value added grow more slowly, a pattern consistent with retirees transmitting purchasing power to destinations whose productive base does not scale with the inflow. These associations are robust to geographic‐amenity controls, pre‐trend conditioning and microregion fixed effects and geographically weighted regressions show they hold across virtually the entire national territory; we are explicit, however, that positive selection of destinations bounds them above any causal effect. We discuss what the Brazilian counter‐current implies for population geography and for other middle‐income countries tracing the same demographic curve.

title: Peer-to-peer accountability and knowledge production in OECD DAC peer reviews
authors: Alice Iannantuoni, Simone Dietrich, Bernhard Reinsberg
abstract: The OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) relies on peer reviews to promote accountability in development cooperation. For peer review to function as an accountability mechanism, it must first satisfy a core requirement: peer review evaluations must accurately reflect donor practices. We examine whether DAC peer reviews interpret donor behavior on tied aid in ways that are consistent with observable aid-tying practices and shared DAC standards. Using a newly collected corpus of 143 DAC peer reviews from 1994 to 2020, we find a strong, systematic relationship between the reviewed donor’s aid-tying practices and the resulting content of the review documents. This linkage is driven primarily by explicit recommendations to untie aid and discussions of the standard, rather than by positive recognition of aid tying. Contrary to concerns that peer reviewers may intentionally soften evaluations and criticism to protect their own interests, we find no evidence that reviewers who themselves exhibit higher levels of aid tying produce evaluations that deviate from actual practice. Our findings demonstrate that DAC peer reviews generate credible peer evaluations that strengthen accountability dynamics in development cooperation. These insights contribute to literatures on peer reviews in global governance, the politics of international organizations, and foreign aid.

title: The power of locality: National staff enhance performance in international organizations
authors: Steffen Eckhard, Sebastian Korb, Daniel Baumann
abstract: International organizations (IOs) rely on locally hired staff to translate global mandates into local action, yet the performance implications of localization remain contested. Addressing this gap, this study combines natural language processing (NLP) with a novel dataset of 5,230 project evaluations and staffing information from five United Nations organizations (2007–2022). Building on current research on local staff employment in IO projects together with insights from expert interviews, we test two dominant competing arguments: local capture versus local knowledge. Multilevel and fixed-effects analyses show that projects with higher shares of local staff perform significantly better, but only once local employees constitute at least 60% of the team. The results advance theory on IO effectiveness by shifting attention from local discretion to staff composition, demonstrating that locally embedded knowledge, when institutionally represented in staffing, constitutes a key organizational resource for adaptive implementation.

title: Bold Claims, Low Wages: Why Voluntary Sustainability Standards ( VSS ) Struggle to Implement Living Wages
abstract: Voluntary sustainability standards (VSS)—such as Fairtrade International and the Forest Stewardship Council—aim to improve sustainability in global supply chains by setting high social and environmental standards and certifying businesses that adopt them. This article examines why some VSS adopt ambitious goals for living wages or living incomes yet continue to certify businesses that only pay a minimum wage. Drawing on previous literature, it offers a typology of five ways that VSS can decouple. Drawing on documents, interviews, and participant observation, it offers detailed case studies of how five VSS have engaged in the coupling and decoupling of wage standards. The research identifies four drivers of decoupling: priorities that complete, costs of coupling, low risk of decoupling, and anticipation that coupling will be easier in the future. It also describes several factors that influence these drivers. Finally, it shows how decoupling may paradoxically facilitate progress, while pressure to fully couple may inhibit transformative change, and concludes with recommendations for avoiding empty claims while harnessing aspirational standards.

title: How considered interests evolve in deliberation: evidence from Swiss citizens’ juries
abstract: Citizens increasingly demand involvement in policymaking, driving the rise of participatory processes like deliberative minipublics. This article introduces a novel longitudinal survey measure to determine the extent to which citizens are more considerate of others’ interests as a result of their participation in such forums. The study explores how participants’ considered interests vary across demographics and process-related factors measured throughout five Swiss minipublics (2019–2023) on different topics and validated using word-embedding techniques on their transcripts. While results show that minipublic participants considered interests different from their own, individuals belonging to less advantaged groups did not consistently show greater consideration of others’ interests. Interest inclusiveness was higher among older individuals, low-income earners and participants in minipublics linked to referendums. This article explains how and why participants in minipublics consider interests beyond their own, which is essential for designing more inclusive participatory processes that engage people from diverse backgrounds in increasingly polarized societies.

title: Who cares about politics under authoritarian rule? Evidence from China
abstract: Departing from mainstream research on political interest in democratic contexts, this study investigates its evolution in an authoritarian setting. To disentangle temporal dynamics, it applies the age–period–cohort interaction model to repeated cross-sectional data from five waves of nationally representative surveys conducted in China. The results demonstrate distinct effects across age, period, and cohort dimensions. Age effects indicate that younger individuals consistently exhibit lower levels of political interest than older adults. Period effects reveal a downward trend in political interest among the Chinese public between 2002 and 2019. Importantly, cohort effects suggest that, contrary to the linear evolutionary predictions of modernization theory, individuals who underwent political socialization during critical historical periods—such as the Great Famine and its aftermath (1959–1963) and the late Cultural Revolution (1974–1978)—as well as those born in the late 1970s and throughout the 1980s, exhibit heightened political interest. These findings contribute to theoretical reflections on the evolution of political interest.

Anti-Elitism Gets the Views: Populist Communication and Popularity on German Political YouTube
abstract: YouTube has become a central venue for political communication, but systematic evidence of how parties employ the platform remains limited. This article examines how German political parties use YouTube and how populist rhetoric shapes engagement. We distinguish between anti-elitism and people-centrism and analyze their prevalence in party videos alongside their effects on video performance. We compile a dataset of official YouTube channels from all major German parties (2017–2025), apply automated transcription, and use a transformer-based model (PopBERT) to detect populist language. Video performance is assessed primarily through views, modeled with quantile regression and hurdle approaches to capture the likelihood of videos reaching the top tier and conditional effects among successful content. Our results show that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) far surpasses other parties in subscribers, video production, and engagement. Content analysis reveals that AfD channels contain markedly higher levels of anti-elitist rhetoric, while people-centrism appears more evenly distributed across the party spectrum. Quantile regression models show that anti-elitism is positively associated with engagement in the upper tail of the view distribution for all parties except the Free Democratic Party (FDP). Hurdle models further indicate that anti-elitism is associated with a higher probability of entering the top performance tier not only for the AfD but also for the Christian Democratic Union / Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), Left, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Results for people-centrism are weaker and less consistent. The study contributes to research on digital populism by showing that anti-elitist rhetoric, more than people-centrism, is associated with video success on YouTube across populist and nonpopulist parties.

title: India's Agricultural Policy Transitions
authors: Avinash Kishore, Bharat Ramaswami, Devesh Roy
abstract: This review traces the evolution of India's agricultural policy regime, centered on price supports, input subsidies, and complex trade policies that oscillate between protectionism and implicit taxation of farmers. It highlights three interlinked challenges: low farm incomes, poor diet quality, and environmental degradation. The policy architecture that ensures food security constrains the pace of agricultural transformation. Reform requires repurposing subsidies and restoring credibility to trade policy. While the digital infrastructure is in place to begin the shift to smarter subsidies, the political path is risky, as policy must seek credible ways to signal protection of farmer interests. Despite these policy rigidities, economic growth and urbanization continue to drive structural changes in agriculture. Diversification away from cereals, new food value chains, and rising integration with nonfarm employment are the key dynamic forces shaping agricultural outcomes. Future outcomes will depend on policy responses to emerging food value chains and new agricultural technologies.

title: Framing Extremist Narratives: A Multi‐Stage Computational Analysis of Discourse Structures, Emotional Mobilization, and Cross‐Platform Migration
authors: Xiaotian Hou, Xiaohan Liu, Mingyu Liu
abstract: Online extremism poses a particularly difficult governance challenge when radical actors adapt and spread grievance, authority, enemy, and recruitment narratives across heterogeneous platforms. This study develops a multi‐stage computational framework for analyzing extremist narratives across platforms. Using a corpus of 22,347 English‐language documents from Twitter/X, Telegram, Gab, public web archives, and extremist‐adjacent forums posted between 2020 and 2023, the study integrates topic modeling, frame classification, psycholinguistic and emotion scoring, semantic cross‐platform matching, qualitative validation, and negative‐control checks. The findings identify eight topic clusters, six recurring narrative frames, and a platform‐migration pattern associated with semantic drift and stronger enemy‐focused framing in less‐moderated destination spaces. The results are consistent with a displacement‐and‐intensification mechanism, although they do not establish causal effects of deplatforming or individual radicalization. The study contributes to computational discourse analysis, coordinated platform governance, and frame‐aware counter‐narrative design.

title: How patronage communicates: information campaigns and government responsiveness in China
abstract: How do social relationships among government officials shape information flows within bureaucratic hierarchies? Classic principal–agent theories emphasize information asymmetries as a source of inefficiency, yet we know far less about the actual nature of communication within bureaucracies. We argue that patron–client ties embedded within formal hierarchies play a central role in structuring internal information flows. Lower-level officials with patronage ties to higher-level leaders have incentives to conduct informal information campaigns that signal diligence and competence as a way to compete for political favors. Using newly assembled data from China—including a rare corpus of internal emails between city-level patrons and county-level clients, as well as original datasets on county governments’ public responses to citizen complaints—we find that client counties communicate more frequently with higher-level officials, more often highlight their diligence in addressing complaints, and more actively defend themselves against accusations. However, client and non-client counties perform similarly in how they respond publicly to citizen complaints. These findings reveal how patronage relations can increase upward information flows without impacting public-facing performance. More broadly, these results suggest that communication in nondemocratic settings may serve to strengthen informal political ties.

title: Policymaking activities of caretaker governments in Western Europe
abstract: In parliamentary democracies, coalition government formation often takes a certain amount of time, during which the outgoing incumbent government remains in office as the “caretaker” until the new government can be formed. While the literature has reached a consensus that caretaker governments retain the policy status quo, empirical evidence remains limited. This article uses original data on government bills from 238 cabinets in 11 Western European countries as descriptive evidence to challenge this long-standing assumption. I propose a timeframe-based, political definition of the caretaking period within the coalition lifecycle and discuss the normative issues with its presence. The over-generalization of the prevalent policy status quo assumption raises critical issues concerning practical caretaking rules, as well as coalition governance and bargaining.

title: Racialization of the democratic peace in foundational embedding models
abstract: One of the most prominent theories in modern international relations is the democratic peace theory, which posits that democracies tend not to engage in armed conflicts with fellow democracies. Recently, Rathbun, Parker, and Pomeroy examined this effect at a microstructural level, performing surveys, computational studies, and meta-analysis. Of particular originality in their work was embedding analysis, which I review and offer a systematic critique of. Then, I propose a new and improved methodology that addresses its issues while leveraging foundational embedding models. My replication results agree with their findings that the democratic peace effect is racialized, that is, it is associated with racial and ethnocentric motivations. The findings offer a timely guide in conducting embedding analysis in political science research.

title: A multilingual, multi-country dataset on gardening and biodiversity awareness across Central and Eastern Europe
authors: Zsófia Varga-Szilay, Lucija Šerić Jelaska, Silva Vilumets, Arvīds Barševskis, Klára Benedek, Danilo Bevk, Agata Jojczyk, Anton Krištín, Jana Růžičková, Eve Veromann, Kinga Gabriela Fetykó, Gergely Szövényi, Gábor Pozsgai
abstract: We present a multi-country and multilingual dataset on garden characteristics, gardening practices, and gardeners’ environmental attitudes based on a questionnaire survey conducted across nine Central and Eastern European countries: Croatia, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. The survey was collaboratively designed and translated into ten languages by native speakers to ensure cultural and linguistic accuracy. It was distributed online through diverse channels, yielding 5511 responses. The dataset enables exploration of relationships between gardening practices and socio-cultural factors at local, national, and regional scales. The questionnaire covered topics such as garden characteristics, management practices, pesticide use, biodiversity-supporting actions, and environmental awareness, offering a comprehensive overview of gardening in the region. The dataset is suitable for cross-country comparisons, machine learning analyses, and the development of indices that quantify ecological value or management intensity. The multilingual questionnaire supports reuse in future studies, facilitating replication or adaptation elsewhere. By making the dataset openly available, we provide a resource for researchers and practitioners interested in urban biodiversity, sustainability, and human–nature interactions.

title: Origin, gender and academic age diversity indicators for UK research communities
abstract: This paper describes a dataset of community-level diversity indicators for origin, gender and academic age across research communities in UK higher education institutions. The indicators were constructed from individual-level bibliometric metadata for 535,456 research-active individuals in OpenAlex, using onomastic inference for gender and country of origin and publication histories for academic age, with confidence-based filtering to manage inference uncertainty. The unit of analysis is the institution–Unit of Assessment pair defined by the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021, and the resulting REF 2021-Diversity dataset comprises 1,848 records across 155 institutions and 34 Units of Assessment. The indicators range from simple compositional statistics through standard entropy-based indices to multidimensional Leinster–Cobbold indices to accommodate various use cases and assumptions. The dataset can support benchmarking of research community composition, methodological comparison of diversity measures, and cautiously specified association analyses between community-level diversity indicators and REF-linked quality profiles.

title: From the courtroom to the public: Judicial influence on People’s attitudes toward same-sex marriage in Japan
authors: Robert Nordström, Sou Shinomoto, Antonio Benasaglio Berlucchi
abstract: Can judicial action change public attitudes? While most empirical studies on the societal impact of court rulings have focused on the United States, particularly its Supreme Court, the influence of courts in other contexts remains largely unexplored. This study examines Japan—the only G7 country that does not legally recognize same-sex marriage—and explores how judicial rulings on same-sex marriage influence public attitudes. Using data from an original survey incorporating natural and experimental treatments, the analysis finds that while a court decision has no significant effect in a natural environment, experimental exposure to a reminder of the ruling can shift respondents’ views. The findings suggest that judicial action on same-sex marriage may have limited but measurable impacts on public attitudes, even in unconventional settings, and therefore contribute to discussions of external validity regarding the societal influence of courts.

title: Revisiting the Communication Mediation Model in the Age of Social Media: Longitudinal Evidence From Climate Misinformation Responses in China
authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
abstract: The Communication Mediation Model (CMM) posits that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which shapes attitudes and behaviors. Yet its assumptions of linear sequencing and universal applicability remain underexamined. In the era of social media, communication flows are increasingly reciprocal and socially embedded, and response behaviors such as misinformation correction and fact-checking represent new forms of media engagement rather than merely offline actions. Using a three-wave panel survey in China ( n = 499), this study revises the CMM in the context of climate change misinformation on social media by testing temporal pathways and audience heterogeneity. Results show that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which in turn predicts correction, though these relationships unfold concurrently within a single time interval rather than following a staggered temporal order. Multigroup analysis reveals that public self-consciousness conditions pathway activation. Findings highlight how social media environments extend the behavioral scope of the CMM and complicate its assumed temporal order. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

title: Scaling Down: Notes From the Laundry Room
abstract: This essay tells the story of a personal experiment in deploying a “deliberative technology” called Polis to start a conversation about the norms of my apartment building’s shared laundry room—a small, quasi-public space ordinarily governed mostly by unspoken rules. The Polis conversation drew meaningful engagement from neighbors, who both voted on shared norms for the space and suggested concrete (and ultimately effective) ways to improve it. Reflecting on this example, I argue that beyond their familiar promise of “scaling up” deliberation, tools like Polis can also facilitate “scaling down,” making it feasible to convene conversations and build a sense of shared interest even in small-scale, everyday settings like the apartment laundry room.

title: Anthropomorphizing AI: Perceptions, Interpretations, and the Humanization of Generative AI
authors: Mohammad Hossein Jarrahi, Amir Karami, Lisa Park, Ensieh Jarrahi, Christoph Lutz
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly advanced AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, has transformed human–AI interactions by providing unprecedentedly natural interaction environments. These developments have significantly heightened user perceptions of AI as human-like, making anthropomorphism, a tendency to attribute human traits to non-humans, increasingly prevalent. Despite the recognition of the rising anthropomorphism in these interaction modalities, little is known about how people anthropomorphize generative AI, especially in social media discourse. Using Twitter/X as a discursive space, we systematically analyze how users described and engaged with ChatGPT, identifying distinct categories and recurring forms of anthropomorphism. Findings reveal diverse anthropomorphic perceptions, including personification, emotional attributions, cognitive and human-like attributes, social interactions, and human-like personality traits. Building on the observation that social media platforms not only reflect but also actively shape and reinforce anthropomorphic narratives, this study raises important implications for trust, misinformation, user expectations, and human–AI interactions.

title: Unpacking the Relationship Between Algorithmic Literacy and Misinformation: A Multidimensional Approach Using Two Sequential Studies
authors: Teresa Correa, Sebastián Valenzuela, Ingrid Bachmann, Nicolás Tobar Jorquera, Natalia Solís-Valdés, Isabel Pavez
abstract: Digital literacy is often proposed as a remedy for misinformation, yet empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness remains mixed. One reason for these inconsistencies lies in the multidimensional nature of both literacy and misinformation. This article focuses on algorithmic literacy, a distinct and increasingly central form of digital literacy in platform-mediated communication, and examines how its cognitive and behavioral dimensions relate to multiple facets of misinformation engagement. Drawing on two probabilistic survey studies conducted in Chile—a nationally representative face-to-face survey ( N = 1,200) and a random-digit-dial telephone survey of urban adults ( N = 2,265)—we analyze how cognitive (algorithmic awareness and knowledge) and behavioral (strategic actions to navigate algorithmic systems) dimensions of algorithmic literacy relate to perceived misinformation exposure, misinformation sharing, objective and subjective news knowledge, and knowledge miscalibration. Across both studies, a consistent pattern emerges: algorithmic literacy is more strongly associated with cognitive outcomes—especially perceived misinformation exposure and knowledge—than with behavioral outcomes like sharing. Higher algorithmic awareness consistently predicts greater perceived exposure, suggesting heightened recognition, while its link to sharing behavior is less consistent. These studies highlight the relevance of distinguishing cognitive from behavioral dimensions of literacy across different stages of misinformation engagement.

title: “Hearing My People, but Not Seeing My People”: Boundaries of Blackness on TikTok
abstract: Social media is a valuable tool that enables Black individuals to contest their racialized experiences and engage in counterpublic discourse. Importantly, this opens up cultural property and closed conversations to out-group visibility and appropriation. With this in mind, I ask: How do Black social media users engage in boundary work on TikTok? I create a typology of boundary enforcement on the platform, identifying nine video subtypes, and analyze each subtype using Critical Technocultural Discourse Analysis. The findings suggest that Black TikTok users employ various discursive strategies to maintain group boundaries. This study explores how new technologies may impact racialized experiences and identity formation.

title: Policing Queer and Racialized Identities: An Intersectional Approach to Study Police Bias
abstract: Queer people in the United States have been historically over-policed, in a long-standing history of criminalization and oppression by law enforcement. Despite scholars having extensively used administrative records of police stops to uncover racial disparities and bias in law enforcement practices, virtually no studies exist doing the same to examine the discriminatory policing of queerness—by itself, and in the intersection with race. In this article, I fill this gap by analyzing administrative records of ∼3,100,000 stops in the United States between 2018 and 2025, looking at whether civilians perceived as LGBTQ+ are disproportionately targeted by the police in post-stop decisions. Through multiple tests, I find consistent evidence that being queer is associated with a higher probability of being searched, arrested, and be victims of police use of force. Then, using an intersectional approach, I test whether the interaction of race with queerness worsens police discrimination. Results show that bias gets worse for racial minorities who are also LGBTQ+, indicating that a dynamic of intersectional, double disadvantage can be found in police discrimination. This research underscores the importance of applying an intersectional framework to police studies, and the ongoing role of policing in reproducing the marginalization of historically oppressed communities.

title: More Inclusive, Less Attentive: How Digital Intermediaries Expand News Audiences but Facilitate Inequalities in News Attentiveness
Migration information campaigns as bureaucratic performances: governing through visibility
abstract: Drawing on a mixed-methods analysis of 97 migration information campaigns implemented across Europe between 2019 and 2026 and more than thirty interviews with migration governance practitioners, policymakers, and international organization staff, this article reconceptualizes migration information campaigns as bureaucratic performances. Rather than informing migrants, campaigns operate as visible governance outputs through which states, international organizations, and implementing agencies stage action, secure legitimacy, and reproduce migration governance systems. The analysis shows that migration information campaigns have become routinized instruments of migration governance whose design is structured around risk framing and strategic ambiguity, and whose primary audiences are often institutional rather than migrant populations. Across governance contexts, campaigns perform distinct functions: signaling cooperation in countries of origin, demonstrating compliance in transit settings, and projecting responsiveness in destination countries. The article argues that migration information campaigns persist not because they influence migration decisions, but because they are institutionally useful. Their value lies in producing visibility, legitimacy, and auditable evidence of action in contexts where governing migration outcomes is difficult. In doing so, the article challenges dominant evaluative approaches in migration studies by showing that policy instruments may endure even when they are widely acknowledged to have uncertain or limited behavioural effects. Migration information campaigns, it concludes, are not failed interventions; they are successful performances of governance.

title: Assessing pedestrian responses to autonomous and personal mobility robots in crowded public spaces
authors: Dominik Wojcikiewicz, Aude Billard, Diego Paez-Granados
abstract: Robots increasingly share spaces with people, supporting delivery services and mobility for the aging populations, yet their ability to share space comfortably lacks understanding and benchmarks for designers and policy-makers. We compared human-robot (HRI) and human-human (HHI) interactions across four real-world crowd datasets spanning Europe, North America, and Asia, using a unified pipeline to detect interactions, stratify by crowd density, and model pedestrian behavior. Local motion patterns (speed, acceleration, and jerk) remained closely matched between HRI and HHI across all densities. In contrast, proxemics diverged, with effects that grew approximately linearly with robot speed and weakened under higher crowding: In the dataset with the faster navigating robot, pedestrians maintained about 0.23 meters more clearance around the robot than around other pedestrians under less crowded conditions and about 0.05 meters more under more crowded conditions, while in the dataset with the predominantly stationary robot, the corresponding differences were small and inconsistent across crowding levels. The main conclusions were robust to parameter variations and remained stable across a broad range of motion-processing and interaction-labeling settings. Our findings provide density- and speed-aware benchmarks for proxemics in social robot navigation and empirically grounded targets for design, evaluation, and modeling across robotics and urban mobility.

title: Escalation dynamics and the severity of wars
authors: Aaron Clauset, Barbara F. Walter, Lars-Erik Cederman, Kristian Skrede Gleditsch
abstract: Although very large wars remain an enduring threat in global politics, we lack a clear understanding of how some wars become large and costly, while most do not. There are three possibilities: Large conflicts begin with intense fighting, accumulate severity over a long duration, or escalate in intensity over time. Using detailed within-conflict data on civil and interstate wars (1946–2008), we show that escalation dynamics—variations in fighting intensity within an armed conflict—are the primary mechanism for producing large conflicts. Civil wars, however, tend to deescalate once they become very large, limiting their overall severity, while interstate wars exhibit a persistent risk of continual escalation. Simple models of within-conflict severity dynamics show that this distinction compactly explains the historical size distributions of civil and interstate wars, and unconditioned escalation is a plausible mechanism for Richardson’s law—the power law pattern in the frequency and severity of interstate conflicts. The dynamics of escalation within conflicts have broad implications for conflict theory and risk assessment.

title: Most people who agree with you won’t protest: Predictors of marches and demonstrations from six decades of research
abstract: Protest and activism are endemic and potent features of many nations’ political life and critical potential counters to democratic backsliding and authoritarianism. In this review article, we meta-analytically examine six decades of research findings on what explains participation, focusing particularly on two well-studied protest forms: marches and demonstrations. Focusing on these iconic and common forms of protest participation ensures accurate research comparison, allowing us to identify sets of variables that are consistently important, others that are not consistently important, and still others that need additional research. Our focus on survey-based studies also allows us to compare research that includes both participants and nonparticipants, which is critical for methodologically sound comparisons. Our analysis of 181 survey-based studies (with more than 1800 different estimates) shows that survey research strongly supports the relevance of political interest, political ideology, membership in organizations, and digital/social media use in explaining participation, as well as demographic variables such as education, age, and living in an urban center. Our review also offers important suggestions for future survey research and micromobilization research more broadly.

title: Individual and differential harm in redistricting
Longitudinal effect of early social media use on standardized learning outcomes during school career
authors: Marco Gui, Chiara Respi, Giovanni Abbiati, Cristiana Paladini, Sofia Ercolanoni, Francesca Milzani, Tiziana Pirola, Giovanni Vezzoli
abstract: This study uses difference-in-differences models to evaluate the impact of early social media use on academic performance among children aged 7–16 years. A dataset comprising 5,227 students from northern Italy was constructed by merging data from a questionnaire on lifetime digital media habits with longitudinal standardized test scores in Italian, English and mathematics. Participants who created a personal social media account in 6th, 7th or 8th grade were separately matched with late adopters who initiated their first social media account in the 9th grade or later. The findings provide compelling evidence that early engagement with social media adversely affects learning outcomes. Additional findings on the effects of early social media use on other academic outcomes for which we do not have longitudinal data are in line with our main findings. We also find supporting evidence that a substantial part of this negative effect is mediated by students’ smartphone pervasiveness in key moments of the day.

title: Lucid Dream Control: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Future Directions
abstract: Lucid dreaming (LD) is the phenomenon during which dreamers are aware they are dreaming and may be able to influence dream content. Dream manipulation, or dream control, plays a critical role in the applications of LD across both clinical and non-clinical domains and may be a key determinant of therapeutic success. However, not all lucid dreamers are able to effectively influence their dreams, and achieving dream lucidity does not automatically translate into meaningful control. Despite the growing interest in LD, research on the mechanisms, reliability, and effectiveness of dream manipulation remains limited. This work critically reviews the current state of research on dream manipulation within LD, identifies gaps in knowledge, and proposes future directions for addressing challenges in reliably controlling lucid dreams. We begin by exploring the elements of dreams that can be influenced through dream manipulation (including dream environment, body, and narrative) and discuss strategies, challenges, and individual differences in dream control. Additionally, we explore the clinical and non-clinical applications of manipulating lucid dreams and call for future research that focuses on standardizing dream control assessment methods, empirical studies evaluating dream manipulation strategies, and a deeper understanding of the cognitive, emotional, and neurophysiological factors that contribute to successful dream manipulation. Finally, the Lucid Dream Control General (LDC-G) and Lucid Dream Control for Specific Experiences (LDC-SE) scales are proposed as new standardized methods to evaluate dream control during LD. These questionnaires provide individual scores for specific aspects of LD control and overall dream control proficiency.

title: Experimental Evidence on the Effect of Mixed-Mode Survey Designs on Item Measurement and Variable Correlations
authors: Liam Wright, Georgia D Tomova, Matt Brown, Konstantinos G. Tsigaridis, Morag Henderson, Richard J. Silverwood
abstract: Background: Mixed-mode designs can generate bias in all types of analysis of survey data due to systematic differences in how survey participants may respond according to mode – a phenomenon referred to as a mode effect. There is widespread evidence of mode effects upon item measurement (e.g., item means and proportions), but less on associations between survey items, despite estimating associations being a primary use of survey data. Methods: We estimated average differences (means and proportions) in item responses according to mode using data from an experiment in which participants were randomized to respond via web questionnaire, video interview, or in-person interview. We then used these estimates to simulate (counterfactual) data from two web-then-in-person sequential mixed-mode surveys of young adults in the United Kingdom (Next Steps and the Millennium Cohort Study, MCS) as if they were collected using a single mode, web. We estimated associations between variables using this simulated data and compared these against associations obtained using the observed (i.e., factual) data; the difference between the two provides a measure of variation in variable correlations reflecting the mixed-mode survey design. Results: Mode effects were observed for an array of items comparing web with in-person and video modes; differences between video and in-person were more muted. Participants in web were more likely to report negatively valent values for sensitive items, in particular (e.g., poorer physical and mental health, lower life satisfaction, and greater financial difficulty), though effect sizes were generally small with few exceeding 0.2 SD and all below 0.3 SD. The impact of mode effects on variable associations in the mixed-mode surveys was also generally small: a 0.004 SD change in absolute effect sizes on average in both Next Steps and the MCS. Conclusion: Items related to sensitive characteristics showed small mode effects when comparing web and in-person or video interview modes. Mode effects did not appear to translate into substantial changes to associations between variables as assessed in a sequential web-then-in-person mixed-mode survey compared with a counterfactual web-only survey.

title: From international dissemination to encountering epistemic diversity: communication about art and the art of communication in the Comprehensive Collection of Ancient Chinese paintings.
abstract: This paper reconceptualizes the international dissemination of A Comprehensive Collection of Ancient Chinese Paintings (the Series) not merely as cultural transmission or global circulation, but as an epistemic practice of exchange that transcends disciplinary, professional, and geographical, and cultural boundaries. Drawing on perspectives from communication science, intercultural exchange, and art–science interaction, the paper examines how dissemination functions as an epistemic practice that both translates and generates knowledge. First, it situates art communication and dissemination as a site of knowledge creation and epistemic encounter rather than a passive transfer of information to audiences (communicating about art). Second, it argues that the Series enables epistemic innovation and diversity through the interaction between multiple, heterogeneous knowledge practices, facilitated by cross-cultural dialogue and inter- and transdisciplinary exchange. Finally, it discusses the interactive and engaging dissemination practices through which the Series is translated to broader audiences, focusing on experiential, sensory, and narrative forms of engagement in immersive exhibitions and digital media platforms (the art of communication). The paper argues that a significant value of the Series lies in its capacity to function as an epistemic infrastructure: one that not only transmits and circulates knowledge on Chinese art and cultural heritage, but also enables encounters between different ways of knowing and, as a result, generates new forms of understanding and epistemic diversity.

title: Conclusion: reflections on and conditions for meaningful art-science interaction
abstract: This conclusion brings together the diverse reflections on meaningful art–science interactions that have emerged throughout the chapters, exploring key takeaways from each contribution. It presents a colorful palette of disciplinary, professional, and artistic perspectives, showing how different ways of knowing meet, contrast, and resonate, while highlighting experiences, insights, emerging practices, and recurring questions across the volume. This journey of discovery through varied perspectives and topics culminates in an outline of possible future directions, not as prescriptions or a manual, but as invitations for readers to explore new pathways beyond the scope of this book, and to embark on further journeys of encounter, co-creation, and epistemic exchange.

title: Working across and beyond boundaries: a journey in art – science collaborations
abstract: This chapter, written in the form of a dialogue, features an in-depth interview with professor Johan Wagemans, a renowned perception researcher and principal investigator of the Palettes project. Over nearly two decades, Wagemans has been at the forefront of interdisciplinary research bridging science and art. In this conversation, he reflects on his personal journey working with artists across disciplinary boundaries and explores how his understanding of art–science relationships has transformed from his earliest collaboration (Parallellepipeda in 2008) to his current work in Palettes. Through a series of anecdotes and critical reflections, the chapter highlights both the strengths and the challenges of conducting long-term art–science collaborations. Wagemans discusses what has worked, what has not, and why, offering insights into the subtle dynamics of interdisciplinary exchange and the conditions that foster meaningful interaction. Looking ahead, he considers emerging pathways, ambitions, and opportunities for future art–science engagement, particularly beyond formal academic structures. The chapter is complemented by selected artworks that symbolize key turning points in his journey and visually illustrate themes raised in the dialogue. Together, the narrative and visual materials illuminate how art–science collaborations can evolve, deepen, and open new directions for research and creative practice.

title: A practical guide to perform an Interdisciplinary Scoping Review
abstract: The growth of interdisciplinary research has brought with it an increasing demand for robust methods to map and synthesize diverse bodies of evidence. Among these, scoping reviews have emerged as a particularly valuable tool. They allow researchers to systematically explore complex, cross-cutting topics, clarify definitions, identify gaps, and build foundations for future inquiry. This guide was developed to respond to that need. It provides a step-by-step framework for conducting an interdisciplinary scoping review, illustrated with the example of digitalisation and its effects on the physical health of older workers. By walking through each stage of the process—from formulating research questions to reporting and publishing findings—the guide aims to make the methodology transparent, practical, and replicable for researchers at different career stages and across disciplines. The approach presented here is rooted in established frameworks and aligned with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to ensure rigour and clarity. At the same time, it reflects the lessons learned from my own experience conducting interdisciplinary reviews in practice. I hope this guide encourages researchers to approach scoping reviews in a more systematic and transparent way, while also fostering collaboration across disciplines.

title: Beyond technical thinking: revealing reflections on technology, media art, logocentrism, and epistemic diversity
abstract: This chapter examines art–science-technology interactions and epistemic diversity in a world shaped by technological progress and scientific knowledge, which are deeply intertwined. While technology is often understood as the use and development of instruments, a means to an end, it is not only something we use; it also shapes how we understand and engage with reality. In this technological ‘revealing’ of reality, the world increasingly presents itself as measurable, controllable, and exploitable: as a resource. This chapter refers to this instrumentalization of reality as technical thinking. In this chapter, we first show that within artistic practice, the use of technology does not necessarily lead to technical thinking. When engaged within artistic practice, it can open non-technical, contemplative ways of relating to the world. The chapter then reverses this perspective by showing that technical thinking can also operate without visible machines, particularly through logocentric language in scientific practice, where articulation and description function as a technology of ordering and control and become conditions for what counts as knowledge. Ultimately, the chapter asks how artistic and other ways of knowing can enter scientific contexts without being assimilated into technical thinking, and reflects on the conditions for sustaining epistemic diversity in contemporary knowledge institutions.

title: Meritocracy, Legitimation and Belonging on the University of Cambridge’s Foundation Year
abstract: Widening participation spans the whole student lifecycle, from access through to success within higher education and progression beyond it, yet policy and evaluation have concentrated on the access stage alone. Far less is known about how students admitted through widened access routes come to understand the legitimacy of their place once inside an elite university. Reporting twenty-one (n=21) walking interviews with students who entered the University of Cambridge through its Foundation Year, a one-year pre-degree programme for applicants whose educational opportunities have been constrained by structural disadvantage, this article examines a tension at the heart of meritocracy. Participants recognized that admissions standards are shaped by unequal opportunity, though the recognition appeared not to weaken their commitment to meritocratic judgement, and they endeavored to suffuse their belonging with proof of deservingness. Such a pattern sits uneasily with Bourdieusian accounts of symbolic domination grounded in misrecognition, and points towards a compliance sustained through lucid perception of meritocracy and its ideological demands. Analysis of the walks suggests that the route organizes this tension by marking students publicly as different, by tying belonging to a competitive progression threshold, by collapsing heterogeneous experiences into a single administrative category, and by locating institutional judgement in everyday encounters with teaching staff. Belonging emerges less as a settled outcome of admission than as a conditional status that must be repeatedly earned. Widening access may therefore secure entry without securing the later stages of participation, so long as the legitimacy of membership continues to be organized through meritocratic evaluation that students simultaneously critique and reproduce.

title: Cognitive and Proactive Building Operation: Current Status and an Eight-Gap Research Agenda
abstract: Buildings dominate final energy demand, but operation remains reactive. This paper reviews cognitive and proactive building operation and derives a research agenda. Two questions guide the analysis: RQ1, the current status of seven constituent streams; RQ2, the gaps explaining the persistent distance between concept and practice. A critical review (July 2026) covers cognitive building concepts, MPC, RL/data-driven control, OCC, AFDD, cognitive digital twins with semantic infrastructure, and LLM-based agentic systems. Retrieval prioritised recent reviews and field deployments, with snowballing. An explicit evidence hierarchy and gap-derivation rule are stated, and bibliographic records were verified against metadata. An independent bibliometric strand uses a documented Web of Science query on cognitive, adaptive, cybernetic, and AI vocabulary, yielding 113 records (2011-2026). This corpus is profiled bibliometrically and mapped onto the gap taxonomy. The query string is reproduced verbatim, its retrieval behaviour is audited, and two artefacts materially affecting interpretation are discussed. The status pattern is consistent: conceptually rich, simulation-mature, field-poor. Bibliometrics sharpen this: 49% of records are from 2024-2026; a single 2020 review accounts for 49% of citations; only 20% are building-related (rest in software, manufacturing, general digital twins); cybernetic-building intersections contain only three records, the latest from 2015; co-word analysis reveals structural zeros, with cybernetics and self-adaptive systems never co-occurring. The query audit confirms: although the viable system model is named, exactly one of 113 records engages Beer's model, and it does not concern buildings. Outside the database, this organizing principle is applied in production management, software architecture, and agentic AI, but not in contemporary building operation. Eight gaps are derived: G1 definitional/theoretical, G2 reactive-to-proactive practice, G3 simulation-to-reality, G4 fragmentation, G5 architectural mechanism, G6 evaluation, G7 longevity/resilience, and G8 human factors/governance. G1-G4 and G6-G8 restate explicit deficits; G5 is an interpretive synthesis. The paper argues G5, the absence of an organizing principle for allocating sensing, computation, and actuation across subsystems, spatial scales, and time horizons, is structurally prior to several other gaps, and candidate principles are compared. Contributions include a cross-stream status consolidation, an evidence-anchored gap taxonomy with derivation rules, bibliometric quantitative support, and a defended keystone-gap argument. The review is evaluative rather than exhaustive and positions its findings as an evidence-based hypothesis set for a subsequent protocol-driven systematic review.

title: Is Entrepreneurship Legitimate Where the State Is Not? Insights from Machine Learning Methods
abstract: Does the political environment influence people’s perceptions of entrepreneurship? Should there be any correlation between state legitimacy and that of entrepreneurship? These questions are crucial, as the success of any developmental tool, including entrepreneurship, depends on its public approval. To find the answers, the present paper examines Iran as an extreme case of a state facing recurring episodes of legitimacy crisis while simultaneously deeply involved in promoting entrepreneurship and penetrating the entrepreneurial ecosystem. The paper reveals that Iranians’ perceptions of entrepreneurship essentially mirror the polarized political atmosphere in society, divided between those who support the country’s entrepreneurial achievements and those who challenge them. Nonetheless, pragmatic reasons, rather than anti-state emotions, such as the state’s problematic intervention in the ecosystem, fueled these criticisms. More crucially, the paper contributes to the literature on institutional determinants of entrepreneurship legitimacy by demonstrating a direct and meaningful association between state and entrepreneurship legitimacy.

title: Energy Security vs. Food Inflation: An Empirical Analysis of Crop-Substitution and Price Spillover Effects in India's E20 Ethanol Expansion
abstract: India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme has advanced from a marginal 1.14–1.53 per cent blending rate in 2013–14 to the statutory 20 per cent (E20) target by Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025–26, five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. This rapid scale-up has been accompanied by an equally rapid structural shift in feedstock composition: official data show the share of grain-based ethanol (maize, rice, and damaged food grain) rising from roughly 9 per cent of total procurement in ESY 2020–21 to nearly 60 per cent by early ESY 2024–25, with industry-association estimates placing maize's individual share alone at approximately 50 per cent by ESY 2024–25, up from 6.2 per cent two years earlier. This paper examines the resulting energy-security-versus-food-inflation trade-off using officially reported and peer-reviewed data. It synthesises the National Policy on Biofuels (2018, amended 2022), the NITI Aayog Roadmap for Ethanol Blending in India 2020–25, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) blending statistics, USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) maize market data, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and Ministry of Finance inflation reporting, and a 2026 peer-reviewed partial-equilibrium modelling study (published in PLOS One by researchers at the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, and the FABLE Consortium). The analysis finds credible evidence of crop-substitution pressure — a 14.7 per cent year-on-year decline in maize production coinciding with record consumption, an 84 per cent collapse in maize exports, and open-market maize prices exceeding the government's minimum support price by approximately 11 per cent in April 2024 — alongside documented cumulative energy-security gains of over ₹1.36–1.59 lakh crore in foreign exchange savings. However, the paper finds that a direct, India-specific econometric (VAR/Granger) estimate of ethanol-to-food-price transmission does not yet exist in the peer-reviewed literature; this study is accordingly framed as a literature- and data-grounded empirical synthesis rather than primary econometric estimation, and it explicitly flags this gap as a priority for future research. Policy recommendations centre on feedstock diversification toward 2G/cellulosic ethanol, protection of grain buffer stocks, and integration of food-price monitoring into the biofuel roadmap.

title: Validation of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale and Autonomy Scale among People with Long-Term Care Needs
authors: Takazumi Ono, Hiroko Costantini, Shinichiro Kumagaya, Ikuko Sugawara, Katsuya Iijima, Misato Nihei
abstract: Social relationships with surrounding people and an individual's autonomy are fundamental components of age-friendly community and long-term care (LTC). The objective of the present study was to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale (TSS) and Autonomy Scales (AS) among people with LTC needs. We distributed a self-administered questionnaire to four daycare/day-services facilities and three home-visit nurse stations in Japan. The TSS consists of 20 items under 4 factors and the AS includes 20 items based on 3 factors. These scales were previously validated in the Japanese general population. 259 people participated in the survey. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated model fit for the TSS was good, whereas that for the AS was acceptable. In addition, explanatory factor analysis demonstrated that the AS had 2-factor structure specified for people with LTC. The regression coefficients for subjective well-being were 0.43 (95%CI 0.23, 0.62) and 0.73 (95%CI 0.50, 0.96), respectively. The alphas in the TSS and the AS ranged from 0.75 to 0.88, from 0.53 to 0.91, respectively. The alphas of the AS in first and second factors specified for people with LTC needs were 0.91 and 0.70, respectively. In conclusion, the TSS and the AS were valid and reliable in people with LTC needs. However, regarding the AS, different factor structures should be used (the structure in general population and that specified in people with LTC needs) depending on the purpose of the assessment. In addition, further studies to assess test-retest reliability and measurement error are needed.

title: Von Neumann’s Blurry Elephant: On The Need for Care and Clarity in Modeling Complex Social Systems
abstract: Wildman and Shults have laid out an ambitious scope for their book, Modeling Religion: Simulating the Transformation of Worldviews, Lifeways, and Civilization. I laud their aims and echo their enthusiasm for modeling. However, I also believe that Wildman and Shults largely fail to achieve their goals. Their models are neither clear nor well justified, and so their results are not compelling. The book’s value is in the attempt, and in the discussions which are based more on interpretations of empirical data than on conclusions from the published models. I believe it will be instructive to explain why I think the goals of the book were not achieved. To do so, I will first explain a bit about how the models work. I will then discuss general guidelines for the use of formal models to understand complex social dynamics, and how Wildman Shults fail to meet them.

title: Resilience: Understand Breakdown, Foster Recovery, and Choose the Right Perspective
abstract: Resilience denotes the capacity of a system to withstand shocks and to recover from them. We distinguish between two different types of dynamics. The first allows for a separation between phases of normalcy and phases of rapid breakdown followed by slow recovery. The second applies to volatile organizations in which such phases are intertwined. Breakdown is often self-inflicted. Situation awareness is impaired by psychological mechanisms that lead to incorrect expectations regarding societal dynamics. Through positive feedback, the failure of a few elements is amplified into a failure cascade. However, positive feedback can also be harnessed to enable recovery. In volatile systems, resilience must be understood as an emergent property arising from the interaction of agents. This necessitates a data-driven approach to inform agent-based models, drawing on repositories, knowledge graphs, or tools from artificial intelligence. Such models help demonstrate that resilience represents a compromise between robustness and adaptivity. Maximizing performance frequently comes at the expense of resilience, and second-order solutions aimed at transforming the system prove more promising than attempts to reconstruct past conditions.

title: Varieties of democratic vulnerability: a comparative study of checks and balances and popular acceptance of transgressions
authors: Honorata Mazepus, Magnus Feldmann, Giovanni D'Agostino
abstract: The recent wave of democratic backsliding has demonstrated that liberal democracies are vulnerable to subversion by authoritarian leaders. Research showed that democratically elected leaders remove checks and balances that constrain their power. One of the explanations why leaders can violate democratic rules focuses on the response of citizens who trade off democracy for partisan and policy gains. This article investigates cross-country differences in vulnerabilities to democratic backsliding by comparing democratic priority profiles of citizens and the patterns of approval for transgressions of democratic rules. We use observational evidence from online surveys with large quota-based samples of citizens in a two-party presidential system (USA, N > 1700), a multi-party parliamentary system based on proportional representation with some semi-presidential features (Poland, N >1800), and a consociational parliamentary system based on proportional representation (Netherlands, N = > 2100). To complement observational evidence, we test experimentally some of these aggregate-level differences: next to partisanship and policy gains, we also manipulate different democratic transgressions (protest rights and decree powers) and measure their effects on government approval in the three countries. Our results show that citizens of different countries have different democratic priority profiles and differ in their disapproval of specific transgressions. Although overall transgressions are not rewarded, and citizens are mostly vigilant and disapproving of violating democratic rules, we find both observational and experimental evidence indicating that liberal democracies can have different vulnerabilities that relate to the democratic attitudes of citizens.

title: Catch the Patient, Not the AI: Collective Sensemaking in an Online Health Community
abstract: Patients and caregivers increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical reports, weigh care decisions, and seek emotional support. Yet most research treats patient-facing AI as a private exchange between a user and a system, leaving open how AI-related content is taken up once users carry it back into the peer communities where they already make sense of illness. This study examines collective sensemaking around AI in House086, China's largest online community for lymphoma patients and caregivers. We identified roughly 400 publicly accessible discussion threads (2014 to 2026) through AI-related keyword searches and manual screening, extracted them into structured case profiles using a schema-prompted large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, deployed via AWS Bedrock), and conducted mixed-method analysis. After quality control, the verified analytic sample comprised 337 post-ChatGPT records focused on widespread conversational-AI use. Members most often reported using AI for informational support, followed by second opinions and psychosocial support. Although members often introduced AI favorably, roughly one in six described feeling overwhelmed by AI output. When other members responded, they frequently engaged the poster's underlying medical or emotional intent while leaving the AI dimension unaddressed. The tendency to bypass AI persisted even in threads seeking triangulation between AI output and other information sources, and when posters shared overwhelmed or unfavorable experiences with AI. On the occasions when members did discuss the AI, they were more often cautious than endorsing. Rather than auditing AI output for factual accuracy, the community more often worked to deflate the false certainty it produced, placing a single AI answer back among multiple sources of judgment. This study argues that AI does not replace the interpretive work of online health communities, nor is it systematically audited by them. Instead, it shifts the locus of sensemaking downstream, so that the community continues to catch the person even when it does not catch the AI, and the interpretive authority that follows does not settle in any single place. We discuss implications for CSCW theory, online-community norms, and patient-facing AI design.

title: Full Reporting in Empirical Asset Pricing: A Statistical Decision-Theoretic Approach
abstract: This study develops a full-reporting framework for empirical asset pricing grounded in statistical decision theory. In the abductive stage, simulated pseudo-factor model spaces are used to evaluate whether candidate test scores can distinguish valid from invalid model states through likelihood behavior, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and classification metrics. In the inductive stage, realized sample scores are mapped to likelihood ratios, error rates, and decision criteria, translating observed evidence into model-state predictions. Reporting this complete inferential chain enables test performance and realized evidence to be integrated into transparent assessments of factor-model validity.

title: Brechas de observabilidad en la vigilancia del riesgo psicosocial laboral en América Latina: fundamentos para una arquitectura dinámica con evidencia desde Chile
abstract: Periodic psychosocial risk assessment systems share a limitation that is architectural rather than psychometric: the aggregation function that produces the organizational indicator irreversibly destroys spatial information about the state of the internal units composing it, regardless of instrument quality or measurement frequency. This paper reports a simulation study with empirical calibration that tests four confirmatory hypotheses, declared a priori, using an agent-based model formalized under the ODD 2020 protocol and calibrated with CEAL-SM 2023 data (N=768,505 Chilean workers). The model demonstrates that concentrated deterioration in a minority of organizational units produces a Spatial Dilution Ratio of up to 4.11×, rendering it either fully invisible (existential gap) or detectable but unlocalizable (granularity gap) to periodic aggregate assessment, while uniformly distributed deterioration produces convergence between architectures — confirming by inversion that the gap is spatial, not temporal. This paper proposes DYNOR (Dynamic Organizational Risk Surveillance Framework) to occupy the follow-up step of the standard five-step preventive cycle in Latin America, operating continuously between periodic assessment anchors rather than replacing them. The framework is directly relevant for normative systems in Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru, Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil.

title: The Changing Role of Major Stakeholders: A Review of Publisher, Vendor, and Institutional Adaptation in the Scholarly Communication Ecosystem
abstract: This article reviews the changing roles of major stakeholders in the scholarly communication ecosystem, focusing on publishers, vendors, and academic institutions. The rapid growth of digital technologies, open access initiatives, and evolving researcher expectations have significantly transformed traditional scholarly communication practices. Through a critical review of existing literature, this study examines how these stakeholders redefine their responsibilities and adopt adaptation strategies to remain relevant in a dynamic academic environment. The analysis highlights key strategies such as business model innovation, service redesign, policy reform, and technological integration as central to effective adaptation. The findings indicate that publishers increasingly function as service providers, vendors play a vital role in technological infrastructure and analytics, and institutions adopt more active roles in research dissemination and support. This review concludes that sustained collaboration and continuous adaptation among publishers, vendors, and institutions are essential for developing an efficient, accessible, and sustainable scholarly communication ecosystem.

title: A Certification Gate for Emerging-Topic Detection: Pre-Registration, Negative Controls, and a Second-Domain Transfer Test on arXiv
abstract: Methods for detecting emerging research topics keep multiplying, but they are rarely validated against ground truth chosen independently of the method: most are assessed on internal coherence or a few hand-picked success stories. This paper contributes not a new detector but a certification gate, a pre-registered, negative-controlled validation protocol any emergence detector can be run through. Before results are seen, the gate fixes (i) a binary "flagged rising" criterion, (ii) an externally-sourced positive set and a matched negative-control set, and (iii) Wilson-95% reporting of recall, specificity and precision. Applied to the temporal component of a five-dimension emergence system over arXiv stat.ML (2018–2023; 76 topics), the gate yields recall 93% (14/15, Wilson 95% [70,99]) and specificity 100% (13/13, [77,100]). The identical protocol is then run on a second, structurally different domain (arXiv cs.CR; 2018–2023; 129 topics) under a benchmark frozen and timestamped before scoring. This is a transfer test, not a replication: with only two domains it characterises how the protocol behaves out-of-corpus, not whether the first result reproduces. Recall falls to 62% (10/16, [39,82]) and specificity to 69% (9/13, [42,87]); pooled, recall is 77% (24/31, [60,89]) and specificity 85% (22/26, [66,94]). The intervals are wide by construction: at these n the benchmark is underpowered to rank detectors and demonstrates only the gate. The honest degradation is the point: a validation that reported 100% on one corpus and hid the second would be the overfitting it claims to detect. The protocol, both benchmarks with timestamp proofs, and a disclosed pre-scoring amendment are released, and the gate's numbers are reported with and without that amendment.

title: Reconstructing Sexual Economy: The role of Women in the subsistence of Sex Work and Tourism and the Rise of Single Mothers in The Philippines
abstract: This paper examines the Philippine sexual economy through a structural sociological and historical lens, arguing that commercial sex work is not merely an outcome of individual choice or moral failure but a rational adaptation to intersecting historical, economic, and institutional constraints. Drawing upon interdisciplinary literature from sociology, history, gender studies, public policy, and human rights, the study traces the evolution of the Philippine sexual economy from Spanish colonial rule and the institutionalization of prostitution around American military bases to its contemporary integration within global tourism. It demonstrates how persistent poverty, gender-segmented labor markets, discriminatory employment practices, and inadequate social welfare systems have made sex work a significant strategy of female household subsistence. The paper further examines how these structural conditions contribute to the growth of solo motherhood and the enduring marginalization of Amerasian children abandoned by foreign military personnel and tourists. It argues that the coexistence of criminalization, anti-trafficking legislation, and external geopolitical influence has produced a policy framework that simultaneously punishes, victimizes, and silences sex workers while denying them labor rights and limiting effective public health interventions. Rather than framing prostitution solely as a criminal justice or moral issue, the analysis situates it within broader systems of political economy, gender inequality, and postcolonial governance. The paper concludes by proposing evidence-based structural reforms, including labor market expansion, strengthened support for solo mothers, rights-based legal reform, and greater accountability for the historical legacies of foreign military intervention. By reframing the Philippine sexual economy as a structural rather than individual phenomenon, this study contributes to broader debates on gender, labor, postcolonial development, and the sociology of informal economies.

title: The Precarious Center: Structural Vulnerability and the Economic Squeeze of South Asia’s Lower Middle Class
abstract: This paper examines the lower middle class in South Asia as a structurally vulnerable “missing middle” caught between extreme poverty and genuine income security. It argues that conventional middle-class definitions often obscure the fragility of households that earn too much to qualify for targeted welfare yet too little to access private health care, quality education, or reliable financial protection. Drawing on evidence from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and West Bengal, the paper shows how this group is squeezed by informal employment, exclusion from social protection, catastrophic out-of-pocket health costs, rising education expenses, regressive taxation, inflation, and debt dependence. It also highlights how remittances, asset ownership, and consumer goods can create a false impression of security while masking deep exposure to economic shocks. The paper concludes that although the extreme poor remain the most deprived in absolute terms, the lower middle class is arguably the most systemically neglected and precariously positioned segment in South Asia, trapped in a cycle of permanent vulnerability without a stable path to upward mobility.

title: Equal Protection or Conceptual Conformity? Global Gender Governance, Norm Translation and Cultural Sovereignty
abstract: Global gender governance has expanded from instruments centred on women’s legal equality and protection from sex-based discrimination to a heterogeneous field encompassing gender mainstreaming, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, sexuality education, institutional inclusion and gender-transformative programming. This article asks when such expansion represents legitimate human-rights protection and when transnational norm transfer risks becoming conceptual conformity. It combines a critical integrative review of 42 scholarly works with structured analysis of 29 primary policy instruments issued by global, regional and national institutions. Searches were conducted through five pre-specified OpenAlex queries and reported using a PRISMA-adapted, transparently bounded design. The analysis distinguishes a universal protection floor, context-dependent institutional measures and contested anthropological propositions. It finds no evidence of a single, centrally coordinated global command structure. It does identify polycentric conceptual expansion, soft-law diffusion, donor and reputational leverage, and forms of localisation whose practical openness varies considerably. Global norms have provided indispensable resources against violence, exclusion and sex-based inequality; they can also blur the boundary between protecting persons and requiring assent to disputed accounts of sex, identity, embodiment and family. The article develops a fifteen-test Conceptual Sovereignty and Gender Governance Framework to assess dignity, safety, evidence, authority, participation, translation, non-compulsion, proportionality, women’s rights, minority protection, conscience, democratic legitimacy, conditionality and reviewability. Equal dignity, it argues, requires robust protection without making conceptual uniformity the price of civic inclusion.

title: Introduction: a palette of meaningful art-science interactions
abstract: This introductory chapter frames the central question guiding the volume: what makes an art–science interaction meaningful? It outlines how this guiding question emerged within the PALETTES research environment, an inter- and transdisciplinary project that brings together researchers from different backgrounds, artists, and cultural practitioners in collaborative exchanges within and beyond academia. Recognizing that art-science interactions are multifaceted and context-dependent, the book explores meaningfulness through different disciplinary and practice-based perspectives. Against this background, the chapter positions the book within ongoing debates on art–science collaboration and epistemic diversity, and situates its scope, rationale, and distinctive features in relation to the current state of the art (and science). It discusses the positioning of art as an epistemic practice in its own right as central to the book’s approach, critically addressing the risk of instrumentalization when art is reduced to serving as a tool for predefined scientific goals. The book examines how art and science can enrich one another as distinct yet interacting ways of knowing. The chapter also reflects on the collaborative conditions under which the chapters were developed, showing how they emerged through sustained dialogue, co-creative activities, and iterative exchange. The contributions thus reflect the very collaborative processes they seek to examine at a meta-level. The chapter further clarifies its intended audiences and concludes with a reflection on the approach to composing the book, including the principles that guided the selection and development of the contributions, as well as on the composition and structure of the book itself, explaining how the volume is organized without fixed thematic divisions, and how this structuring can be understood as a curatorial practice that makes visible the relations between contributions. It also provides a brief overview of the chapters and their respective lenses, followed by cross-chapter connections that offer orientation for navigating the volume as a whole.

title: The Halo of Presentation: A Six-Month Autoethnographic Case Study of Self-Presentation, Peer Perception, and Social Evaluation Among Adolescent Peers
abstract: Human beings continually evaluate one another using observable cues such as appearance, clothing, grooming, posture, confidence, and interpersonal behavior. These evaluations frequently dictate the trajectory of social interactions long before substantial verbal communication occurs. Although psychological research has extensively examined first impressions and interpersonal perception in controlled laboratory settings, comparatively few qualitative studies explore how deliberate alterations in self-presentation influence everyday social dynamics within an established adolescent peer group over an extended longitudinal period. This six-month qualitative autoethnographic case study (January–June 2026) investigates these dynamics within a naturally occurring secondary school environment. Acting simultaneously as researcher and participant within a stable core friendship group, I systematically modified outward self-presentation across two equal, contrasting phases. Phase One (January–March) established a baseline characterized by disciplined grooming, regular exercise, curated clothing, confident posture, and low approval-seeking behavior.
