Phase Two (April–June) introduced deliberate reductions in grooming, repetitive clothing usage, unmaintained hair growth, lower social confidence, and heightened people-pleasing behaviors. Digital field notes documented everyday interactions. Qualitative thematic comparison revealed marked shifts: Phase One corresponded with higher perceived respect, frequent social invitations, and sustained conversational engagement. Conversely, Phase Two corresponded with increased teasing, social distancing, and diminished conversational engagement, with shifts becoming noticeable 11–17 days post-modification. These findings are analyzed through established sociopsychological frameworks, including the Halo Effect, Impression Management, Expectancy Violations Theory, and Status Characteristics Theory. While acknowledging the inherent limitations of a single-subject autoethnographic design, this study provides a transparent lived account demonstrating how outward presentation actively negotiates adolescent peer evaluation.

title: THE FORMATION OF THE U.S. HEGEMONIC REVOLUTIONARY BLOC
abstract: This article examines the formation and transformation of the revolutionary hegemonic bloc in colonial America during the period 1763-1776. Drawing on Antonio Gramsci's theory of hegemony, the analysis conceptualizes the American Revolution as a process of formation of class alliances among heterogeneous social classes under conditions of crisis. The article argues that revolutionary unity did not emerge spontaneously nor through elite manipulation alone, but through a prolonged and conflictual process in which merchants, large landowners, and lawyers articulated a hegemonic project capable of incorporating artisans and yeomen, while simultaneously containing popular radicalism. Using a structural-historical approach, the article distinguishes between two phases of the revolutionary crisis: an initial phase characterized by a fragmented and decentralized bloc organized around negative unity and resistance to British taxation (1763-1774), and a second phase marked by the institutionalization of the hegemonic bloc through the Continental Congress, provincial conventions, and committees of safety (1774-1776). The analysis highlights the central role of institutional mediation, the relative autonomy of political and ideological processes, and the strategic sacrifice of short-term economic interests by leading classes in order to sustain bloc cohesion. By demonstrating how hegemony can be constructed and exercised in the absence of a consolidated state, the article contributes to historical sociology and offers a theoretically grounded reinterpretation of the American Revolution as a case of pre-state hegemonic formation.

title: Consumer Protection Governance in Gendered Markets: Appearance Pressure, Consumer Awareness, and Gender-Differentiated Pricing in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula Tricity, India
abstract: Gender-differentiated pricing, commonly termed the "Pink Tax," describes situations in which comparable products or services are priced differently by gender. While prior research has documented such price differences, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms shaping how consumers experience them. Drawing on the Political Economy of Beauty and consumer protection governance frameworks, this study examines how appearance pressure, gendered consumption behavior, and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior relate to experienced gender-differentiated pricing among 151 consumers surveyed in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula tricity, India. Using exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the results indicate that appearance pressure (β = .407, p < .001) and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior (β = .320, p < .001) significantly predicted experienced gender-differentiated pricing, while gendered consumption behavior did not (β = .128, p = .120), together explaining 44.6% of the variance. These findings suggest that consumers' experiences of differential pricing are shaped more by social expectations around appearance and price awareness than by purchasing behavior alone. Robustness checks (Harman's single-factor test, variance inflation factors, and bootstrapped confidence intervals) support the stability of these results. Given the study's convenience sample and cross-sectional design, findings are presented as exploratory rather than generalizable, with implications framed as hypotheses for future regulatory attention rather than settled policy prescriptions. The study contributes an interdisciplinary behavioral perspective to consumer protection governance research in the Indian context.

title: Evaluating the Youth Outcomes and Change Pathways of “Walk With Me”, a Peer Support Programme for Youths With or at Risk of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Singapore
authors: Lyon Koh, Gerard Chung, Elizabeth Yee Min Chia, Anusha Agarwal, Sophie Cheng
abstract: Introduction: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is common among youth and often serves social functions, yet most young people avoid formal services and turn to peers first. Walk With Me (WWM), a journey-based peer support programme in Singapore, pairs trained volunteers with youths who have or are at risk of NSSI. This study evaluated youth outcomes. Methods: Using a mixed-method, single-group, pre–post design, 36 youths (aged 15–25; 72% female) completed surveys before and after the programme. Eight outcomes spanning interpersonal and emotion-regulation domains were assessed, four theory-of-change pathways were tested and open-ended responses were analysed qualitatively. Results: All outcomes improved significantly from pre- to post-test, with medium to large effects; the largest gains were in emotion regulation and coping, and younger participants showed greater resilience gains. The four hypothesised change pathways were supported or partially supported; notably, encouragement to reach out predicted increased support-seeking. Youths rated their peer-supporter relationship highly, and qualitative accounts echoed these gains. Conclusion: WWM is linked to meaningful improvements in youths' social skills, support-seeking, communication, and emotion regulation, appearing to operate through a gradual peer relationship. As one of the first studies to test these mechanisms, it offers a promising foundation for rigorous evaluation.

title: Dynamics of Skill Mismatch in the Workplace: Longitudinal Evidence from a Medium-Sized Japanese Company
abstract: Although skill mismatch in the labor market is an important topic of discussion and research worldwide, that phenomenon in the Japanese labor market or organizations remains to be fully elucidated, despite the fact that Japan has a distinctive employment system. Therefore, using newly available data, such as longitudinal personnel data and employee satisfaction survey data, this study investigates the existence and determinants of vertical skill mismatch in a typical medium-sized Japanese company in order to address the dearth of similar literature in Japan. As a result, this study shows the vertical skill mismatch of frequent occurrence. Additionally, empirical results reveal: 1) job autonomy decreases the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; 2) supervisors’ precise advice related to business activities for their subordinates reduces the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; and 3) communication among employees in the workplace increases accessibility to skill matched roles. Career development in the Japanese company may not reflect a linear progression from easy work to more difficult work, but may rather be more of a mixed change involving under- and over-skilled mismatching.

title: Lessons from Tanzania’s Ujamaa for Smart Settlements in Nepal: Social Justice and Economic Development
abstract: This article examines lessons Nepal can draw from Tanzania’s experience with Ujamaa, the African socialist development model initiated by President Nyerere in 1967. Using comparative policy analysis, published research, official documents, and exploratory field observations from selected Tanzanian locations, including the capital and villages in the Iringa Region, the study evaluates Ujamaa’s achievements and limitations. It assesses their relevance for Nepal’s landless populations and smart-settlement initiatives. The analysis focuses primarily on rural and peri-urban development and does not examine urban squatter housing and rural-to-urban migration. The comparison demonstrates that some lessons from Tanzania can be considered for Nepal’s own program. Ujamaa contributed to national integration, a shared linguistic identity, literacy, primary education, and rural services. However, it also reduced household autonomy, disrupted existing livelihood systems, and failed to achieve sustained agricultural productivity, employment generation, and income growth. The article also briefly discusses Nepal’s own Go to the Village Campaign of 1967, which had mixed success, and Korea’s generally successful 1970 Saemaul Undong movement for a comparative perspective of village-oriented national programs. The article proposes a Smart Settlement Framework for Nepal based on verified beneficiary identification, differentiated tenure and housing options, voluntary participation, livelihood-oriented site selection, serviced land, cooperative enterprise, accountable local governance, and measurable pathways from social protection to economic mobility.

title: A New Prescription, Not a New Frame: Single Religious Belonging in Taiwan
abstract: Social surveys commonly measure single religious belonging (SRB). Critics suggest SRB fails to group religionists meaningfully outside the West, where hybrid religiosity is normal. This study challenges that premise. Using the 2023 Taiwan Social Change Survey, I find SRB predicts 25 of 27 religiosity outcomes. Its power may vary. SRB separates Christians from everyone else almost perfectly, and Yiguandao just as well. Protestants and Chinese traditions rarely cross the Jesus worshipping boundary. And while Buddhists, Daoists and folk religionists share one pantheon, they rank it differently and follow different rules on diet, pilgrimage and initiation, so plural worship may mark syncretism rather than plural belonging. I then test whether granularity of SRB matters. Asking more denomination and taking refuge questions moves Buddhists and folk religionists between categories, but does not change the predicted pattern. Where SRB is thin, the remedy is a finer question about practice, not more boxes.

title: Family Systems Intelligence in Neurodevelopmental Disability Care: A Conceptual Framework for Family-Centered Service
abstract: Systems intelligence (Doherty, 2024; Doherty et al., 2026) offers a pathway for understanding how people perceive and act within complex interconnected systems. This article applies that concept to neurodevelopmental disability (NDD) service systems, where families and professionals coordinate care across clinical, educational, disability, and community contexts. We propose six components of family-centered interventions that build systems intelligence: systemic perception and self-positioning, shared interpretation, role negotiation, coordinated action, feedback responsiveness, and transferable capability. Three examples of family-centered approaches illustrate complementary pathways for developing systems intelligence across family, professional, and service-system relationships. The framework describes systems intelligence as a shared family-service capacity and identifies practical directions for research, training, service design, and equity.

title: The Illiberal Academy: Typologies of Illiberal Institutions of Higher Learning
abstract: As political illiberalism becomes a more prominent feature of contemporary democratic and hybrid political systems, the consequences that these emerging political forces have for institutions of higher education are only beginning to be explored. Universities occupy a central position in the ideological struggle for cultural hegemony: they produce knowledge, train elites, socialize large numbers of students, and shape the discursive environment. Illiberal movements recognize this and in addition to restricting the academic freedoms of university systems at large, also use these institutions as metapolitical instruments for achieving hegemony in both liberal democratic and authoritarian settings. Existing research offers little in terms of systematic frameworks for understanding the diversity of these organizations, which tend to be analyzed using case studies. This article addresses this gap by comparing illiberal universities across the US, EU and Russia and classifies them into four ideal types based on two primary factors: their origins and their funding sources which, we argue, influence the functions, incentive structures, and relations to political power for these universities. According to these two primary factors, we show that each ideal type operates according to a specific organizational logic. These findings demonstrate cross-national evidence for the multifaceted way in which illiberal movements engage with universities in the “third wave of autocratization.”

title: Climate Action At Any Cost? Environmental Concern, Economic Trade-offs, and Regime Preferences
abstract: Climate change confronts democratic governments with a difficult tension between effective climate action, economic prosperity, and democracy. But does this political trilemma also appear in citizens’ regime preferences? This paper examines how perceived climate threat and willingness to prioritize environmental protection over economic growth relate with support for democracy, technocracy, autocracy, and military rule. Using original comparative survey data collected in 2025 across eight European countries, I identify five profiles of regime preferences through cluster analysis and use multinomial regressions to examine how climate attitudes relate to profile membership. I find that low willingness to prioritize environmental protection over economic growth is associated with greater openness to autocratic forms of rule, including military rule, and that this association becomes substantially stronger as perceived climate threat increases. By contrast, when high climate threat is accompanied by high willingness to prioritize environmental protection even at the expense of economic growth, technocratic orientations prevail. These findings suggest that the institutional climate-growth-democracy trilemma may indeed have an individual-level counterpart: climate urgency is associated with different regime-preference profiles depending on citizens’ willingness to trade economic growth for environmental protection.

title: The state of the research on parents with disabilities' involvement in the child protection system: A comprehensive review
abstract: Background: This article provides a comprehensive overview of the global peer-reviewed research literature on the involvement of parents with disabilities in child protection. Materials: Using a systematic scoping review methodology that initially retrieved 10,471 articles, we identified 135 peer-reviewed articles. We charted the articles based on publication year, location of study, discipline, type of parental disability, methods, aspect of child protection studies, and whose voice was centered in the study. Results: We found a sharp global and cross-disciplinary increase in articles on this topic since 2010, with studies conducted in 17 countries and published in journals related to disability, child welfare, social work, mental health, and health. The majority focus on parents with intellectual and developmental disabilities or mental health disabilities. The most common areas of inquiry were the prevalence of child protection involvement and out-of-home care. Less common were articles about child protection processes, such as reporting, assessment, substantiation, services, case disposition, court processes, recurrence, and intervention. Most of the data used in the studies came from the professionals’ perspectives. Conclusion: Our study highlights significant gaps in the research and underscores the need for new directions in this field.

title: From Business Accounting to Market Valuations
abstract: In this study, we examine how accounting variables represent the core elements of firm activity and how the relations among these variables connect business accounting to market valuation. Building on this account, we develop a unified framework that expresses market values in accounting terms. A key contribution of this framework is that it places market-based and book-based measures of return within a single coherent structure. This unification, in turn, provides a new theoretical basis for refining central principles in corporate finance and valuation.

title: Exact Linear Present Value
abstract: In this study, we propose an exact, level-based counterpart to the widely used loglinear present value framework. This level-based framework preserves the core economic content of the loglinear approach while eliminating the need for approximation. The framework, however, goes beyond exactness. It also allows a richer analysis of price dynamics. Price changes are separated into anticipated movements and expectation revisions, and each component is further decomposed into cash-flow and discount-rate contributions. We apply the framework empirically to characterize aggregate stock price movements.

title: Changing Relationship and Marriage Beliefs Across Partnership Formation Transitions in Germany
abstract: This study explores changes in partnership and marriage beliefs across the life course in Germany. We conceptualize and empirically investigate relationship formation transitions as a mechanism for changing partnership and marriage beliefs, as they may reinforce or weaken cohort replacement effects. Adaptations in relationship beliefs may result either from increasing correspondence or unplanned contradictions of own relationship trajectories with “chrononormative” ideals around the standardized life cycle. We use fixed-effects panel data models based on the German pairfam data (2008-2022, N=11,705 respondents) to study how individuals’ partnership and marriage beliefs change across relationship formation transitions. Across LAT-entry and entry into cohabitation, beliefs in emotional benefits of partnerships increase, while beliefs in restrictions and stress decrease. Beliefs in financial benefits of partnerships increase when individuals enter cohabitation or marriage. Already with entry into LAT-relationships and cohabitation, support for marriage as a lifelong union rises moderately. Across entry into marriage, approval of marriage increases further, while nonmarital alternatives are viewed more critically. These adaptations following entry into marriage are more pronounced in East than West Germany. Our findings point to a strong couple norm and only partial deinstitutionalization and widespread approval of marriage.

title: Characterizing Canadian Out-of-district Political Donations from 2015 to 2024
abstract: Federal political representation in Canada is geographical: one Member of Parliament (MP) represents one electoral district. Despite this representational structure, Canadians can legally donate to a host of political entities, regardless of proximity. Using a public dataset from Elections Canada’s Open Data on Contributions matched with census data from Statistics Canada, we characterize broad patterns in Canadian out-of-district donation from 2015 to 2024. We find that out-of-district donations form a persistent share of donor-sourced funding to both candidates and district associations, averaging 40% across time, election periods, and party lines. While relatively constant through time, the propensity for out-of-district donation varies substantially across districts, beyond what spatial proximity alone would predict. Districts with higher population density, median household income, educational attainment, and visible minority proportions see higher rates of out-of-district giving, the same traits that predict donor prevalence generally in Canada. Despite its frequency, out-of-district donation in Canada remain largely regionalized; nearly half of donations that leave their district are received by a political entity in a neighbouring one, and few cross provincial lines. These and other findings provide a helpful characterization of this largely undocumented facet of Canadian political financing, and inform further research on effective representation in Canada and other nations with similar representational structures.

title: Science through an artistic lens: scientific aesthetics and aesthetic exhibition practices with kinetic art installations in science museums
authors: Na Zhang, Priscilla Van Even, Huang Yaping
abstract: This chapter examines scientific aesthetics and the role of artistic mediation in contemporary science exhibitions, with a particular focus on kinetic art installations, a dynamic form of art that relies on movement and expressive motion. It situates aesthetic exhibition practices within the growing paradigm of experiential learning in science museums, which marks a shift from traditional top-down information transfer toward interactive exchange, as well as cognitive, sensorial, and aesthetic engagement of museum visitors through exhibition design. Rather than presenting science as static information to be passively absorbed, such exhibitions invite visitors to feel, reflect, and interpret through sensorial stimulation and meaningful cognitive engagement, reshaping how scientific knowledge is communicated, experienced, and understood. Drawing on the vision of the Exploratorium, a museum of science, art, and human perception founded by Frank Oppenheimer, the chapter approaches art and science as complementary modes of revealing and exploring natural phenomena. Through a series of case studies in science museums where kinetic art installations function as artistic mediation, the chapter explores how these artworks communicate scientific ideas through metaphor, movement, and interaction. These examples demonstrate how artistic mediation can render complex processes tangible and participatory. Together, they show how aesthetic exhibition practices foster active meaning-making and position science as a dynamic, interpretative process.

title: The Politics of Crime Prevention: Evidence from Colombia
abstract: Why do governments prevent crime in some places while neglecting others? Crime prevention policies are often viewed as too slow, diffuse, and politically intangible to generate electoral rewards. When implemented, existing research suggests they primarily serve to reward co-partisans or mobilize ideologically aligned voters. This article challenges that view by arguing that incumbents allocate crime-prevention resources to electorally competitive municipalities because these investments yield electoral returns. Using detailed project-level data from Colombia, I show that national incumbents disproportionately direct crime-prevention funds to municipalities where recent presidential elections were closely contested, rather than to areas with higher crime rates or strong partisan loyalties. I then demonstrate that these allocations increase the vote share of the right-wing incumbent coalition in subsequent elections. Drawing on quantitative analyses and interviews with policymakers and bureaucrats, I argue that these effects operate primarily through the visibility and attribution of crime prevention projects, particularly those aligned with right-wing issue ownership of public security.

title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

title: Stable Contexts Are Not Static Causes: A Latent Variable Approach to Time-Varying Consequences of Stable Unobserved Heterogeneity
abstract: Urban-health studies increasingly examine environmental co-occurrences, but longitudinal analyses often rely on fixed-effects (FE) models whose assumptions about stable unobserved heterogeneity are left implicit. This article uses a structural equation modeling (SEM) representation of FE to clarify a narrow but important point: stable, time-invariant, unobserved heterogeneity is controlled by conventional FE only when its contribution to repeated outcomes is also constant across waves. When stable histories of segregation, infrastructure, or governance have changing consequences as environmental co-occurrence configurations are reorganized, conventional FE models may leave residual confounding. I review the classical fixed-effects structural equation modeling (FE-SEM) representation, then present two diagnostic extensions: time-varying-loading FE-SEM (TVL-FE-SEM), a single-latent-dimension model with wave-specific loadings, and constant-and-deviation-loading FE-SEM (CDL-FE-SEM), a two-latent-dimension model that adapts the intercept/slope logic of latent growth modeling to separate common and deviation-loading profiles. A compact Monte Carlo simulation shows that classical FE-SEM recovers the true effect only when stable unobserved heterogeneity enters repeated outcomes with constant loadings, TVL-FE-SEM performs well when the same single latent source has changing loadings, and CDL-FE-SEM helps diagnose whether stable heterogeneity operates through more than one loading profile under a fixed-effects specification, though with finite-sample instability. An empirical illustration using Korean community-health data from 2021–2024 demonstrates the sequence as a diagnostic workflow.

title: Dealing with Factor Mismeasurement
abstract: Empirical implementation of asset pricing models faces a fundamental constraint. The true pricing factors implied by theory are unobservable, so researchers must rely on observable empirical factors. Because these factors are only proxies, they may contain measurement errors that distort estimated factor exposures, risk premia, and assessments of model performance. This study examines factor measurement errors and develops a methodology for assessing their empirical consequences. The methodology allows researchers to evaluate the reliability of asset pricing tests more carefully and draw more credible conclusions from empirical evidence.

title: Shifting toward a Micro ICAPM
abstract: Intertemporal asset pricing models typically begin with the market factor and introduce additional state variables to capture changes in investment opportunities over time. Empirically, these state variables have traditionally been proxied by macroeconomic variables because they reflect broad shifts in economic conditions affecting the aggregate opportunity set. These proxies are useful at the aggregate level, but less suited to representing variation in investment opportunities across individual assets. This study therefore develops a micro-level approach that replaces macroeconomic proxies with asset-specific variables. The central idea is that a broad set of such variables can more fully represent individual, time-varying investment opportunities.

title: Out of the APT Shadow
abstract: In empirical asset pricing, researchers often evaluate a pricing theory through its empirical factor model. This practice is widespread, but rests on a strong premise: the factor model must be a valid empirical proxy for the theory it claims to implement. In most applications, this premise is assumed rather than verified. Good performance alone is not decisive, because a factor model may reflect equilibrium pricing, arbitrage pricing, or both. This study addresses this ambiguity by separating risks arising solely from arbitrage considerations from those relevant to equilibrium pricing. It then tests whether a factor model truly represents equilibrium pricing theory.

title: Operationalizing Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis for Short-Form Video: A Methods and Data Study of Grooming Precursors Masked as Relationship Advice
abstract: Objective: This methods and data article operationalizes qualitative multimedia content analysis (QMCA) for short-form video posts on TikTok and Instagram Reels, focusing on the method's execution and the frequency structure of observable grooming-precursor cues masked as relationship advice. Method: A purposive corpus of 100 public short-form videos, evenly split between TikTok and Instagram, was archived, de-identified, and coded using MAXQDA 24 for time-segment coding and Excel for the codebook, audit trail, and thresholds. A five-pass routine separated visual features, audio features, on-screen text, and relational/boundary cues. Category development relied on same-document co-occurrence, with recurrence requiring five or more distinct posts. Results: The final codebook contained 289 codes and produced 1,233 post-level feature hits. Recurrence concentrated in presentation-layer categories: Parasocial Proximity and Platform Normalization appeared in all 100 posts, and Intimate Setting Cues in 80. Covert precursor categories recurred less often: Power Imbalance Normalization in 30 posts, Coercive Reframing in 15, Boundary Erosion in 14, and Isolation and Secrecy in 10. Conclusions: QMCA provides an auditable method for documenting how short-form advice content packages relational scripts through camera, voice, setting, captioning, and platform conventions. The taxonomy supports prevention-oriented screening without inferring creator intent or labeling any post as grooming.

title: The missing quadrant: perceived voluntariness, option sets and the acceptance of green digital tools
authors: Maha Jehanzeb, Talha Murtaza, Rida Safdar
abstract: Technology acceptance research measures voluntariness as a perception and, in its consumer flagship, assumes it outright, while parallel stream studies explicitly mandate use. It is between the perception and the mandate that a state lies which neither can classify: a use that is formally optional and reported as chosen while the adopter’s set of viable alternatives has been closed off by conditions beyond their control. This paper names that state foreclosed adoption, where the voluntariness assumption of acceptance research is adapted through the lens of the self-determination theory, whose definition of autonomy as endorsement rather than independence entails that the experience of free adoption cannot certify that alternatives existed. The paper goes on to develop a typology of adoption states (volitional, foreclosed, mandated), three foreclosure mechanisms (economic, architectural, relational) with distinct sources and visibilities, an account of leadership style as the mechanism converting foreclosure into internalisation or bare compliance, and eight propositions with an operationalisation agenda. Green digital technology is argued to be the domain where the resulting misclassification costs most, because foreclosed green adoptions are counted twice over, as voluntary and as value driven, inflating estimates of environmental motivation in research and in organisational sustainability metrics.

title: Humanity after the peak: long-run population and human-capital pathways for global environmental change
abstract: Population and human-capital pathways are central to global environmental change research, yet most widely used demographic projections end in 2100. This creates a time-horizon problem for slow-moving environmental processes, including sea-level rise, land-use change, long-lived infrastructure, food-system transformation and adaptation across generations. We extend Shared Socioeconomic Pathways population and human-capital scenarios to 2300 and examine how peak population gives way to long-run demographic decline, aging and regional redistribution. In the middle-of-the-road pathway, the global population declines to about 4.2 billion by 2300. In the sustainability pathway, it approaches 1 billion. These are not extinction scenarios, but they describe a profound change in the social and demographic setting in which environmental demand, exposure, adaptation and policy operate. The results show that the post-2100 period cannot be treated as a simple continuation of twentieth-century population growth. A smaller, older and more educated world may reduce some overall pressures while intensifying others, especially around labor, care, migration and uneven regional change. Long-run environmental analysis, therefore, needs population pathways that extend beyond 2100 and include not only population size, but also age, education, spatial distribution and demographic momentum.

title: Social spending and democratic institutions in Southeast Asia: A comparative study between Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries. Furthermore, this essay will also challenge the theory that the government system (majoritarian versus consensus democracy) influences the magnitude of social spending and welfare commitment, especially in Southeast Asian democracies, namely, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines. Design/methodology/approach This research uses descriptive statistics and qualitative data to match social spending with the development of democratisation in four cases. Findings The main argument is whether the presence of democratic institutions encourages the government to be more open, citizen-oriented and responsive or whether the inclusive political conditions will create more open public participation in the policymaking process. Thus, in the context of developing countries, public participation will be more likely to demand social policies. Research limitations/implications It has not been able to undertake a more detailed impact evaluation assessment of the development and change of democratic institutions towards policy outcomes within a shorter temporal scope. In addition, this thesis does not also provide details or explanations about the interaction process between particular democratic institutions and specific social policy sectors. Practical implications The process of interactions between particular electoral systems. For instance, the contribution to the emergence of policy in the health services sector or conducting research in normative democratic institutions such as public awareness of the importance of public participation in shaping and directing the implementation of poverty reduction policies could be studied, by using the historical institutionalism approach. Originality/value The impact of certain political institutions on public policy has become a very important discussion in the new institutionalism perspective. Social policy (social spending) as a manifestation of government’s commitment towards welfare is the result of institutional arrangement. In the context of developing countries, where social policy is needed to fulfill the basic needs of citizens, it is important to identify what kind of institutional formations are conducive to the development of social policy. This essay will analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries.

title: A Rejoinder to 'Still Instrumentally Inclusive' (Turnbull-Dugarte & López Ortega)
abstract: Turnbull-Dugarte and López Ortega's "Still Instrumentally Inclusive" (the Response) answers my replication (the Comment) of their 2024 American Political Science Review paper (the Article) with, among other things, a multiverse of 2,970 analyses based on eighteen different weighting schemes, randomization inference, and a trichotomous moderator. As I show in this rejoinder, each is undermined by bona fide errors in their code, their writing, and their interpretation. First, the multiverse is just many correlated variants of the same test. This is in large part due to the weighting schemes which suffer multiple problems (some due to code errors, some intrinsic), and are largely correlated variations on one weighting scheme. Second, due to code errors the randomization inference compares a weighted statistic against an unweighted null and, in the two heterogeneity tests, permutes the interaction column rather than treatment assignment column. Every permutation p-value the Response reports is therefore computed against the wrong reference distribution; when they are recomputed correctly, two of the five it reports as significant are no longer so, and they are the two the Response emphasizes. Third, the trichotomous moderator is erroneously described as terciles, but it is in fact based on non-tercile cutpoints. The key subgroup effect reported in the Response thus rests on comparing just thirty high-weight control respondents against thirty-one high-weight treated respondents, and ends up reaffirming my original point that the heterogeneity in study 2 is with respect to weights, and not immigration sentiment as their theory predicts. I close by documenting seven claims in the Response that are untrue or misleading.

title: Designing engagement: A Research through Design approach to cultivating relational motivation for community-supported agriculture
authors: Sota Takagi, Maoko Fujisaki, Mitsuyo Toyoda, Takumi Ohashi
abstract: Global challenges such as climate change and food insecurity are closely linked to the unsustainable structures of dominant food systems. These systems are reinforced by entrenched mental models that treat consumers as passive buyers and agriculture as mere market transaction. Community-Supported Agriculture (CSA) offers a locally grounded model in which producers and consumers share the risks and benefits of production, holding potential to challenge these structures and foster new relationships and behaviors that contribute to systemic food system change. However, CSA remains underdeveloped in Japan, and how participation motivations are relationally generated through design remains poorly understood. This study examines how design interventions can cultivate relational motivation: forms of engagement arising through social connection and shared values rather than individual preference alone. A Research through Design (RtD) approach was employed to examine a collaborative design intervention in Isumi, Chiba, Japan (October 2025). It followed five phases: (1) educational sessions on CSA and natural farming, (2) a chef-curated meal featuring locally grown produce, (3) a farm field tour, (4) a facilitated Philosophy for Children (p4c) dialogue, and (5) a co-creation workshop. Eleven participants attended, supported by eight collaborators including a producer, a chef, local staff, and researchers. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires (seven-point Likert scales) and thematic analysis of dialogue and workshop data were used for analysis. Quantitative analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) showed a significant increase in participants’ ethical food-selection intention (p = .046, r = .63), and eight of ten reported increased willingness to join CSA despite half having had no prior awareness. Thematic analysis identified three themes: deepened understanding of natural farming, intergenerational responsibility for food culture, and critical reflection on production structures. These themes were translated into concrete CSA visions in the co-creation workshop. Through RtD, the study derived design principles for an entry-point intervention to cultivate participation intentions toward CSA: (1) sequential integration of learning, experience, and reflection; (2) cross-domain intermediary collaboration as social infrastructure; and (3) embodied and relational ethics that translate abstract values into situated action. These principles offer actionable guidance for designers, educators, and policymakers seeking to lower barriers to CSA participation within local communities.

title: Cheap Labor, Expensive Consequences: Determinants Behind Persisting Exploitative Labor Practices in India's Labor Market
abstract: India’s recent economic trajectory has been marked by a striking paradox. Periods of high aggregate growth, expanding urbanization, and integration into domestic and global value chains have coexisted with mass labor informality, insecure employment, weak bargaining power, and uneven access to legal protection. This paper examines whether India’s economic growth has substantially been dependent on exploitative labor, understood not merely as low pay, but as a labor regime characterized by precarity, restricted worker voice, externalization of social costs, and structurally unequal exposure to risk, while recognizing the link between labor exploitation and the architecture of growth rather than treating it solely as a distributive or moral problem. The paper recommends further policy to prevent exploitative labor practices for socio-economic development, calling for the inclusion in development planning to promote cultural identity, economic resilience, diversity, and community participation as a structural support in multiple sectors through responsible governance and business practices.

title: Combining survey questions with a Bayesian bootstrap method improves election forecasts
authors: Henrik Olsson, Wandi Bruine de Bruin, Mirta Galesic, Drazen Prelec
abstract: We present a Bayesian bootstrap method for election forecasting that integrates traditional own-intention questions with wisdom-of-crowds questions, which ask for social-circle expectations and election forecasts. Across the 2018, 2020, and 2024 U.S. elections, wisdom-of-crowds questions consistently outperformed own-intention questions in predicting vote shares. The Bayesian bootstrap combines these questions in a theoretically justified way, assigning weights based on their inferred informational value. The main assumption is that election winner expectations for a given participant are themselves an optimal Bayesian forecast in light of all evidence available to that participant. Social-circle expectations contribute the most to the Bayesian bootstrap forecast, as they reduce demographic biases and capture hidden voter preferences. The method improves forecast accuracy across diverse electoral contexts, offering a principled approach to combining polling questions and suggesting applicability to forecasting other social phenomena.

title: Directing internal attention during sentence reading
authors: Rhianna Lowri Watt, Sage Boettcher, Anna C Nobre, Kate Nation, Dejan Draschkow, Blaine Butler
abstract: Selective attention plays a central role in identifying and prioritising relevant memories (internal attention), but internal attention’s involvement in selecting relevant content for language comprehension is not understood. In two preregistered experiments, we tested the utility of anaphoric expressions as retrodictive cues to guide content selection. Participants read sentences, followed by anaphoric expressions (retrocues) that referred back to one of two target words contained in the sentence. Subsequently, participants were prompted to identify which target word had been referred to. We manipulated the predictability of the anaphoric expression across experiments (Experiment 1: predictive; Experiment 2: non-predictive). We show improved response performance for cued words, even when the retrocue was non-predictive. This parallels classic patterns of automatic attentional selection of memory contents in visual working memory. Our findings suggest that anaphoric devices act through internal attention to select language content maintained in memory to serve ongoing comprehension.

title: Title: Sport for Preventing Violent Extremism: A Systematic Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Violent Extremism is a global threat, prompting both the United Nations and its member states to prioritize prevention efforts. The growth of Violent Extremism prevention through sport or sport-based interventions has been reported in several scholarly studies and en dorsed by the United Nations. These studies have also reported a shift in efforts to prevent future forms of Violent Extremism towards targeting potential future violent extremists and preventing radicalization through Sport programs. Though, there is a lack of knowledge regarding the poten tial mechanisms, methods and approaches for preventing Violent Extremism (PVE) through SDP. This study aims to explore the best practices for using SDP/Sport as a tool in PVE. Methods: A systematic scoping review was conducted by using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) template by (Tricco et al., 2018) on five databases (i.e., Scopus, SportDiscus, Scielo, Sociological ABS, SocIndex) between 2000 and February 2025. A total of 1,284 records were identified and were narrowed to 12 references for full extraction. Results: The review found that SDP/sport and PVE research gained momentum after 2019, with publications focusing on countering and preventing violent extremism, resilience building, and youth deradicalization, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals 3, 10, and 16. Six of the included studies were empirical, five were literature reviews, and one was a personal experience of the researcher. Empirical studies were conducted in Russia, Australia, India, Tajikistan, Jordan, Europe, Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda. Therefore, peace education curricula were implemented in Nigeria, India, Tajikistan and Jordan, though girls/women were notably absent as beneficiaries. The findings emphasize the need for updated methodologies and inclusive approaches to enhance intervention effectiveness. Conclusion: This review demonstrates that sport can play a powerful role in preventing violent extremism by fostering youth resilience and community belonging. Conversely, current research lacks consistency, clear frameworks, and meaningful inclusion of local voices. To advance the field, future studies should broaden the scope of PVE to include related concepts, such as crime and violence prevention, and draw on grey literature to build a more comprehensive and grounded understanding.

title: When the Well-Off Feel Left Behind: Income Misperception and Populist Attitudes
authors: Thilo N.H. Albers, Daniel Bischof, Felix Kersting, Fabian Kosse
abstract: Why do materially secure citizens embrace populist attitudes? Research on the populist right has focused primarily on economically vulnerable voters and left-behind places, leaving unclear why support extends to citizens who are objectively well off. We argue that a belief-based source of grievance helps explain this puzzle: citizens may underestimate their relative economic standing and feel deprived despite material security. Using a survey module embedded in the Innovation Sample of the German Socio-Economic Panel, we show that pessimistic income-rank misperceptions predict stronger populist attitudes conditional on actual rank. Instrumental-variable and within-household analyses strengthen a causal interpretation. A preregistered survey experiment randomly provides personalized information about respondents' actual income percentile. The control arm replicates the observational pattern; the treatment corrects beliefs and shifts income satisfaction, but does not reduce populist attitudes. Economic grievance can therefore travel upward through perceived status, while becoming politically resistant once organized by populist narratives.

title: What Is Coercion?
abstract: A brief monograph investigating the subject of coercion, comparing the perspectives of Sarah Conly's "Seduction, Rape, and Coercion", Patrick Bratton's "When Is Coercion Successful?: And Why Can’t We Agree on It?", and H.J. McCloskey's "Coercion: Its Nature and Significance". It is concluded that coercion is separate from persuasion by its method of action in that coercion threatens identity and persuasion does not. There is also a distinction between legitimate and illegitimate coercion.

title: Tool or Trend? Workload, Confidence, and the Conditions for Generative AI Adoption in Research Administration
abstract: Generative AI is rapidly transforming white-collar work; however, little is known about its uptake in research administration, a specialized field of non-routine, judgement-dependent labour. This study reports the findings from a cross-sectional survey of researchers and research administrative staff at a large academic research hospital in Toronto, Canada (n = 119). Almost three-quarters of respondents (73%) reported using generative AI tools for research administrative work. Four outcome variables, Frequency, Effectiveness, Impact, and Quality of generative AI use, were strongly intercorrelated, indicating that respondents who used the tools more frequently also rated them more favourably across all three evaluative dimensions. Self-assessed confidence positively predicted evaluations of the tools, whereas job security concern was negatively associated with evaluations of generative AI. Respondents who iteratively refined outputs rated the tools more favourably than those who abandoned their attempts at using them, while heavier workloads were associated with less favourable quality perceptions. These findings suggest that realizing generative AI’s potential in administrative work depends on the user’s skills, confidence, and working conditions, rather than the tools themselves.

title: Is the Future Modular? Mapping Preferences, Benefits, and Risks of Modular Journalism across three Audience Segments
authors: Sophie Morosoli, Hannes Cools, Natali Helberger
abstract: One of the ways in which GenAI could change the future of news is modular journalism (MJ) – presenting news in novel, more fluid, personalized and interactive formats that respond and adjust to the individual preferences of users. Being more responsive to users' individual needs through AI-supported forms of personalization could unlock new ways of catering to diverse or underserved audiences, and potentially even reduce news avoidance and information overload or serve as the foundation for new news experiences. This study investigates audience evaluations and willingness to pay for MJ through focus groups (N=26) with three diverse user segments: basic subscribers, adolescents, and individuals with migration backgrounds. Findings reveal that particularly young adults and individuals with migration backgrounds are interested in MJ, valuing flexibility and engagement, though concerns exist about oversimplification of serious topics. Participants favor personalization with user agency over algorithmic curation to preserve content diversity. Willingness to pay is mixed; MJ alone has limited appeal but adds value when integrated into existing subscriptions. Young adults are most willing to pay, especially with trial access. These findings illustrate that there is a potential for MJ to engage audiences with customizable formats, user-controlled personalization, and editorial integrity, and in doing so enhance accessibility, and potentially reduce news avoidance.

title: Recursive Requisite Variety: A Cross-Level Theory of Regulatory Capacity and Control Loss
abstract: Control is lost in structurally similar ways across systems that share no subject matter: an individual who can no longer check what a machine produced, a building whose automation degrades along the dimension it does not sense, a project organization that adds reviewers without adding scrutiny, and a workforce that delegates judgment to a system it cannot audit. These failures are ordinarily explained by four unconnected literatures. This article argues that they instantiate a common mechanism, and it offers that mechanism as a theoretical proposal rather than a tested account. Regulatory capacity is finite and must be allocated across scale, time, and dimension. Delegation does not remove regulatory load; it converts execution load into verification load, while the capability that discharges verification load is maintained largely as a by-product of execution and therefore decays under delegation. Because the allocation decision draws on the same bounded budget, the locally rational response to overload increases the load that produced it, and recovery requires a capacity injection exceeding the original deficit. The resulting structure is termed recursive requisite variety: the same allocation failure recurs at every level of a nested system, and a regulator’s effective variety is bounded by the effective rather than the nominal variety of the regulators beneath it. Seven falsifiable propositions are derived; none is tested here. The instantiations are conceptual recoveries with illustrative evidence rather than tests of the mechanism, and the article states at each level which of the two it is offering. Three of the propositions were not located, in the form stated here, in the scoping audit reported below: redundant regulators drawing on a shared source add effective variety only in proportion to their independent failure share; artefacts carrying neither recoverable provenance nor an independently checkable criterion impose verification load that no capacity can discharge; and overload is characteristically not registered by the actor experiencing it, because the delegate’s output exhibits the surface properties of reliable feedback.

title: Reliability-Aware Sexism Detection: Combining DPO with Annotator Agreement and Token-Level Confidence Scoring
authors: Hadi Mohammadi, Shihan Wang, Masoume M. Raeissi, Anastasia Giachanou
abstract: The detection of online sexism remains an open problem. Sexism detection is inherently subjective, yet most existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority decision and treat all instances uniformly. This ignores two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), which integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. RA-DPO uses this score to select high-value preference pairs during training and to support inference-time abstention, which allows the model to trade coverage for accuracy. We evaluate RA-DPO on 6,920 multilingual posts from EXIST 2023, fine-tune OpenAI gpt-4o base via DPO, and validate on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen). Results show that training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO which indicates that reliability-aware selection can reduce training cost without sacrificing performance. At inference, selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage in the true-agreement setting and 88.7% in the deployable predicted-agreement setting, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline. These results suggest that accounting for annotation uncertainty is beneficial for both efficient training and reliable deployment in subjective classification.

title: Effects of Questionnaire Notifications on Engagement and Attrition in an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study: Longitudinal Observational Study
authors: Daniel Dvořák, Martin Kreidl, Martin Tancoš
abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies are widely used in mobile health (mHealth) research and interventions. EMA requires participants to repeatedly open short questionnaires announced by smartphone notifications, so notification scheduling is a central design decision. Yet evidence on how repeated prompts shape short-term engagement and long-term attrition remains fragmented. We examined (a) how notification order within a measurement window relates to the timing and likelihood of questionnaire opening, and (b) whether the number of notifications within a burst relates to permanent disengagement, in a 12-month, multi-burst smartphone EMA study of Czech adolescents. We analyzed paradata from the FUTURE project, an observational EMA study of 201 adolescents (13–17 years). Four 14-day bursts each contained up to four short questionnaires per day, with up to 10 notifications per questionnaire window. Time from first notification to opening was modeled with Cox survival models with respondent-level frailty. Permanent dropout was modeled with logistic regression at the person-burst level. We tested whether demographics, timing, and the momentary phone context (screen activity, app use) moderated the notification effects. Analyses used Stata 18. A total of 26,007 questionnaires were notified. Of these, 17,668 (67.9%) were opened. Within a measurement window, among questionnaires still unopened, later reminders were associated with a slightly higher chance of opening (hazard ratio [HR] 1.13, 95% CI 1.06–1.19; P<.001), and this estimate was stable across all models, and we found no sign of within-window reminder fatigue. Gender, age, and socioeconomic status changed this pattern only marginally. The phone context mattered more. When the screen was already on (interaction HR 0.862, 95% CI 0.846–0.878), or social media (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.856–0.913) or messaging (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.844–0.926) was in use (all P<.001), reminders were less efficient. Regarding study dropout, 86 of 201 participants (43%) disengaged permanently. More reminders within a burst were associated with slightly lower odds of study dropout (fully adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.996; P=.01), a small association that was stable across all model specifications (OR 0.978–0.984). In this adolescent EMA study, engagement was front-loaded: most openings came soon after the first prompt, but even later notifications had a positive effect on questionnaire engagement. So, within each measurement window, more prompts are better. This holds across all socio-demographics. Repeated reminders showed no sign of backfiring on study dropout. In fact, more reminders went with slightly lower study dropout. Responsiveness depended on what the phone was doing just before the first prompt. Context-aware prompting (avoiding prompts especially if a social media or a messaging app are open) is a more efficient design lever than simply adding reminders.

title: State and local attitudes toward household electrification in California: evidence from a large survey
authors: Gabriel De Roche, Sophia Tomany de Brito, Yohan Min, Sanjay Poudel, Madalsa Singh, Patricia Hidalgo-Gonzalez, Ranjit Deshmukh, Grace C. Wu, Matto Mildenberger
abstract: Decarbonizing residential energy depends on millions of households making millions of purchasing decisions across multiple household electrification technologies, especially solar and storage systems, electric vehicles, heat pumps, and induction stoves. This paper describes consumer attitudes towards household electrification using a large representative survey of 7,158 households in California, with data collected in Spring 2025 from a stratified sample that includes large subgroups across all of California's climate zones as well as from census tracts designated as Disadvantaged Communities by the state. Alongside a wide range of sociodemographic and attitudinal predictors of current adoption, we measure future adoption interest with a personalized contingent-valuation measure of the minimum financial incentive/subsidy required to adopt along a technology-specific subsidy ladder. Leveraging the large statewide sample size, we also use multilevel regression with post-stratification (MRP) to estimate future adoption rates for each of California's 9,129 census tracts for every threshold along this subsidy ladder. We find substantial latent demand, especially for technologies with low current adoption. We also find heterogeneity across technologies in consumers' sensitivity to subsidies and that attitudinal predictors (and especially beliefs about cost, health, and safety benefits) dominate sociodemographic predictors. These results have direct implications for active policy design. Information campaigns designed to shift beliefs about health and safety play an important complementary role alongside cost-focused messages. Our geographically fine-grained estimates of future adoption at the census tract level provide rich local data for policy-makers, researchers, and practitioners designing incentive programs and planning grid infrastructure as California households continue to electrify.

title: What Does Frontier Access Buy? Benchmarking LLM Access Tiers and the Reproducibility Case for Open Weights in Survey Coding
abstract: Social scientists coding open-ended survey responses with large language models (LLMs) face a tradeoff between proprietary frontier systems, cheaper commercial alternatives, and open-weight models that can be audited and self-hosted. This study benchmarks eighteen LLMs across four access tiers, from proprietary flagships to open-weight models small enough to run on a laptop, zero-shot against a human consensus on three open-ended questions from a probability-sampled U.S. panel. External validation adds a British Election Study task and an online-comment emotion task (GoEmotions), spanning five tasks in three contexts. The flagship proprietary models' average margin over their cheaper counterparts is statistically indistinguishable from zero, despite stronger general-benchmark performance. Pricing tells the same story: frontier models cost 1.3–6× more per token, yet for most of them some cheaper model is also more accurate, and the field's second-best macro F1 comes from its cheapest closed model. Open-weight models have largely caught up. The largest ones match both proprietary tiers on cell-level agreement, while on the stricter macro F1 they trail by about two points on average. They reach this at no per-call cost, with the reproducibility and data-privacy advantages of self-hosting. Both patterns hold out of domain. The leading models, closed and open alike, agree with a trained human coder about as well as the two coders agree with each other. Failure is patterned. Errors concentrate on interpretive categories where the human coders themselves disagreed, and on longer responses, penalties from which frontier prices buy little relief. The caveat is scale. Laptop-scale models show strong cell-level agreement but trail further on macro F1, so fully local deployment carries a modest, task-dependent accuracy cost. Hardware scale and question difficulty, not price or license, are the binding constraints on these tasks.

title: Request routing services undermine the reproducibility of open weight LLMs
authors: Joe Higton, Joshua A. Tucker, Christopher Barrie
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard tool for classifying text in social science. To make these classifications reproducible, researchers are often advised to use open weight models and to set the sampling temperature to zero. We show that this advice is insufficient when models are accessed through a request-routing service, in which queries are sent to different hosting providers through a single API. Using a popular request-routing service, OpenRouter, we classify British manifesto sentences for ideology 100 times per sentence across eight models and 33 hosting providers, alongside five model configurations served on our own hardware, generating approximately 1m classification draws. When using the request-routing service, open weight models consistently fail to return deterministic outputs. Depending on the model, only 26% to 92% of sentences receive the same label in all repeated classifications. This variation is not solely due to different providers fielding queries: for five of the eight models, the majority of classification variance arises within providers. On our own hardware, the same task is perfectly reproducible at temperature=0. We conclude that reproducibility depends on the entire model hosting environment, and recommend that researchers report the fullest available metadata and raw responses when using LLMs.

title: Same Facts, Different Meanings: Factual Information, Interpretation, and Attitude Change
abstract: A key puzzle in the political information literature is why factual information reliably updates citizens’ beliefs about the fact in question but rarely shifts downstream political attitudes. Using two preregistered survey experiments (N ≈ 3,250) covering eleven issues across economic indicators and misstatements by prominent political figures, this paper makes two contributions. First, we test whether the muted effect of factual information on downstream attitudes holds for outcomes that are less entrenched and more proximate to the information than those tested in prior work—such as economic evaluations and perceptions of politicians’ honesty and competence—and find that even these outcomes respond only modestly. Second, we develop and empirically test a framework of six adjacent belief dimensions—regarding causes, relevance, and intent—through which factual information may be reinterpreted in ways that reshape its political meaning. We find evidence of adjacent belief updating, although concentrated on specific dimensions rather than widespread. The strongest finding is that individuals who learn that a favored politician made an inaccurate claim concede the inaccuracy but shift toward viewing the statement as figurative, with sizable effects across two independent studies. Importantly, where adjacent belief adjustment occurs, its direction is contingent on individuals’ predispositions. Uncongenial information triggers adjustment that attenuates the political implications of the fact, while congenial information triggers no such adjustment or small shifts in the opposite direction. Together, the results illustrate how parallel trends in factual accuracy can coexist with divergent trends in how those facts are politically interpreted.

title: Measuring Perceptions of Extreme Weather Events and Climate Change
authors: Clara Brügge, Patrick Kraft, Franziska Quoß
abstract: As climate change increases the frequency and severity of extreme weather events (EWEs), people worldwide are beginning to experience these impacts firsthand. While a growing body of research has explored how this direct experience of EWEs affects public perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, findings remain inconclusive. A central challenge in this literature is the large researcher degrees of freedom in operationalizing EWEs. This inconsistency partly stems from a lack of theoretical and empirical clarity regarding what the public actually perceives as an EWE. Previous work has shown a low correspondence between subjective perceptions and objective meteorological data, highlighting a disconnect between scientific definitions and the experience of laypeople. To address this gap, we investigate how average citizens conceptualize EWEs using a high-quality panel survey conducted in Switzerland. We field an open-ended survey question with experimental variation in its wording and use large language models (LLMs) to classify the content of responses across multiple dimensions – including the type of event, its regional focus, and its relation to climate change. Validating the classification against human coding and benchmarking it against fine-grained objective weather data, we find that respondents draw on a wide range of considerations, that question wording – especially a local cue – strongly shapes responses while explicit climate-change priming does not, and that open-ended responses correspond at least as closely to objective weather data as a targeted closed-ended item. We discuss the promise and limitations of LLM-based measurement for research on climate and extreme weather perceptions.

title: Long-run political change after the Great Recession
abstract: What are the long-run political consequences of economic crises? We study the Great Recession in the United States, exploiting geographic variation in unemployment shocks. Harder-hit counties shifted toward Democratic candidates. House gains persisted through 2022, after the shock's employment effects had dissipated, while presidential gains attenuated after 2016. House gains did not track local recovery or Republican incumbency, which weighs against simple retrospective voting accounts. Harder-hit places also showed no shift toward right-wing populist candidates or movements. Instead, survey and ballot measure evidence points to economic scarring and demand for protection: residents of harder-hit places remained pessimistic about their economic prospects, even as personal finances recovered, and became more supportive of social protection. Taken together, the findings suggest that a crisis can durably reshape what affected communities demand from government after acute local labor market distress has subsided.

title: Social norms solve coordination problems paradoxically created by shared interests
authors: Minhua Yan, Yuanmei Li, Zhizhong Li, Robert Boyd, Sarah Mathew
abstract: Human cooperation is motivated both by shared interests arising from kinship and friendship and by social norms, but whether these mechanisms substitute for or complement one another remains debated. Cooperative farming among Derung horticulturalists offers an ideal study context, because most cofarming occurs among kin or friends, and a norm prescribes equal harvest division by household regardless of contributions. We show that this norm solves two problems that shared interests cannot solve, or may even exacerbate. First, shared interests expand the range of acceptable divisions, making coordination harder. By specifying a salient division, the norm resolves this problem. Second, cofarmers often misperceive how much their partner benefits. By prescribing a division independent of cost-benefit assessments, the norm prevents these differences from unraveling cooperation. The complementary action of norms and shared interests may explain why humans cooperate with kin and friends more than other animals.

title: Poverty and Caregiver Mental Health are Related to Infant and Toddler Resting State Brain Networks: Insights from fNIRS
authors: Kaja K. Jasińska, Hannah Whitehead, Sharon Wolf, Dr Fabrice Tanoh, Stephanie Bugden, Brooke Wortsman, Amy Ogan
abstract: Significance: The first three years of life represent a period of heightened neural plasticity, during which early adversity—such as poverty and maternal stress—can shape long-term developmental trajectories. However, little is known about how these adversities are linked to neural network organization in infants and toddlers living in low-resource settings. Aim: This study examined how prenatal exposure to maternal poverty and mental health symptoms relates to neural network organization in early childhood. Approach: We conducted a longitudinal study with 42 children (6–36 months old) from economically-vulnerable households in rural Côte d’Ivoire. Maternal multidimensional poverty and mental health symptoms were assessed around conception and during pregnancy. Two years later, children’s development was measured using the Caregiver Reported Early Development Instruments (CREDI), and resting-state brain activity was recorded using portable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Graph-theoretic metrics of functional connectivity, including segregation, integration, and small-worldness, were computed to characterize neural network organization. Results: Greater exposure to poverty was associated with reduced network segregation and integration. In contrast, higher maternal mental health symptoms were linked to increased segregation and integration. These findings suggest that deprivation and maternal stress differentially relate to early neural network architecture. Conclusions: Our results align with dimensional models of adversity, and suggest that deprivation (related to poverty) and threat/unpredictability (related to maternal mental health and caregiving) may become biologically embedded. These findings underscore the importance of addressing both structural poverty and maternal mental health during pregnancy and early childhood to promote healthy brain development in high-adversity contexts.

title: Bayesian estimation in multiple comparisons
abstract: Traditional regression models typically estimate parameters for a factor F by designating one level as a reference (intercept) and calculating slopes for other levels of F. While this approach often aligns with our research question(s), it limits direct comparisons between all pairs of levels within F and requires additional procedures for generating these comparisons. Moreover, Frequentist methods often rely on corrections (e.g., Bonferroni or Tukey), which can reduce statistical power and inflate uncertainty by mechanically widening confidence intervals. This paper demonstrates how Bayesian hierarchical models provide a robust framework for parameter estimation in the context of multiple comparisons. By leveraging entire posterior distributions, these models produce estimates for all pairwise comparisons without requiring post hoc adjustments. The hierarchical structure, combined with the use of priors, naturally incorporates shrinkage, pulling extreme estimates toward the overall mean. This regularization improves the stability and reliability of estimates, particularly in the presence of sparse or noisy data, and leads to more conservative comparisons. Bayesian models also offer a flexible framework for addressing heteroscedasticity by directly modeling variance structures and incorporating them into the posterior distribution. The result is a coherent approach to exploring differences between levels of F, where parameter estimates reflect the full uncertainty of the data.

title: Who Pays for the Church? Religious Clientelism and Broker Compensation in Postwar Italy
abstract: In many contexts, religious leaders mobilize support for allied politicians. These mobilization efforts are often assumed to be part of brokerage agreements in which politicians provide material compensation once elected. Despite how common these arrangements are, little is known about how and when politicians compensate religious leaders for their electoral brokerage. We argue that politicians reward organization-embedded religious brokers by providing status-enhancing goods that increase their standing within the organization and the local community. We illustrate this type of compensation by investigating exchanges between Christian Democratic politicians and personally connected Catholic bishops in postwar Italy. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate that elected politicians reward connected bishops with investments in church renovations, that these investments are targeted to increase the prestige of bishops, and that electoral incentives shape patterns of broker compensation. These findings shed light on the reciprocal exchanges that underpin politician-clergy alliances in electoral democracies.

title: The Spread of High-Speed Internet and Gender-Based Violence within Families in Mexico
authors: Daniela R. Urbina, Julia A Behrman
abstract: The relationship between internet access and gender-based violence (GBV) remains contested: theories of global diffusion sustain that online media spreads gender-egalitarian norms and condemns violence against women, whereas digital platforms can also normalize misogyny and enable coercive control. To test these hypotheses, we exploit temporal and geographic variation in the rollout of high-speed internet across Mexican municipalities between 2011 and 2021, distinguishing violence by intimate partners from that by other family members. Combining three waves of Mexico’s ENDIREH survey, with time-varying georeferenced coverage measures, we estimate two-way fixed-effects, difference-in-differences, and triple-difference models. We find that rapid internet expansion reduced family-perpetrated violence—particularly emotional and physical violence —but had no effect on intimate-partner violence. Further analyses reveal that one pathway through which increased digital access decreased family-level GBV was by enhancing women’s decision-making power, especially among those living with their parents. Our findings highlight the value of adopting a broad definition of GBV that reaches beyond intimate partners, particularly in contexts where multigenerational households are common.

title: Resistance to territorial stigmatization: the mechanisms linking place-based social movement engagement and people's perceptions of place
abstract: Scholars of territorial stigma have assumed that resistance efforts should improve how stigmatized neighborhoods are perceived. Findings from a two-and-a-half-year ethnographic study of a place-based social movement in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, challenge this assumption: the same organization's resistance efforts can produce fundamentally different effects depending on how audiences are positioned to encounter the neighborhood. For those with little direct contact, a consistent counternarrative reshaped how the neighborhood was symbolically imagined. For occasional visitors, direct exposure introduced complexity that secondhand accounts could not provide. For residents who engaged deeply with the organization, material and relational support gradually reshaped how the neighborhood was experienced from within. And for residents with high neighborhood familiarity but low organizational engagement, none of these mechanisms took hold. These findings reveal that resistance to territorial stigma and perception change are distinct processes, connected by mechanisms that vary with the nature and depth of contact between people and place, which shows how inequality is reproduced not only through material conditions but also through unequal processes of knowing place.

title: What Citizens Mean by Democracy: Partisan Differences in Open-Ended Survey Responses
authors: Mirko Wegemann, Elena Leuschner, Tim Lars Allinger, Daniel Bischof, Kristian Frederiksen, Morgan Le Corre Juratic
abstract: Do voters from different partisan camps understand democracy in the same way? We analyze more than 25,000 open-ended survey responses from representative samples in 14 countries, classifying answers with a fine-tuned language model and sentence embeddings. Citizens most often define democracy through individual and civil rights; multidimensional definitions are rare, and elections are mentioned by only 17% of respondents. Yet shared vocabulary masks partisan divergence.
