Far-right voters and non-voters are less likely to mention civil rights, elections, and horizontal accountability, while far-right voters more often invoke majoritarian principles. Among respondents mentioning rights, left voters connect rights to equality and citizenship, whereas right voters emphasize freedom of speech. Democratic contestation thus unfolds within democratic language, creating openings for selective elite reframing.

title: The impact of product placement on sales of plant-based meat alternatives: A controlled interrupted time series analysis of an in-store intervention
authors: Alice Kininmonth, Francesca Pontin, Victoria Jenneson, William Young, Alison Fildes, Michelle Morris
abstract: Background: Reducing meat consumption and substituting red and processed meats with plant-proteins could have positive health and environmental impacts. This study examined the impact of an in-store product positioning intervention on sales of plant-based meat alternatives (PBMA) and meat-based products. Methods: Between September 2021 and January 2022, a major UK supermarket retailer implemented a product placement intervention that moved 25 chilled PBMAs from a separate dedicated PBMA bay within the meat aisle to being shelved next to their meat-based counterparts and the original dedicated PBMA bay was removed. No changes were made in control stores. To examine the effectiveness of the intervention on sales of PBMAs and meat-based products, controlled interrupted time series analysis was conducted using 538 days of sales data from 6 intervention stores and 6 matched control stores. Results: Overall, there was a significant difference between intervention and control stores in the change in sales of PBMAs attributable to the intervention (-51.18 units, 95% CI: -97.15, -5.21, indicating that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts led to a measurable reduction in PBMA sales in intervention stores. There was no difference between the intervention and control stores in sales of other meat-free products, meat-based products, or products within the protein Eatwell category, indicating that the intervention had no measurable effect on sales of products other than the relocated PBMAs. Price-point comparison analysis revealed that PBMA products were significantly more expensive than their meat-based counterparts. Conclusion: This study revealed that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts was not effective at increasing sales of PBMAs and in fact led to a significant reduction in sales of the repositioned PBMAs. The reduction observed may have resulted from regular PBMA customers not being able to find the relocated PBMAs or from the higher price of PBMAs compared to their meat-based counterparts or both. Future research in real-world settings is needed to better understand the behavioural levers that encourage customers towards healthier and more sustainable purchases. Future research should also examine whether placement-based interventions, such as dual-placement coupled with price promotions, can support meaningful behavioural shifts towards more sustainable choices.

title: Communication Repertoires in Hybrid Office Work: Mediated Channels, Face-to-Face Interaction, and Formal and Informal Exchange
authors: Kai-David Klärner, Sophie-Charlotte Meyer, Anita Tisch
abstract: Research on communication in hybrid work often focuses on individual channels or remote work intensity rather than the broader communication repertoires through which employees interact. This study examines whether the composition of these repertoires is associated with formal and informal collegial exchange beyond employees’ overall communication frequency. Using data from the 2024 DiWaBe 2.0 survey of 7,587 employees, we distinguish overall work-related communication frequency from its distribution across face-to-face interaction and four mediated channels: email, chat, telephone, and video conferencing. A joint five-mode model separates overall communication frequency from mode-specific deviations rela-tive to face-to-face interaction. Parallel measures enable a direct comparison of formal and informal exchange. The findings suggest that greater relative reliance on mediated channels is associated with lower reported formal and informal collegial exchange relative to face-to-face interaction. By contrast, voice/video and text-based channels do not differ significantly in their average associations with either outcome. The mediated-channel deviations also do not differ significantly between formal and informal exchange. Robustness analyses yield sub-stantively similar results across alternative samples, additional controls, and model specifications. The study demonstrates the analytical value of a communication-repertoire perspective on hybrid work. Overall communication frequency and communication-mode composition represent distinct dimensions of employees’ communication repertoires. The findings therefore shift attention from workplace location or individual channels alone to how communication is organised across co-present and mediated forms.

title: Epistemic Intolerance Toward Outpartisans
authors: Seo-young Silvia Kim, Taegyoon Kim, Jeong Hyun Kim, Youngdeuk Park
abstract: We identify and operationalize epistemic intolerance, the belief that outgroup members are epistemically incompetent, violate epistemic norms, and are unworthy of epistemic engagement. In particular, we measure epistemic intolerance toward outpartisans using an original 18-item battery fielded in two U.S. surveys (December 2025 and April 2026; N = 3,386, of whom 2,525 partisans are analyzed). We show that epistemic intolerance is widespread and distinct from affective polarization and that, when measured with the full battery, it predicts democratic norm erosion, outparty dehumanization, and anti-intellectualism toward outparty elites, even when benchmarked against both affective polarization and political sectarianism. Moreover, its overall level is bipartisan, and prevalent even among leaners across both the Democratic and Republican parties. These findings identify epistemic intolerance as a consequential and previously underappreciated dimension of partisan hostility, with downstream implications for designing effective depolarization strategies.

title: Barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK
authors: Vanita Sundaram, Beth Bell, Nadia Jessop, Emma Jackson
abstract: Abstract This paper focuses on barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK. The data are derived from the first UK study of racially minoritised girls’ experiences of public sexual harassment; in this paper we focus specifically on sexual harassment experiences in school. We adopted a qualitative research design that used co-produced, participatory methods to elicit the voices of racially-minoritised girls and young women. Twenty-eight participants from schools, community settings, and universities took part in semi-structured interviews and focus groups that used techniques such as photo elicitation and creative methods to prompt discussion. Barriers to disclosure fall into four thematic categories: feeling dismissed; lack of appropriate adults to disclose to in school; normalisation of sexual harassment; and victim-blaming. The findings make an important contribution to the scant UK literature on the school-level experiences of racially minoritised girls and demonstrate how race/ethnicity shape these experiences. Keywords: sexual harassment, schools, disclosure, barriers, racially-minoritised girls

title: Affordable Health Advice: Rethinking Credibility in Digital Health Communication
abstract: This Global Forum article proposes “affordable health advice” as a complementary lens for understanding credibility and livability in digital health communication. Drawing on my previous research on Egyptian physician vloggers and using a recent Egyptian digital health controversy as an illustrative thread, the article argues that audiences do not evaluate health advice only through scientific validity, source expertise, trust, or health literacy. They may also assess whether advice appears possible to live with. The article identifies three dimensions of affordability: economic, cultural, and emotional. Economic affordability concerns whether advice appears financially attainable and sustainable in contexts where treatment, medication, testing, food, and long-term disease management impose substantial costs. Cultural affordability concerns whether advice speaks from within people’s everyday language, food practices, religious rhythms, humor, and classed realities. Emotional affordability concerns whether advice reduces the psychological burden of illness by promising hope, autonomy, and relief from chronic-patient identity. The article argues that health advice may gain credibility when it appears more compatible with lived realities than conventional recommendations, even when that advice is scientifically contested.

title: Cultural constructions of nature connection: Exploring migrants' experiences of connecting with nature in Australia
authors: Kate Sollis, Bethaney Turner, Lily van Eeden, Kanchana Wiset, Usitha Rajeevan, Pauline Marsh, Emily Flies
abstract: Cultural norms and values influence human-nature connection, shaping then how people use, and interact with natural environments and their nature stewardship actions. This study examines how nature connection varies across migrant communities in Australia and explores the role of cultural factors in shaping human–nature relationships. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyse data from a national survey of 4,006 respondents in Australia, exploring the quantitative measures (CN-12 and Inclusion of Nature in Self) and qualitative responses from the respondents born overseas. Migrants reported higher overall nature connection than non-migrants, with particularly high levels among individuals from North African and Middle Eastern, Southern and Central Asian, Southern and Eastern European, and Sub-Saharan African backgrounds. However, differences in connection were not explained by socio-demographic factors, migration history, or access to nature. Qualitative findings reveal distinct conceptualisations of nature, including everyday interactions, human–nature entanglement, recognition of nature’s agency, reciprocity, and experiences of awe. These findings suggest that both cultural values and lived experiences shape how nature is understood and engaged with, highlighting the need for culturally inclusive approaches to environmental policy and nature-based interventions.

title: Democracy, a Sine Qua Non Tool for Economic Development: The Ghanaian Experience (1950–2022)
abstract: At independence in 1957, Ghana’s per capita income was comparable to South Korea’s, yet decades later the two countries occupy vastly different positions in the global economy. What explains this divergence, and what role has democratic governance played in Ghana’s economic trajectory? This study investigates the relationship between democracy and economic development in Ghana from 1950 to 2022, a period marked by cycles of military rule, economic decline, and democratic transition. While the existing literature extensively debates whether democracy causes development or development enables democracy, far less attention has been given to testing this relationship within a single-country time series that spans both authoritarian and democratic eras. I argue that democratic consolidation in Ghana has had a positive and statistically significant effect on economic growth. Using data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) dataset and a bivariate regression model with GDP as the dependent variable and the V-Dem democracy index as the independent variable, the analysis reveals that a one-unit increase in democratic quality corresponds to a 2.056-unit increase in GDP, with democracy explaining approximately 41.6% of the observed variation in economic output.

title: Properly Initiated: Gangstalking, Targeted Individuals and Digital Cults of Affliction.
abstract: Targeted Individuals (TIs) describe “gangstalking” as coordinated, technologically mediated persecution that profoundly restructures everyday life. While clinical frameworks often interpret these experiences as individual delusion, such approaches overlook their collective and ritual dimensions. Drawing on digital ethnography, multi-platform participant observation, and interviews with TIs, this article reframes online TI communities through Victor Turner’s concept of cults of affliction. I argue that these networks function as contemporary curative cults, guiding participants through a tripartite rite of passage: separation, liminal seclusion, and return. Within this process, influencers act as modern diviners, transforming isolated sufferers into “wounded healers” who diagnose hidden enemies, construct therapeutic narratives, and perform public acts of revelation across digital platforms. This analysis positions gangstalking as a cultural concept of distress and a collective strategy for meaning-making, challenging medicalized models of mental illness and expert authority.

title: Beyond the Billiard Ball: Understanding the Effectiveness of Transnational Politics
abstract: This paper examines the conditions under which transnational political activity translates into measurable shifts in state behavior and the international order. Drawing on the foundational scholarship of Nye and Keohane (1971), Kaiser (1971), Keck and Sikkink (1998), Risse-Kappen (1995), and Vertovec (2009), I argue that the effectiveness of cross-border politics depends not on the existence of transnational actors alone but on the structured conditions through which they operate. The paper identifies persistent gaps in the existing literature, particularly the absence of systematic frameworks for assessing when transnational pressure yields tangible policy outcomes versus symbolic compliance. To address this, I propose the Layered Mediation Framework (LMF), a five-layer sequential model that evaluates transnational effectiveness through political openness, domestic institutional pathways, advocacy and accountability networks, the strength of issue framing, and the policy-to-actualization gap. The LMF offers a comparative analytical tool for measuring the flow, mediation, and ultimate impact of transnational political activity across different cases and regimes.

title: How Do Benjamin Barber and Iris Young Seek to Create Justice?
abstract: This paper examines how Benjamin Barber and Iris Marion Young seek to create justice through democratic reform. Both theorists reject the adequacy of liberal democratic institutions and advocate for deeper, more inclusive forms of public deliberation. Young proposes a transformative approach centered on remedying internal and external exclusions through institutional reform, group representation, and expanded modes of communication—greeting, rhetoric, and narrative— that foster dialogical understanding. Barber advances a more radical vision, calling for the replacement of existing “thin democratic” institutions with new participatory structures, including neighborhood assemblies, election by lot, national referenda, and universal citizen service. The paper identifies significant convergences between the two theorists, particularly their shared emphasis on diverse communicative practices, civic education, and the pursuit of a common will over parochial interests. It also highlights key divergences: Young favors reforming existing institutions to be more representative, while Barber argues such institutions are fundamentally flawed and must be replaced entirely. The paper concludes that Young’s incremental, reform oriented approach offers a more pragmatic and implementable pathway to democratic justice.

title: Between Multifactor and Multi-Beta
abstract: Given extensive evidence that firm characteristics predict expected returns, much of the literature asks whether these characteristics also capture the covariance structure of returns. If so, the next question is which modeling framework best explains the covariance structure revealed by those characteristics. This study addresses that question by comparing two alternative frameworks: a multifactor model and a conditional single-factor model. It formally examines how each specifies the covariance structure and how much overall return covariation each explains. The analysis then considers whether the covariance structure implied by the multifactor model can be nested within the conditional single-factor model.

title: An Algorithmic Multifactor Extension
abstract: Anomaly-based multifactor models have become a major development in empirical asset pricing because they provide a systematic way to expand existing pricing models. This study clarifies the algorithmic logic behind that extension. Specifically, it shows how these models identify pricing errors left unexplained by the factors already included in a model and incorporate additional factors to reduce those errors. This logic matters because it explains how anomaly-based models absorb empirical anomalies while reducing dimensionality. We further show that the method for adding factors closely parallels a classical factor-extraction algorithm in statistical modeling, thereby reinforcing the statistical validity of anomaly-based models.

title: Informational Limits behind the Puzzle
abstract: Some level of consumption is indispensable for survival. Human well-being, however, depends not only on present consumption but also on the expectation that consumption can be sustained in the future. Traditional economic models do not fully capture this forward-looking psychological dimension. This study revises the standard utility specification by incorporating expectation-based satisfaction. It also recognizes that consumers predict their own future consumption better than researchers do. Because utility depends directly on these private predictions, informational asymmetry matters for empirical asset pricing. The study shows how accounting for this asymmetry can help explain empirically high equity premia and low risk-free rates.

title: Shared Governance in Hospitals: Development, Frameworks, and Future Directions for Interprofessional Implementation and Evaluation
authors: Christoph Golz, Kai-Uwe Schmitt, Mirjam Körner
abstract: Shared governance has been recognized for more than three decades as an organizational framework for strengthening nurses’ participation in decision-making, professional autonomy, and accountability. In recent years, the concept has regained attention as healthcare organizations face workforce shortages, increasing care complexity, and growing demands for interprofessional collaboration. This Expert Opinion examines the development, implementation, and evaluation of shared governance from nursing-centered models toward broader professional and interprofessional governance systems. Building on existing conceptual and measurement work, it discusses the conditions under which shared governance can be translated consistently into an explicit interprofessional decision-making system, with clearly defined authority, alignment with existing structures, and robust evaluation. Implementation is complicated by conceptual overlap with frameworks such as the Magnet model, distributed leadership, clinical governance, quality improvement structures, and interprofessional collaboration. These overlaps may blur responsibilities, duplicate structures, and complicate the attribution of outcomes to shared governance. Measurement approaches have advanced but remain fragmented. Instruments such as the Index of Professional (Nursing) Governance and the Verran Professional Governance Scale assess perceptions of governance culture, while the Council Health Survey provides a council-level measure of council functioning. However, current measurement approaches do not yet sufficiently capture interprofessional governance as an operational system, including how authority is distributed across professional groups, how decisions move through organizational structures, and how governance contributes to workforce, patient, and organizational outcomes. We propose a research and practice agenda that emphasizes conceptual clarification, interprofessional alignment with existing organizational frameworks, measurement innovation, and rigorous implementation and evaluation designs. Future work should combine measures of governance culture, council functioning, interprofessional representation, decision pathways, structural characteristics, and outcomes. Such an approach can help shared governance move from symbolic or fragmented implementation toward a measurable and sustainable mechanism for strengthening professional engagement, workforce retention, interprofessional collaboration, and the quality and safety of patient care.

title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate
abstract: During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.

title: International Migration: A Barrier towards Help Seeking for IPV among South Asian Immigrant Women in the US
abstract: The literature review explores the way international migration works as the barrier in seeking help by South Asian immigrant women in the U.S. Significant number of women from these countries experience IPV and suffers from asking for help or support due to different aspects of South Asian culture. This review examines the structural barriers faced by these populations and also, looked into the theoretical perspective of fundamental cause theory. Finally, the review addressed the future scope of study and need for culturally driven services targeted toward these women.

title: Agent-oriented modality in the languages of North America
authors: Jessica K. Ivani, Alexandra Nogina, Taras Zakharko
abstract: This study examines the morphosyntactic and functional encoding of agent-oriented modality in a maximally diverse sample of languages from North America. Focusing on necessity, obligation, ability, and desire, we show that agent-oriented modality is expressed through a wide range of construction types, including tense-aspect-mood morphology, modal verbs, non-verbal formatives, and complex clauses. We show that clustering the constructions by their formal properties yields three groups that align closely with the modal functions of necessity, ability, and desire. We further show that the constructions encoding different modal functions tend to differ in their morphosyntactic profiles, with strong necessity and obligation in particular showing systematic associations with tense marking, and weak and strong necessity with mood marking, respectively. These findings suggest that agent-oriented modality is not a uniform grammatical category, but a structured functional domain whose subtypes recruit material from different areas of grammar. The study contributes to a typological understanding of modality by combining constructional detail and an autotypologizing approach to cross-linguistic comparison.

title: Embodied Knowledge: The Case of Sociology
abstract: Spontaneous Community Research (SCR)—research that draws on experiences accumulated over years or decades of community participation before research questions are formulated—generates valuable sociological knowledge from insider perspectives. Yet current ethical frameworks and journal data requirements often exclude this approach. This article demonstrates that standard expectations—such as prospective research design, informed consent, tangible data deposits, and reproducibility—are incompatible with SCR's distinctive characteristics because its data are embodied: stored in the researcher's memory, inseparable from lived experience, and not amenable to conventional documentation. Rather than excluding SCR from academic discourse, the article argues for epistemic pluralism by recognising multiple legitimate forms of social knowledge production, each requiring ethical standards that are appropriate to its methodology rather than uniformly applied. To this end, it proposes alternative validation strategies that emphasise contextual transparency, collective corroboration, and reflexive acknowledgement of the evolution of the researcher's positionality. Keywords: embodied knowledge, insider research, autoethnography, positionality, data repositories, research ethics

title: BLACK LGBTI+ PENTECOSTAL FAMILIES AND AFFECT OF RESISTANCE: DECOLONIAL PERSPECTIVES FROM THE BRAZILIAN PERIPHERY
abstract: This paper presents key results from doctoral research in Religious Studies on Black LGBTI+ Pentecostal families in Brazil, conceptualized herein as quilombo families (famílias aquilombadas), viewed as ethical-affective expressions of resistance within the religious field. Utilizing an intersectional, decolonial, and affective framework, engaging critical scholars such as Joe Coyle, E. Patrick Johnson, and Beatriz Nascimento, the study deploys the metaphor of the Pentecostal quilombo to analyze inclusive churches as urban territories of affection, freedom, and the restoration of social bonds. Grounded in semi-structured qualitative interviews with 33 Black LGBTI+ individuals and families across inclusive congregations, the findings reveal how these family units challenge traditional Christian heterocisnormative dogmas and articulate a counter-hegemonic spirituality. This framework demonstrates both the transformative potential of affective-political reconstruction and the structural limits of inclusion when racial, moral, and gender hierarchies remain unbroken.

title: LABRASHURIAS: THE PRETOGAYS LANGUAGE OF PENTECOSTAL INCLUSIVE CHURCHES
abstract: The "pretogays" language (Santos, 2022) represents a linguistic manifestation resulting from the intersection of the epistemic category "pretoguês" (Gonzalez, 1988), the vernacular "pajubá" (Lima, 2017), a "dialect" of "resistance" utilized by transvestites and transgender individuals, and "glossolalia" (Sullivan, 2020), the characteristic and mystical speech of Pentecostals. These three communicative modes converge among LGBTI+ individuals within inclusive Pentecostal churches in Brazil, faith communities that do not condemn dissident sexualities but reframe them as divine gifts. Utilizing an intersectional framework (Crenshaw, 2002), further enriched by E. Patrick Johnson's Quare theory, Ashon Crawley's Blackpentecostal Breath, and Black sociolinguistics (Smitherman; Alim), this study demonstrates how race, class, gender, linguistics, and religion intersect to reveal how words and speech acts function as performative signs intrinsically linked to Black, gay, and Pentecostal embodiment.

title: Dual Momentum: Cash Flows and Discount Rates
abstract: Observed continuation in abnormal returns is best understood not as a primitive phenomenon, but as the combined effect of two channels: cash-flow momentum and discount-rate momentum. This two-channel view follows directly from the identity that decomposes abnormal returns into cash-flow news and discount-rate news. We show that these channels imply distinct patterns in the joint behavior of raw returns and normal returns, extending the analysis beyond the canonical facts of momentum. These patterns provide a diagnostic for assessing whether momentum profits are driven more by cash-flow momentum or by discount-rate momentum.

title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Asset Prices
abstract: A basic intuition in asset pricing is that higher perceived risk is associated with higher expected return. Yet this intuition alone does not fully explain how expected return is translated into realized return. An important link is therefore still missing. To address that gap, this study moves beyond the static risk-return tradeoff and focuses on three intertemporal elements: information processing, repricing in response to revisions in perceived risk, and hedging against future reinvestment risk. By bringing these elements together, the study explains how asset prices evolve over time and how returns take shape over time.

title: Speculation-Based Asset Pricing
abstract: This study proposes speculation-based asset pricing, in which valuation is driven by speculative beliefs and return forecasts rather than by risk-based dividend discounting. This shift matters because the theory does not require a dividend stream and therefore applies to non-dividend-paying assets. The key object is a speculative baseline return, defined as the return level investors believe the asset can eventually deliver. This baseline determines the explosive growth rate of the bubble component, which identifies the speculative part of the asset price. The analysis then shows a dynamic implication: faster convergence to this growth potential requires a greater near-term return cost.

title: Institutions and the future African fertility decline
abstract: Africa will account for nearly all global population growth in the 21st century, driven by persistently high fertility rates and substantial demographic momentum. This paper argues that, while many of the distal factors that affect fertility (for example, education, urbanisation, and contraceptive access) are well-understood as important determinants of fertility patterns and levels, demographers have tended to focus on these at the expense of considering the less-quantifiable institutional aspects which mediate the impact of those factors on the pace and timing of fertility declines. Drawing on McNicoll's foundational framework, we argue that weak, contested, or unstable institutions render high fertility a rational household strategy. Without deliberate institution-building — analogous to East Asia's developmental states — a demographic-institutional trap is likely to perpetuate Africa's elevated fertility well into the 21st century.

title: Bringing public attention to disease into global health priority-setting
authors: Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado, Ismael Rafols, Adrian A. Díaz-Faes
abstract: Background: A central concern in global health priority-setting is whether the supply of scientific knowledge aligns with health needs and demands. This alignment is usually assessed by comparing research effort with disease burden, overlooking other type of “social demand” of disease, in particular whether diseases are socially visible and generate public attention. We develop an analytical framework that treats public attention and epidemiological burden as complementary dimensions of health demand and examines their alignment with knowledge supply. Methods: We combine data on publications indexed in OpenAlex, disability-adjusted life years from the Global Burden of Disease, and Wikipedia pageviews for 2016 to 2023, as indicators of research effort, disease burden, and public attention, respectively. We map 19 disease groups and 138 specific diseases across these three dimensions. Ternary plots are used to position diseases according to their relative balance across dimensions and to identify diseases that are over- or under-represented in research effort relative to epidemiological burden and public attention. We compare Global North-South patterns using German, Persian, Swahili, and Vietnamese language areas to assess how these relationships vary across territories. Results: The three dimensions show limited alignment. At the disease group level, cardiovascular diseases account for the largest share of disease burden, mental disorders attract the largest share of public attention, and neoplasms concentrate the largest share of research effort. Public attention and disease burden are weakly correlated at both group and specific disease levels, indicating that Wikipedia pageviews and DALYs capture distinct dimensions of health demand. Ternary plots reveal different forms of misalignment, with some diseases showing plots dominated by burden, others by research effort, and others by public attention. Territorial analyses add a further layer by showing that diseases follow disparate patterns of supply-demand (mis)alignment across different linguistic territories. Conclusions: Public attention provides a complementary dimension for mapping global health needs and demands. Our approach identifies where scientific knowledge supply fails to match epidemiological and/or public attention, supporting more nuanced global health analysis that may be useful for priority-setting.

title: Examining communicative disenfranchisement and the commercialization of perimenopause and menopause on TikTok and Instagram
abstract: Menopause has a contested and complex history as evidenced by cultural representations of women’s health, shifting scientific recommendations for treatment, and challenges with diagnosing this life transition. Women increasingly report experiences with disenfranchised talk, including being silenced, discredited, and stereotyped, all of which prevent timely diagnosis and treatment. Social media has recently commercialized perimenopause and menopause, which contributes to greater confusion. Sensitized by the Theory of Communicative Disenfranchisement, we used content analysis to examine Instagram (n=135) and TikTok (n=134) content about perimenopause and menopause. We document a focus on symptoms, management strategies, commercialization, and disenfranchised talk and its consequences. Practical and theoretical implications for applying TCD in mediated spaces that consider commercialization and self-gaslighting, as well as creating authentic content to reach audiences interested in this life transition, are provided.

title: Formal Improvement and Further Research on Classificatory Kinship Systems (Part 1)
abstract: Abstract ：Social organization and kinship systems are major subjects of study in social anthropology. For over a century, this research has faced considerable challenges, primarily due to the immaturity of formal representations. Formal representations of kinship serve as tools for cognition and logical deduction, much like mathematics is to physics. In many cases, the quality of these formalrepresentations directly determines the accuracy of our understanding of the subject. The quality standards are maximum completeness, accuracy, intuitiveness, and simplicity, facilitating understanding, memorization, and use. This paper focuses on the intermarriage and succession rules of the Australian Kariera type, a system that was once widespread in the early social formations of various peoples around the world. This paper is divided into two parts. The first part, building upon previous research, presents a complete set of formal representation rules (symbols, formulas, and diagrams); it also provides over twenty Australian ethnographic cases (4 Category System and four groups of intermarriage and succession formulas) to demonstrate the verifiability of the formal representations presented in this paper. Based on this, it provides two types of (patrilineal and matrilineal) kinship tracing and derivation tools, illustrated with diagrams. The Kariera case, employing the instrumental diagrams presented in this paper, positively analyzes the 4 Category System kinship system, thereby further demonstrating the instrumental quality of the formal representation presented in this paper. Based on this, the generation process of Classificatory kinship System relationships is discussed.The issue of "double descent" in the Kariera system is a century-old problem, which this paper addresses through a formalized explanation. The conclusion briefly summarizes the composition of the Classificatory kinship System.

title: Predictability in Strategic Asset Allocation
abstract: The benchmark chosen under strategic asset allocation serves as the fund’s long-term target, while the actual portfolio composition fluctuates around that target over time. When active managers adjust portfolio weights in response to forecasts of benchmark returns, return predictability becomes valuable because it creates opportunities for effective short-term tactical adjustment. Predictability therefore enters utility as a distinct source of benefit. This role of predictability is not captured by the traditional mean-variance framework. The study therefore extends that framework by introducing predictability directly into the analysis. The resulting mean-variance-predictability framework defines the benchmark choice problem and reshapes the associated pricing relation.

title: Price Dynamics and Investor Mobility
abstract: This study develops an equilibrium framework for asset price dynamics under heterogeneous investor beliefs. It shows that price changes admit three equivalent representations, each linked to a distinct channel: group dominance, order imbalance, and participation tilt. As an application of the third representation, the study introduces investor mobility as a measure of how actively investors shift their participation across belief groups over time. Higher mobility indicates greater changes in investor composition and, for a given level of forecast dispersion, larger price movements. The study implements this concept empirically by constructing and analyzing a market-wide series of investor mobility.

title: Seeing Amsterdam through Google Maps: Uneven visibility and crowd-based mapping
abstract: How is the city represented and shaped through Google Maps? Through a computational analysis of over 106,000 places in Amsterdam, this paper examines how Google Maps represents and creates urban hierarchies and differences. Drawing on critical cartography and platform studies, we examine how Google Maps’ affordances and modes of crowd-sourced data collection generate uneven platform geographies: consumption-oriented places, scenes, and neighbourhoods stand out while others are pushed to the background. However, we also show that Google Maps intervenes into processes of segregation and gentrification in complex ways; we do not find straightforward platform-promoted displacement. Through a granular analysis of one street, we show that there are synergistic connections between places that may seem to be in competition and that different communities use Google Maps to appraise the street in culturally specific ways. Both our city-wide and street-level analyses demonstrate that Google Maps functions as a constitutive urban infrastructure that creates platform geographies by spawning hierarchies of visibility and marking differences.

title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

title: The affective bases of socialized preferences
abstract: Research on family socialization suggests that the drivers of preferences (such as values and attitudes) are rooted in early life experiences. But the cognitive process that connects past experiences to present thought processes is not well understood or theorized. In this article, I draw on recent cognitive science research on the role of affectively-valenced memories in shaping preferences, and the sensitivity of the involved cognitive processes to top-of-mind concerns. Revisiting socialization theories in light of these ideas suggests that while rooted in affective memories, socialized preferences are results of probabilistic predictions of the brain and are malleable to priming. Across 3 related studies, including a preregistered survey experiment, I examine the empirical case of socialization of inclinations towards parenthood.

title: One Policy, Many Publics: Central Bank Communication and the National Politics of Trust
abstract: Central bank decisions have become politically contested. In response, central banks communicate more with the public, since their effectiveness rests on public trust. Yet whether they reach ordinary citizens is largely unknown. We exploit the European Central Bank’s unexpected announcement of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) during the fieldwork of a March 2020 survey in Germany and Italy. Our results show that the same decisive intervention was rewarded only where it aligned with the perceived national interest: in Italy, trust in the ECB rose, strongest among news-followers and the left; in Germany, trust in the ECB did not move at all, even as trust in national institutions surged. Preferences for central bank goal independence moved in neither country. Citizens thus notice exceptional monetary policy decisions, but their responses are mediated by national interests and discourses, with asymmetric consequences for a central bank that makes one policy for many publics.

title: Legal Threats and Online Dissent: Evidence from Social Media Regulation in Turkey
authors: Arvind Magesan, Juan S. Morales, Arieda Muço
abstract: We study how legal threats to social media platforms shape online political communication. We exploit the sharp implementation of a 2020 Turkish law that required social media companies to establish local offices and provide user data to the government on request. Assembling a panel of over 700 Twitter users and 7 million posts, we use a differences-in-differences design to compare dissenters, individuals publicly critical of the reform when announced, to other groups unlikely to be affected, such as celebrities. We find that dissenters and political exiles post 15-20 percent fewer tweets following implementation, and engagement with their content falls sharply. These short-run chilling effects emerge despite limited platform compliance, indicating that anticipated enforcement risk, rather than actual enforcement, drives the effect. In the long run, the chilling effects dissipate. Our findings suggest that states can govern online speech indirectly, by regulating platforms rather than users, but that such effects may be self-limiting in the absence of visible enforcement.

title: Children’s Art Experiences: Interactive Digital Art
authors: Emilie Bossens, Bieke Zaman, Priscilla Van Even
abstract: Art invites exploratory, multisensory, emotionally rich and context-shaped forms of engagement, yet these experiences are sometimes difficult to capture. This challenge becomes especially pronounced with children, whose meaning-making relies on movement, sensation and play, rather than verbal reflection or evaluative judgements. Because most cultural spaces are designed around adult norms and expectations, children’s distinctive ways of engaging with art often remain overlooked or under supported. This raises questions about how cultural settings can better accommodate what children themselves experience as meaningful aesthetic encounters. In this chapter, we first review research on children’s art engagement from perceptual, cognitive, emotional, bodily, spatial, and social perspectives. We then present a case-study of 215 children aged 3 to 12 years old engaging with an interactive digital artwork at a family arts festival. Through systematic observations, we identify three recurring interaction patterns, demonstrate how social dynamics and contextual factors shape children’s unfolding engagement, and show how children exert agency through their exploratory actions and the artwork’s responsive features. Building on these insights, the chapter concludes with future directions for art research and practice, calling for child-centered methodologies, stronger attention to embodiment and emotion, and closer art-science collaboration to better support meaningful art experiences for children.

title: Rural-Urban Differences in Student Journalism Performance Metrics
abstract: This paper examines rural-urban differences in student journalism performance among higher education institution (HEI) student produced news outlets. With journalism quality frameworks, three article-level dimensions serve as comparisons: textual distinctiveness, Critical Information Needs (CIN) coverage, and localeness. Using a dataset of approximately 15,000 student articles, we utilized outlet-level soft cosine similarity, validated LLM-assisted binary coding, and logistic regression. Our results suggest three findings within our dataset: 1) the textual patterns of articles are not strongly structured by locale, 2) rural articles had substantially higher descriptive rates and odds of addressing a CIN than urban articles, and 3) rural articles had higher descriptive rates and odds of being coded as local. These results suggest that student journalism’s local-news role varies more in their civic ability, corroborating that being locally engaged is not synchronous with addressing CINs and that rural-urban differences could extend beyond institutional capacities into HEIs informational role in surrounding communities.

title: Aid Cuts and the Politics of Refugee Hosting
abstract: In 2025, U.S. aid cuts drove the fastest contraction of foreign aid on record. These cuts threaten the cooperative arrangement underpinning the refugee regime, in which low- and middle-income countries host most refugees while high-income countries finance assistance. As host communities lose aid-related jobs, services, and infrastructure, does citizens’ willingness to host refugees decline? I examine this question in Kenya using two nationwide surveys, a high-frequency panel and vignette experiment near Kakuma camp, and 52 interviews with local leaders, all conducted as the cuts unfolded. Support for hosting declined in refugee- hosting areas as economic losses and insecurity grew, driven by households that lost camp-based benefits. By contrast, national support remained stable, and exploratory evidence suggests that humanitarian concern limited backlash. Yet because refugee policy often responds to pressures in hosting regions, continued cuts may weaken the local foundations of asylum in the countries that host most of the world’s refugees.

title: Chaotic Dynamics of Asset Prices
abstract: This study offers a new perspective on asset price dynamics by showing that seemingly irregular price movements are governed by a common structure. It separates the forces underlying these movements and develops three equivalent representations that make this structure more transparent. A central construct in the study is a time-varying parameter that classifies price dynamics into interpretable regimes. In the empirical analysis of aggregate stock prices, periods of higher parameter values, indicating more turbulent regimes, align closely with major economic downturns. This evidence supports the parameter’s use as a diagnostic tool for detecting regime shifts and periods of macro-financial turbulence.

title: Arbitrage-Induced Mispricing
abstract: Contrary to common belief, arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers are not direct counterparts in trading. Their portfolio positions may instead overlap, amplifying fluctuations in aggregate demand for assets with particular positioning signals and pushing prices away from fundamental values. These deviations, in turn, create additional hedging demand. This study examines whether overlap in position setting between arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers generates mispricing and whether this mispricing becomes a priced source of risk. The empirical findings support both possibilities: they confirm the presence of such mispricing and show that additional pricing factors are needed to account for it.

title: Climate Adaptation as Evolvability
authors: Michael Weisberg, Rachael Brown, Christopher H. Lean
abstract: Standard approaches to climate adaptation, commonly understood as the protection of infrastructure, social systems, and ecosystems from adverse climate impacts,are too closely tied to the biological concept of adaptation and the ecological notion of stability. Instead, we argue that climate adaptation is better articulated by analogy to the concept of evolvability. Adaptation thus understood emphasizes the need for internal capacities of restoration and self-maintenance, preserves flexibility and options for the future, addresses the social, political, and psychological impacts of climate change, and promotes transboundary strategies.

title: A Contract-Based Healthcare Ecosystem for Depopulated Rural Communities: Residential Risk Visibility and Incentive-Linked Health Monitoring
abstract: Debates on healthcare sustainability in depopulated rural communities have focused on technological solutions — telemedicine, drone delivery, remote monitoring. This paper addresses the structural problems technology alone cannot solve: helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) cannot fly at night or in bad weather; severe emergencies admit no alternative to physical transport; and the healthcare costs generated by rural residence remain invisible to both residents and society. We propose a "contract-based healthcare ecosystem": (a) quantifying and visualizing the relationship between residence location and medical access as individual risk; (b) making participation in continuous health monitoring a contractual condition of new residency; and (c) linking participation and risk-management attainment to basic-income-style payments. On ethical grounds the scheme applies only to new residents, with existing residents guaranteed conventional arrangements. Extending the external-balance model of our companion paper (SocArXiv, doi:10.31235/osf.io/rcsq9_v1), we estimate that if 60 high-risk residents of a 500-person community participate in monitoring and severe events fall by 15-35%, incentive payments of 2,500-11,700 yen per person per month are offset by reduced external medical expenditure alone (break-even). This range is realistic for behavior-change incentives, implying that a scheme in which health-risk management directly contributes to community economic self-sufficiency is institutionally feasible. Ethical limits concerning privacy, stigmatization, and freedom of choice are examined from a clinician's perspective. Note: The full manuscript is written in Japanese; an English abstract is provided above.

title: Testing the water: Importance of surface water resources for settlement installation in various climatic contexts using a machine learning approach
abstract: Past human spatial dynamics are strongly influenced by water availability. Since the development of agrarian sedentary societies, water is seen as an essential ressource. Yet quantifying its influence on past populations across different environmental and chronological contexts remains methodologically challenging. This study investigates the relative importance of thirteen water-related variables alongside five additional environmental covariates in shaping archaeological site distributions. Using machine learning model of Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), a total of 461 Bronze Age and Iron Age (3,500 - 50 BCE) sites from four regions with contrasting climatic conditions - the Rhine Valley, Lazio, the Shephelah, and the Kurdistan region of Iraq - were analysed. Results show that distance to water flow and stable topographic variables consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of settlement location. Palaeoclimatic variables, particularly precipitation seasonality and precipitation of the wettest quarter, outperform modern remote sensing indices. Despite contrasting environmental conditions, the four regions share broadly comparable settlement trajectories, with a consistent shift toward greater site density and spatial dispersion from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age. These findings highlight the value of temporally robust environmental proxies for modelling past human-landscape interactions and offer a replicable framework for water-focused archaeological predictive modelling across diverse climatic settings.

title: Constitution-Making After Contested Elections: The Constitutional Legitimacy Threshold and Tanzania’s Post-2025 Reform Dilemma
abstract: Constitution-making after contested elections presents a fundamental dilemma for democratic governance: whether institutions whose own legitimacy is disputed can credibly undertake the task of creating a new constitutional order. This article examines Tanzania’s post-2025 constitutional reform debate through the concept of the constitutional legitimacy threshold, arguing that constitution-making requires a higher level of legitimacy than ordinary legislative governance (Beetham, 1991; Habermas, 1996). Drawing on theories of constituent power and constitutional authority (Sieyès, 1789; Ackerman, 1991), the article distinguishes between formal constitutional competence and substantive constitutional legitimacy. While Tanzania’s Parliament may possess legal authority to initiate constitutional reform under existing constitutional procedures, the article argues that foundational constitutional transformation requires broader conditions of representative credibility, political inclusion, and public confidence (Elster, 1995; Arato, 2016). Using Tanzania as a case study, the article analyses how electoral contestation, institutional distrust, and political polarization affect the legitimacy of constitution-making processes. It demonstrates that disputed electoral mandates can generate a gap between the legal authority of institutions and their capacity to produce a constitutional settlement accepted across society. The analysis draws on comparative constitutional experiences to show that durable constitutional orders are frequently associated with inclusive participation, negotiated legitimacy, and broad societal ownership (Klug, 2000; Ghai & Cottrell, 2010). The article contributes to comparative constitutional politics by developing the constitutional legitimacy threshold as an analytical framework for understanding why some constitution-making processes achieve durability while others remain contested. It argues that successful constitutional reform depends not only on procedural legality but also on the perceived legitimacy of the institutions, actors, and processes responsible for producing the constitutional order. The Tanzanian case illustrates a broader challenge facing emerging democracies: constitutional renewal requires not merely the power to change constitutional rules, but the legitimacy necessary to establish rules that command enduring acceptance.

title: Why Play When AI Can Win: The Non-Transferability of Participation in AI-Assisted Play
abstract: Knowledge work is learning to hand itself over. Drafting, analysis, computation, even the role of a practice opponent can now be delegated to artificial intelligence, and the delegation works: the results come back, often better and faster than one's own. This paper asks what, in that handover, does not move. Drawing on Bernard Suits's analysis of games, I separate the achieved state of an activity from the value of participating in it and defend a non-transferability theorem: parts of an activity can be delegated, but no agent, human or artificial, can take over one's participation itself. When another realises the goal state on my behalf, the fact that I undertook the constitutive constraints and pursued the goal through them does not thereby come into existence. AI can deliver the state of affairs; it cannot deliver the fact of participation. At bottom, then, the central claim is not a claim about AI at all: the theorem is agent-relative, and holds whatever machines become — achievers, players, moral patients, or none of these. What it leaves open is the human question. Whether one can keep playing, lucidly, in full knowledge of the machine's strength, depends not only on individual temperament but on whether a culture grants dignity to those who do unnecessary things in earnest. Japanese professional shogi, which met machine superiority a decade ahead of other knowledge domains and kept its play, is examined as a completed historical case — public evidence that the question in this paper's title has already been answered, once, in the affirmative.

title: Coding choices and short-sequence artefacts undermine claims of a conventional Palaeolithic sign system – a comment on Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026)
abstract: In this comment, I show that methodological and statistical flaws undermine the central conclusions of Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026).

title: Reskilling and Retraining the Water Technology Workforce: An Agentic Generative AI Framework for Water Purification, Nano‑MEMS, and Curriculum Development
abstract: The rapid digitalization of water infrastructure is bringing artificial intelligence, advanced sensing, and membrane materials science into routine water treatment practice. At the same time, utilities, regulators, and training institutions face a persistent workforce challenge: many operators, engineers, and managers are being asked to adopt data-driven tools without a coherent educational pathway that links AI literacy to real treatment workflows. This article synthesizes recent literature on agentic generative AI, reinforcement learning, smart sensing, nano-enabled membranes, and digital twins for water systems, then translates those developments into a structured reskilling model for the water sector. The proposed framework is organized around three competency tiers: foundational AI and data literacy for water professionals; applied agentic AI for decision support, process optimization, and predictive maintenance; and advanced nano-AI integration for sensor-rich treatment trains, membrane design, and digitally enabled R&D. The manuscript further proposes journal-ready tables covering competency architecture, course design, and implementation priorities, alongside conceptual figures illustrating the interaction between water purification processes, AI agents, nano-MEMS monitoring, governance, and workforce outcomes. Rather than treating automation as a substitute for expertise, the framework positions human-in-the-loop supervision, risk management, interoperability, and regulatory compliance as core curriculum requirements. The article argues that reskilling should be embedded in utility modernization strategies, community-college pipelines, professional certificates, and utility-academic partnerships so that adoption of smart water purification systems is matched by operator trust, safety assurance, and practical competence.

title: Digital Infrastructures and Contemporary Governance in Times of Conflict
abstract: Scholarship on internet shutdowns and digital authoritarianism tends to treat digital infrastructure as an instrument of repression, while research on wartime digital government treats it as an instrument of resilience. This article argues that the two are not separable: in conditions of acute interstate war, the same architecture can simultaneously secure a regime’s continuity and restrict the visibility of its population. Drawing on Michael Mann’s concept of infrastructural power and using the 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran war as a revealing single case, it examines connectivity control, command decentralization, cyber pressure on critical systems, and the management of online narratives as one governing logic rather than discrete tactics. A central claim is that wartime decentralization mattered politically as well as militarily: it helped preserve authority after leadership losses and communications disruption, while the same distributed architecture widened the scope for miscalculation and escalation. The article’s contribution is to specify a mechanism the two literatures have tended to treat separately — the co-location of resilience and repression in a single infrastructure, and the double-edged character of the decentralization that sustains continuity.

title: Economic Constitutionalism: Legitimate Authority and the Democratic Governance of Institutional Purpose
abstract: Formally accountable regulation can remain inadequate when its objectives are privately, technically, or distributionally insulated from democratic authorization. This article introduces economic constitutionalism as a second-order framework that extends regulatory legitimacy analysis from the conduct of regulators to the authority to define what regulation is for. The analysis reconstructs authorization assumptions across regulatory legitimacy, capture, public-purpose, and quantification literatures and derives three mechanisms of regulatory-purpose displacement and four design properties for purpose-responsive regulation. Applications to artificial intelligence, platform labor, education, care, and public information demonstrate the framework's comparative diagnostic reach. The argument shifts the regulatory design agenda from procedural compliance alone to the authorization and revision of regulatory purpose.

title: Fuzzy Cross-Database Record Matching for Missing and Unidentified Person Cases: Design and Retrospective Validation of the CAIRN Engine
abstract: Abstract Missing-person (MP) and unidentified-person (UID) records in the United States are fragmented across federal, state, county, and volunteer-maintained systems, and the matching applied within those systems is predominantly exact-field or manual. This paper describes CAIRN (Case Analysis and Intelligent Resolution Network), a hypothesis-generation engine that scores MP-UID candidate pairs using seven weighted, error- tolerant signals (fuzzy name similarity, distinguishing marks, temporal compatibility, geographic distance, age fit, height/weight, and race with subset tolerance), applies two hard filters that eliminate a pair outright rather than scoring it (biological sex, and chronological impossibility), and attaches an explicit confidence tier reflecting how many identity-grade signals supported each score. The engine was validated retrospectively on forty-eight confirmed-solved case pairs assembled from Internet Archive snapshots of Doe Network case pages, current NamUs records, official press materials, and recovered snapshots of NamUs records deleted after resolution. In a ranking benchmark on six solved pairs that took four to forty-two years to resolve in reality - decades combined - the engine ranked the true match first in six of six cases in a matter of seconds. Forty-two additional pairs spanning records-strong, minimal-data, recovered- record, and movement and concealment classes scored between 0.463 and 1.000, each consistent with its evidentiary class. Of the twelve pairs scoring above 0.92, ten required more than a year of human review to connect and five required more than a decade, with a median of approximately three years; the two exceptions, resolved in roughly one month and roughly nine months respectively, are the two most recent cases in the benchmark. Two confirmed matches are eliminated outright by hard filters: one by an incorrectly recorded biological sex, and one by a missing-person report date standing in for a last-contact date, placing the recovery twenty years before the reported disappearance. A separate prospective field test cross-scored 2,508 Florida MP and 869 Florida UID summary records, measuring behaviour under summary-level data rather than match accuracy. It demonstrated that summary- level data alone produces high-scoring but low-confidence false positives; all three top-ranked candidates were disproven under human review, and the failures directly motivated three engine corrections now incorporated. All output is framed as leads for human verification through official channels, never as conclusions.

title: Identifiability limits in rare network count processes: a simulation laboratory with empirical probes in crime, seismology and neural spike trains
abstract: Rare network count data — panels with 90–99% zeros across nodes and time — are common in criminology, seismology and neuroscience, where a fitted Poisson, negative-binomial or zero-inflated model is often read as evidence about mechanism. Using a simulation laboratory of ten stress-test data-generating processes and semi-synthetic probes in UK Police, USGS and Allen Neuropixels data, this work shows that model fingerprints, dispersion, residual autocorrelation and intervention estimates can instead reflect sparsity, the observation operator and effect design. Identifiability is layered: a stable fingerprint is not a mechanism.
